articles.title: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way
articles.summary: The new money repairs what the company owes. The retrenchment is aimed at a different problem.

blocks.text: ABS-CBN Corporation, which has not turned a profit since it lost its broadcast franchise, has P6 billion in new money coming in, the largest show of confidence in the company since the shutdown of 2020. Then on Tuesday, September 15, it announced that around 200 employees will be losing their jobs.

This will be the 6th straight year the workforce shrinks. ABS-CBN went into the shutdown with 11,071 workers, counting regular employees, project and program-based staff, independent contractors and talents together. By the end of 2025, it came down to 3,646, made up of 2,009 regular employees on permanent contracts, 206 project employees, 582 program-based employees and 849 independent contractors. Nearly 5,000 went in the first round alone, a figure that ABS-CBN president and CEO Carlo Katigbak gave shareholders at the 2020 annual meeting.

Those two things were put out side by side in ABS-CBN’s September 15 official statement. It called the new investments “a vote of confidence in the future of the company” in one paragraph, and in the next said it has been “a difficult year for the content industry,” blaming the Middle East conflict, high inflation and low economic growth for weaker advertising and consumer spending. Then it announced “the difficult decision to implement a retrenchment program to keep ABS-CBN on strong financial footing,” covering “around 200 people or 7% of the company’s workforce.” At a town hall meeting on Tuesday, according to sources familiar with the meeting, Katigbak told employees this would be the last retrenchment under his leadership.
So if investors are finally putting P6 billion into ABS-CBN, why are 200 employees going out?

The P6 billion is fresh capital going into a company in trouble. It will arrive in tranches through 2026, released as the existing owners and the new one, I&C Holdings Corp., settle terms between them. Salaries, on the other hand, fall due every month.

I&C is taking P3.5 billion of it. ABS-CBN describes the firm in its own August 12 statement as a fully Filipino-owned private investment holding company “that invests for long-term company turn-around.” Crème Investment Corporation, Mantes Corporation, and Presta Holdings Company Inc., representing three branches of the Lopez family, are taking P2.2 billion between them. Lopez Inc. is taking P300 million. “This substantial investment is a vote of confidence in ABS-CBN,” chairman Mark Lopez said when the agreements were signed.

What the money buys are newly issued common and preferred shares that do not exist yet. They have to come out of an increase in ABS-CBN’s authorized capital stock, which shareholders are due to vote on at a special meeting on September 30 and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has to approve afterward. ABS-CBN has told the exchange the public float will be diluted, meaning the shares held by ordinary investors will account for a smaller slice of the company. The same meeting is expected to expand the board from seven directors to nine.

ABS-CBN told the exchange the proceeds are for working capital, for strengthening the balance sheet and for general corporate purposes. In plain terms, most of it is for paying what the company already owes. Some of it will likely go to repaying the bank loans coming due.

The books show how much that is. At the end of June, ABS-CBN held P1.31 billion in cash against P8.64 billion in loans falling due within 12 months. Its short-term obligations exceeded the assets it could quickly turn into cash by P14.2 billion, a gap that had widened from P12.4 billion at the end of December. Shareholders’ equity, which is what would be left if the company sold everything and paid everyone, had gone below zero, to minus P1.08 billion from a positive P747 million six months earlier.
So the P6 billion dropped into that picture pushes equity back above zero and gives the company something to show its banks. It will not change what the business earns next year.

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN makes room for new owners

blocks.text: The media company itself was not only losing money. It was losing more than the year before, and by the middle of this year, its everyday operations had stopped producing any cash at all.

Revenues in the first half of 2026 fell 17% to P6.88 billion, and the net loss more than doubled to P1.83 billion. The clearest measure was EBITDA, which strips out interest and the paper cost of ageing equipment to show whether a business generates cash from running itself. In the first half of 2025, it was positive P568 million. In the first half of 2026, it was negative P498 million.

ABS-CBN has a fair answer to part of this. The first half of 2025 carried election advertising, BINI‘s sold-out Philippine Arena concert, and a strong Star Cinema release, none of which repeated. And the company says that setting political advertising aside, content revenues were flat. It expects the second half to improve on the back of BINI’s world tour and the rest of its film and live-events slate. But that does not explain the cost side, where salaries and wages rose to P2.5 billion from P2.4 billion. Personnel and talent costs rose to P1.82 billion from P1.65 billion, even as revenue fell.
The easy explanation would be Sky Cable, whose cable and broadband revenues fell 42% to ₱1.12 billion as subscribers kept leaving.

The numbers point elsewhere. Sky cut its operating costs 25% in the first half and halved the personnel costs to P257 million. And it ended the period still generating cash from operations with EBITDA of positive P11 million. The content business went the other way, to negative P509 million, with a net loss of P1.24 billion against P535 million a year earlier.
The heavier pressure sits in the part of ABS-CBN that is supposed to be its future.

The cutting started in 2020, years before any new investor appeared. Katigbak set out the scale himself at the August 2026 annual meeting. Leaving Sky aside, general and administrative expenses plus manpower costs fell from around P15 billion in 2019 to P6.9 billion in 2025, a reduction of 54%, while debt fell from P20.5 billion to just under P8.5 billion, a reduction of 58%.

The workforce came down with it. After the 2020 retrenchment the company and its subsidiaries counted 5,870 people at the end of 2021, then 5,701, then 5,279, then 4,022 after the restructuring that followed the collapse of the Sky Cable sale to PLDT, and 3,646 at the end of 2025. Regular employees, the ones on permanent contracts, fell from 3,899 to 2,009 over those 4 years. In its 2025 sustainability report, ABS-CBN puts its employees at 2,797 and its attrition rate, including retrenchment, at 32%.
“We recognize that we are not yet where we need to be,” Katigbak told shareholders in August.

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN talks up its ‘new’ future, but its new owners weren’t in the room

blocks.text: Retrenchment is not a saving that starts immediately. Separation pay goes out first and the lower payroll shows up afterward, which is why a company short of cash can find it hard to afford.

ABS-CBN has been carrying that cost for years. It paid roughly P1.1 billion in separation benefits during the 2020 retrenchment. Its audited 2025 financials show that the parent company still owes P874 million to employees retrenched and separated in earlier rounds, down only P70 million from the P944 million owed a year before.

The ABS-CBN retirement fund that normally pays those benefits is nearly empty. At the end of June, it held P61 million against P3.53 billion owed to employees. Two years earlier, the fund held P228.5 million. For 2026, ABS-CBN expects to put P60.4 million back in.

A company holding P1.31 billion in cash against P8.64 billion in loans coming due cannot easily write separation checks for 200 employees, while a company with P6 billion committed incoming capital can. This means the new money is not what makes the retrenchment unnecessary but part of what makes it payable.

There is a 3rd audience for the announcement. Almost all of ABS-CBN’s debt now sits in the column for obligations due within a year, P8.4 billion of it at the parent company, because a standstill agreement with its lenders ran out at the end of 2025. The P5 billion owed to the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) and the P4.75 billion owed to UnionBank have been extended in short increments since, most recently to May 31 and June 30 of this year.

The company is in talks to refinance those loans on longer terms, including removing the requirement that it hold a broadcast franchise. Its interim accounts still carry a formal warning that there is material uncertainty over whether ABS-CBN can continue operating as a going concern, and among the steps management lists in response is continuing cost control that reduces general and administrative expenses and employee costs.

blocks.caption: Banks, retirees, the business: Where will ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue go?

blocks.text: The statement gave a number and stopped. The company has not said which divisions the 200 come from or how many will go from each, how much it expects to save every year, or how much the separation packages will cost. It has not given a current headcount, or a headcount that separates ABS-CBN from Sky. Nor has it said how the P6 billion will be split between the loans falling due, the money owed to employees from earlier rounds, and the day-to-day running of the business.

And one question the disclosures do not touch: Was this reduction already in the plans and projections shown to I&C Holdings and the Lopez investors before they signed? There is no evidence any of them demanded it, and ABS-CBN was cutting costs long before I&C appeared. But money that arrives in tranches, on conditions, from an investor that describes itself as backing long-term turnarounds, comes with a view about what a company should cost to run.

Katigbak’s promise to employees at the town hall meeting — that this would be the last retrenchment under his leadership — can mean two different things. It can mean ABS-CBN has finally reached a size it can sustain, or it can mean only that there will be no further retrenchment for as long as he is chief executive. Only the first is a statement about the business.
The test is the arithmetic. The company has to reach the point where what it earns covers what it spends, and the first half of 2026 moved away from that point rather than toward it.
The 200 will not be the first to leave with money still owed to them. People let go in the earlier rounds are still owed money years later.

Strengthening a balance sheet means paying down what a company owes, and the money owed to former employees sits on that balance sheet alongside bank loans. The P6 billion may well be what clears both.

“We owe it to our banks, our employees, our partners to make good on all our obligations to them,” Katigbak told shareholders in August. On September 30, the shareholders are due to vote on the capital increase the P6 billion depends on. ABS-CBN has not said which divisions the 200 come from, or how much of the new money goes to the people it has already let go. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: #EmmysSoWhite again: No actors of colour win during 2026 Primetime Emmys
articles.summary: There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted…

image.caption: Host Mariska Hargitay speaks onstage during the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Monday. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted awards going to white performers.
All acting category winners during TV's biggest night were white
In 2015, activist and writer April Reign created the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag.
Now, she says she doesn't really watch award shows live, and last night's Emmys was an example of why.

There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Primetime Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted awards going to white performers.
"It's not a regression, it's definitely a stall," said Reign.

items: Emmys 2026 winners list: Widow's Bay, The Pitt take top honours

blocks.text: The other two major acting categories — supporting actor and supporting actress in a limited series — were given out last week at the Creative Arts Emmys, but those winners didn't change the tally.
'A pattern, not a moment'
By Tuesday morning, #EmmysSoWhite was trending, with users calling out the Television Academy on social media.

"The academy saw that three black women made history at the Emmys winning the big categories of the night and how happy everybody was and said never again," one user wrote on X, referencing the 2024 Emmy awards, "so now we’re stuck with #EmmysSOWhite for the foreseeable future 🫩"
"What is this... #EmmysSoWhite" wrote another, alongside a photo composite of the winners.

Reign started the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag in 2015, when all 20 acting nominees for the Academy Awards that year were white, sparking a conversation and a movement about the Academy and its voting body.
While there have been some changes in the following years aimed at addressing these discrepancies, Reign called out Monday's results.
"This is a pattern, not a moment," Reign said in an interview with CBC News. "A single snub is an accident. A pattern this consistent is a design feature of how the institution votes."

The Television Academy released a transparency report in February revealing that the majority of its members in 2026 — 67 per cent — were white. It publishes this report annually, with the first official one coming out in 2021.

At the same time, the academy pointed to steady year-over-year growth in its membership among people identifying as biracial, multiracial, East Asian and Southeast Asian, as well as women, non-binary, transgender and intersex voters.

items: 2026 Emmys: Widow's Bay upsets, The Pitt triumphs at Canada-preoccupied ceremony

blocks.text: Reign said the conversation around representation needs to begin long before awards season, pointing to the writers, casting directors and behind-the-scenes decision-makers who shape which stories and characters make it to the screen.

"We can't wait until we get to the award shows to have this conversation when, you know, the pipeline starts before a single word is written on the page," she said. She suggests asking questions like who the casting directors and show-runners are, and who is saying a white character couldn't be queer or a person of colour.

"Those are the questions that we need to ask from the very beginning so that we're not having these conversations again in February or March for the Oscars, and in September for the Emmys, because it's too late."

It's worth noting that outside of the primetime broadcast, Ernest Harden Jr. picked up an acting win Monday night for his guest-starring role as Louie Cloverfield on The Pitt. But the guest acting categories weren't presented during the broadcast. Octavia Spencer also won for narrating Lost Women of Alaska.

And while Monday night's show was a complete shutout for actors of colour, director Hiro Murai won a golden statuette for Widow's Bay. He's now the first Asian filmmaker to win best directing for a comedy series at the Emmys and only the third to win a primetime Emmy in any category, joining Emmy-winning directors Lee Sung Jin, who won for Beef, and Hwang Dong-hyuk, who won for Squid Game.
How does this compare to previous years?
Representation at the Emmys was actually down before Monday's ceremony even started.
Variety reports only 17 performers of colour scored acting nominations this year — a sharp drop from 28 last year.
The Emmys made headlines for diverse nominations in 2021, however every single lead and supporting acting winner that year ended up being white, also prompting the hashtag #EmmysSoWhite.
Let's look at how things have shaken out over the last few years for diverse winners at the Emmys.

Last year (2025): One of the 12 acting races went to a person of color — Tramell Tillman won for Severance and made history as the first Black man to take home outstanding supporting actor in a drama series.
2024: Four out of the dozen acting trophies went to diverse winners (including Liza Colón-Zayas, Lamorne Morris and Shōgun stars Hiroyuki Sanada and Anna Sawai).

2024 (January): This delayed ceremony was the peak of diversity for acting wins, with five actors of colour taking the stage to claim trophies: Quinta Brunson, Ayo Edebiri, Niecy Nash-Betts, Steven Yeun and Ali Wong.
2022: We saw three diverse performers win: Lee Jung-jae, Zendaya and Sheryl Lee Ralph.
2021: This was the last time all of the primetime acting winners were white.

On the Television Academy's official site, it says the academy is "dedicated to honouring excellence in television while promoting creativity and diversity, and empowering storytellers through recognition, education and leadership"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Local party dominates race for BARMM district seats in Lanao del Sur
articles.summary: MARAWI CITY, Lanao del Sur—Local political allies of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao Grand Coalition (BGC) dominated the parliamentary district races in Lanao del Sur province,…

blocks.text: MARAWI CITY, Lanao del Sur—Local political allies of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao Grand Coalition (BGC) dominated the parliamentary district races in Lanao del Sur province, securing six of the nine available seats in last Monday’s historic first-ever Bangsamoro parliamentary elections.

Provincial Election Supervisor Mohammad Nabil Mutia, as chair of the provincial board of canvassers, proclaimed all nine winners, including Princess Pala Amera Gandamra, wife of Marawi City Vice Mayor Majul Gandamra, at the Provincial Capitol Social Hall on Tuesday morning.

Gandamra, who ran under the banner of Serbisyong Inklusibong-Alyansang Progresibo (SIAP) Party for the first district of Lanao del Sur, garnered 62,086 votes over her closest rival, Abdulrahman Tahir, candidate for the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), who took only 8,293 votes. The district covers the provincial capital of Marawi.

The eight other winning candidates are Hamza Gauraki (UBJP), second district; Rauf Adiong (SIAP), nephew of Lanao del Sur Governor Mamintal Adiong Jr., third district; Lampa Pandi (UBJP), fourth district; Arimao Asumi (SIAP), fifth district; Hosni Macapodi (SIAP), sixth district; Rayyan Mindalano (SIAP) seventh district; Arrie Balindong (UBJP), eighth district; and Rashdi Adiong (SIAP), ninth district.
Following the victory, Governor Adiong issued a call for unity and reconciliation among all political parties that took part in the historic BARMM parliamentary vote.
“Let us stop thinking of alliances yet. Let us enjoy this historic vote<’ Adiong told reporters.

SIAP is allied with the BGC which Adiong, Basilan Governor Mujiv Hataman, Suu Vice Governor Abdusakur Tan, former Maguindanao del Norte governor Bai Mariam Mangudadatu and his husband, former Sultan Kudarat governor Suharto Mangudadatu, founded on April 24, 2024.
Colonel Caezar Cabuhat, Lanao del Sur police director, told reporters that, for the first time, the elections in the province were peaceful, with no violent incidents reported on election day.

“Unlike in the past when elections were always marred with violent incidents, last Monday went without an incident reported. We used to have an average of 15 incidents that always resulted in a failure of election in several towns,” Cabuhat said.
He credited the intensive security preparations, close inter-agency coordination and a shared community commitment to conduct a peaceful election.
The Armed Forces of the Philippines deployed three Army brigades to secure the political exercise in Marawi City and 39 towns in the province.

Mutia said the peaceful elections were only marred by the no-show of 79 teachers who were to serve as poll managers in five towns, but the gap was immediately filled by police officers trained to serve as election inspectors. /jpv

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte's camp concerned about Trillanes' links to ICC prosecution's 8 new incidents
articles.summary: Rodrigo Duterte"s camp concerned about Trillanes" links to ICC prosecution"s 8 new incidents
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 7:03am

THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Lawyers of former President Rodrigo Duterte are asking the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to "determine the admissibilityof the eight new incidents included by the Office of the Prosecutor in its Trial Brief, while questioning their documentary evidence as "linked" to former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV.

Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes requests the Trial Chamber for a “judicial determination” of Incidents 50 to 57 mentioned by the prosecution in its 143-page Trial Brief—whether for the latter to file an amended version or remove the incidents entirely from the document.
Haynes argues that the eight new incidents were added by the prosecution without prior judicial authorization.

“In its Trial Brief, the Prosecution justified its addition of these eight new incidents as falling within the scope of the confirmed charges ‘because they were perpetrated in a ‘time during which and an area where criminal acts were allegedly committed by an identifiable group of perpetrators against an identifiable group of victims,’” Haynes said.
Evidence source

The Document Containing the Charges (DCC) specified 49 incidents in Duterte’s three counts of crimes against humanity. The prosecution’s Trial Brief now lists 57, with the additions at the center of the defense challenge.
Duterte’s defense team said it was notified by the prosecution of the new incidents through an email on August 31 regarding the latter’s submission of its Trial Brief.
Available information about the new incidents show that several happened in the National Capital Region and Region IV-A in 2016, or were victims on an “illegal drug personalities’ watchlist.”
The defense expressed concern over the authenticity and sources of evidence, which they linked to Trillanes, who is known as a critic of the former president.

“The chain of custody reveals that the documentary evidence cited in the Trial Brief in relation to the eight new incidents has a single political opponent of Mr Duterte, Antonio Trillanes, as its source, and these documents – which include purported internal PNP documentation – bear no indication of authenticity.”

In their argument, the defense claimed that Trillanes “has produced all of the newly disclosed PNP Incident Record Forms underpinning these eight incidents” despite having “no known legitimate means of accessing internal PNP documentation.”
Duterte’s lawyers also questioned the new Incident Record Forms for lacking signatures or “an official stamp indicating that they are a ‘certified true copy’ of the original.”

“In light of these evidentiary deficiencies, questions may be raised as to whether these eight incidents would have passed the lower standard of proof applicable at confirmation, had they been included in the original pre-confirmation brief and document containing the charges,” the defense argued.
Judicial oversight

Citing previous ICC cases that discussed adding incidents or amending charges before trial, Duterte’s defense argued that a trial chamber could authorize the prosecution to “add a victim without recourse to Article 61(9)” but not extend it to include a “new incident setting out a new time, place, individual criminal act, principal perpetrator, and victim.”
Haynes also added that “other criminal acts not mentioned in the document containing the charges” should “fall squarely within the facts and circumstances of the charges.”
“It is abundantly clear that judicial oversight is essential, and that the Prosecution cannot merely add to the confirmed charges proprio motu and without judicial authorisation,” Haynes said.
Timing of addition

The defense also submitted that the document containing the charges “no longer match” the current Trial Brief due to the eight new incidents, which they also argue “exceed the scope of the confirmation decision.”
”The Prosecution is now seeking to add eight new incidents based upon fresh evidence that constitute new material facts, not ‘further specification’ of the confirmed charges,” the defense argued.
They also questioned the timing of the prosecution’s addition of the new incidents, which were disclosed only around three months before Duterte’s trial is scheduled to start on November 30.
“Each incident rests upon fresh evidence and seeks to introduce an entirely new set of material facts, meaning authorisation is required,” Haynes said.
No public response from the Office of the Prosecutor to the defense submission has been published as of writing.
Trial Chamber III is also set to hold a status conference today. It remains to be seen whether the dispute over the eight additional incidents will be taken up during the hearing. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers
articles.summary:
More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says

About 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they…

blocks.text: About 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they try to balance their vulnerable relatives’ growing care needs with declining access to state-funded social care services.

Research estimates that more than a million people have left the workplace to look after ageing, ill and disabled loved ones in the past two years, highlighting the social challenges caused by UK’s rapidly changing demographic profile.

Unpaid caring is now a “widespread social and economic reality” for UK households, it says, with one in five employees – equivalent to 6.7 million people – facing career and financial sacrifices as they juggle paid work and care for family or friends.

Over a fifth of those surveyed (22%) had reduced their job hours to juggle work and care, with over a third (34%) working less than eight hours a week. Around one in 10 carers said they had turned down promotions or taken on lower-paid roles to stay in work.

Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy at Carers UK, said: “These figures represent real people who have had to make difficult decisions about their careers, their financial security and their futures due to the pressures of balancing work and care.”

Carers UK, which published the report, called on government to strengthen employment rights for unpaid carers, including introducing a statutory entitlement to 10 days’ annual paid carer’s leave for employees.

It urged Louise Casey’s independent review of adult social care, expected to report in the next few months, to recommend policy changes putting carers at the centre of a reformed system, by making it easier for carers to combine work and unpaid care.
Midwife Jacqui Hylton, aged 58, gave up her 30-year NHS career to become a full-time carer two years ago when her then 86-year-old mother Winnie’s health took a serious turn for the worse.

Hylton moved from Hertfordshire to Leeds to live with Winnie and become her full-time carer. But she is frustrated that her professional skills are going to waste when the NHS faces a midwife shortage.

Caring will make it harder for her to return to midwifery as she is unable to work the required number of hours a year to maintain her professional accreditation. Enhanced respite allowance would potentially enable her to keep her hand in at work.

“I don’t regret caring for my mum. But financially I’m worse off, my pension will be less than it should have been. It’s lonely at times and its extremely hard work – harder than working in the NHS,” she said.

The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Around one in five (20%) of UK adults, equivalent to 11 million people, report unpaid care duties.

As well as affecting carers’ finances, careers and wellbeing, the report estimates the doubling in the number of people quitting paid work to care over the past seven years comes at an annual £37bn economic cost to the UK.

A government spokesperson said: “Unpaid carers make an extraordinary contribution to families, our communities and the economy, and I would like to personally thank Carers UK for their invaluable work in supporting unpaid carers and championing the issues they face every day.

“We want to ensure there are good jobs for carers who want to work alongside managing their caring responsibilities. This is why we are exploring how best to support unpaid carers through our review of employment rights.”

articles.title: Billions on paper: How much of Luzon Corridor’s $20-B pipeline will become real?
articles.summary: Rappler worked with an independent research analyst to see how much of the Luzon Economic Corridor pipeline is actually moving from pitch to pavement, and found that most of it is still in the…

blocks.text: First of 2 parts
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself offered perhaps the best test for the billions of dollars in projects pitched to investors under the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC).

“The success of the LEC will not be measured by the number of meetings that we hold or projects that we announce,” Marcos told investors and officials packed into the Grand Hyatt Manila on Thursday, September 10. “It will be measured by what we finance, by what we build, what we place into operation.”

That’s a demanding standard for the investment dealbook unveiled at the inaugural LEC Investment Forum, which lays out opportunities across the economic belt stretching from Subic Bay and Clark through Metro Manila all the way to Batangas.

On paper, there’s plenty to build. The dealbook contains 31 individually detailed opportunities, plus 13 industrial parks seeking businesses and locators. But only 18 of the 31 projects disclose an opportunity value. Rappler’s tally puts those at roughly $17.6 billion to $20.7 billion (P1.11 trillion to P1.30 trillion)*, depending on which end of disclosed ranges is used, while 13 projects still have no price tag at all.
Much of the pipeline is the basic machinery an industrial economy needs: railways, ports, airports, power plants, pipelines, warehouses, water systems, and telecommunications.
Rappler visualized the projects with disclosed values below, using the upper end where the dealbook gives a range. Click on a sector or hover over a project for more details.
Only four projects account for roughly four-fifths of the dealbook’s disclosed value at the upper end:

items: $4.1 billion (P257.6 billion) Sangley Point International Airport
$4 billion (P251.3 billion) North-South Commuter Railway operations and maintenance opportunity
$3 billion (P188.5 billion) Metro Manila Subway O&M concession
$3 billion to $6 billion (P188.5 billion to P377.0 billion) Subic-Clark natural gas ecosystem

blocks.text: Looking at these highlighted projects alone also shows that much of the pipeline is not made up of entirely new projects created under the LEC. Several of the biggest transport and energy projects were already in the government’s infrastructure pipeline before being folded into the corridor.
Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan flagged this as another reason to be cautious about treating the dealbook as a fresh wave of investments.

“I also flag that much of the pipeline is not new. Many of the transport and energy entries are long-standing JICA, ADB, and DOTr projects now rebranded under the corridor,” Punongbayan told Rappler. “All in all, there remains a huge gap between the corridor’s vision and its promised pipeline.”

To look beyond the headline values, Rappler collaborated with Cesar Tolentino, an independent research analyst and strategic adviser, to assess how far the projects have actually progressed using the dealbook and other publicly available project information.

Tolentino’s analysis quantified about $21.4 billion (P1.34 trillion) across 20 projects with identifiable investment values. But only about $5.1 billion (P320.4 billion) could be classified as pledged, already being spent or implemented, or completed. Roughly $15.5 billion (P973.8 billion) remained at what Tolentino groups in the visualization as the planning stage, where the stated project value could not yet be verified as committed investment.

blocks.caption: hierarchy visualization

blocks.text: “Even if there is documentation confirming a minimum investment amount of $21.4 billion for the Luzon Economic Corridor, [only about] $5 billion is either pledged, work-in-progress (being spent), or completed (spent). A majority of the declared investment amount is up ‘in the air’ and cannot be confirmed as committed,” Tolentino told Rappler.

That does not necessarily mean the projects will not push through. Many are still at the point where investors are being sought, procurement has yet to happen, or feasibility studies and other project preparation are still underway.
Tolentino said this makes it difficult to treat the full value of the project list as investment that can already be expected to enter the country.

“There’s a rule of thumb that Chinese businessmen use: ‘You only count the money that is on-hand,’” he said, referring to funds already received or backed by a contract. A pledge without a contract, by comparison, remains work in progress.

Being listed in the dealbook itself also does not mean an investor has already written a check, or that the project itself is new to the LEC. Some of the corridor’s largest entries are longstanding government infrastructure projects that have since been grouped under the initiative. The document also does not provide a common methodology for what it calls an “opportunity value.”

In some cases, the figure appears tied to building or expanding infrastructure; in others, it is attached to a long-term operations and maintenance concession. For projects looking mainly for customers or offtakers, it’s not always clear whether the number refers to capital expenditure, total project value, expected contract revenues, or another measure.

In other words, the roughly $20-billion (P1.26 trillion) headline is better understood as the scale of opportunities being marketed, rather than an actual $20-billion investment already committed to the Philippines.

blocks.caption: table visualization

blocks.text: The projects are also at very different stages. For instance, the proposed 212-kilometer Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas freight railway is undergoing studies expected to finish only in early 2029. Feasibility work for the Metro Manila Subway Phase 2 is likewise targeted for 2029, while the $175-million (P11-billion) National Data Center remains at pre-feasibility stage.

Others are further along. The Department of Agriculture has secured an initial $65 million (P4.08 billion) for the Clark National Food Hub. A $20-million to $25-million (P1.26-billion to P1.57-billion) insulated-panel factory expansion in Pampanga already has civil works completed and equipment in transit, while development of a $30-million (P1.88-billion) Subic fuel depot began in May.

That wide gap between early-stage concepts and implemented projects is exactly the challenge the government now has to close. US Ambassador Lee Lipton said it best during the forum: “Ideas are easy. Closing a deal is hard. Getting projects to the finish line is even harder.”
The Philippines urgently needs to attract more capital, with foreign investment already weak and continuing to lose momentum.

Foreign direct investment net inflows reached just $3.38 billion (P212.36 billion) from January to June 2026, down 17.8% from $4.12 billion (P258.86 billion) in the same period a year earlier, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Full-year FDI had already fallen 13.6% in 2025 from 2024.

blocks.caption: DECLINE. Data form the BSP shows that foreign investments in the Philippines have been declining since 2024, with H1 2026 also being lower than the same period from 2025. Chart from BSP.

blocks.text: Economy Secretary Arsenio Balisacan has also repeatedly said the country needs stronger investment if it wants to generate more productive, better-paying jobs rather than depend so heavily on consumption and services.

The LEC is one attempt to solve that problem by packaging infrastructure, industrial land, incentives. and government support into a single investment proposition backed initially by the Philippines, US, and Japan, and now a wider group of partner countries.

blocks.caption: MAP: Where Filipino families earn the most and least

blocks.text: There was also genuinely new money around the forum. The Philippines and the US signed a $60-million (P3.77-billion) Millennium Challenge Corporation Threshold Program grant, while the US Trade and Development Agency announced project-preparation support for Subic ship repair expansion and an AI-enhanced public Wi-Fi pilot. Those commitments are more concrete than expressions of interest, although project-preparation funding should still not be considered financing for the eventual full-scale infrastructure.
At the same time, Manila is not putting all its eggs in the US-led basket.

Just days before the LEC forum, the government’s economic team was in Hong Kong for the Belt and Road Summit, pitching the Philippines to investors and seeking deeper investment ties with the Hong Kong and China market.

“Hong Kong is a global financial center and a gateway to Asia. The Philippines is a fast-growing economy with talent, scale, resources, and a strategic location in the region. Our strengths complement each other,” Finance Secretary Frederick Go said at the Philipping-Hong Kong briefing.

The finance chief also emphasized that the country’s next chapter of growth would be built with the private sector and partners across the international business community, a chapter the government hopes will eventually be driven by AI, data centers and other high-tech industries.
But can the Philippines move beyond today’s pipeline of mostly basic infrastructure and actually attract the high-tech investments it’s banking on? (To be concluded) – Rappler.com

*$1 = P62.829 based on the September 14, 2026 rate of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

articles.title: Thirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigation
articles.summary:
PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station

A 13th serving Metropolitan police officer has been dismissed in relation to an…

blocks.text: A 13th serving Metropolitan police officer has been dismissed in relation to an undercover BBC investigation into misogyny and racism at Charing Cross police station.
PC Mason O’Connor was found to have committed discreditable conduct and breached professional behaviour standards, linked to a comment he made towards a female colleague, according to the Met.

The Panorama investigation aired in October 2025 and followed seven months of undercover filming. It included footage of officers calling for immigrants to be shot and boasting about using violence against suspects.
On Tuesday, a disciplinary panel heard that O’Connor told a female colleague in October 2024 that he “hope[d] you get raped on your way to Waterloo”, while he was off-duty in a pub.
The incident was reported as part of a witness appeal and “proactive wider investigation” launched after the broadcast of the Panorama film.
At the time, the Met police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said the footage was “vile to watch” and featured “incontrovertible evidence” that would enable the fast-tracking of misconduct hearings.

O’Connor’s sacking comes a few weeks after the dismissal of PC Lloyd Hunter, who was found to have made comments that trivialised the use of force and suggested that he would enjoy using force against members of the public. Hunter also said he “hated” homeless people.
Commander Simon Messinger, from the Met’s professionalism department, said: “Two more officers have now been dismissed for their appalling comments and attitudes.
“I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met’s determination to improve our culture across the organisation.
“We continue to support the ongoing IOPC [Independent Office for Police Conduct] investigation.”

The IOPC confirmed that investigations were continuing against 15 other officers or police staff and that misconduct had been identified from footage provided by the BBC which had not been included in the Panorama broadcast.
after newsletter promotion
A gross misconduct hearing is scheduled for later this month over comments made by a detention officer regarding the treatment of people being held in police custody.

Amanda Rowe, the IOPC’s director of engagement, said: “This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated, and the sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter.”
Both O’Connor and Hunter will be barred from rejoining the police force.

Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 26: What to expect

Legal luminaries will take center stage on Wednesday not as witnesses in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, but as amici curiae, or friends of the court, who will help resolve questions on the conviction vote threshold.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said there will be no trial on Wednesday to give ample time to the four retired Supreme Court justices who will provide expert legal advice following the ruling on the 16-vote threshold to convict the Vice President.

Set to appear before the court to give their position on the matter and take questions from the senator-judges are three former magistrates — Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban, Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Reynato Puno, and Retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna.
Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. will also participate, but through a legal memorandum instead of a physical appearance.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 6:43am

Legal luminaries will take center stage on Wednesday not as witnesses in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, but as amici curiae, or friends of the court, who will help resolve questions on the conviction vote threshold.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said there will be no trial on Wednesday to give ample time to the four retired Supreme Court justices who will provide expert legal advice following the ruling on the 16-vote threshold to convict the Vice President.

Set to appear before the court to give their position on the matter and take questions from the senator-judges are three former magistrates — Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban, Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Reynato Puno, and Retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna.
Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. will also participate, but through a legal memorandum instead of a physical appearance.
Copies of Davide’s legal memorandum, as well as the position paper from San Beda University School of Law dean Fr. Ranhilio Aquino, were earlier given to senator-judges and the parties.
Escudero said that senator-judges will be given five minutes each to ask questions to all or either of the three amici curiae present.
The defense and prosecution counsels are likewise allowed to ask questions coursed through the presiding officer.

Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol said the amici curiae are expected to answer questions on whether the phrase “all the Members of the Senate,” as stated in Article XI, Section 3, Paragraph 6 of the Constitution, should refer to the Senate’s full membership of 24 senators or only those “who are legally and physically capacitated to participate and vote on the final question in an impeachment trial.”

The amici curiae are also set to face questions related to the Avelino v. Cuenco case, particularly whether its treatment of members beyond the Senate’s coercive jurisdiction applies to senators who are detained, abroad, suspended or whose whereabouts are unknown.
The questions will seek to determine whether such senators should be included in the phrase “all the Members of the Senate” for purposes of the two-thirds vote required under the Constitution.

They are also expected to give their views on whether a senator-judge who did not attend or substantially participate in the impeachment proceedings, including in propounding questions to and observing the demeanor of witnesses, may nevertheless validly cast a vote on the final question in an impeachment trial. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: AI leaders call for regulations, Trump dismisses 'hoaxes'
articles.summary: AI giants are working to create a standards body amid rising alarms about the dangers of the industry. Meanwhile, Trump has dismissed the warnings, and a divided US Congress has failed to act.

image.caption: Anthropic, Google and OpenAI say they are working on a self-regulatory body to supervise the fast-growing industry Image: IMAGO/ZUMA Press

blocks.text: Some of the top names in AI are working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers and an apparent US reluctance to police its speedy development.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI on Tuesday said it was working with top competitors Anthropic and Google on a self-regulatory body.

This comes amid rising calls for stricter control on the technology that is growing at lightning speed and not without dangerous precedents, calls that have thus far gone unanswered by the Donald Trump administration.
What do we know about the proposed self-regulatory body?
The regulatory body, proposed by Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, would be modeled after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which oversees US brokers and investment firms.
Hassabis had called in July for a federal organization that would test the most powerful AI systems before they are released to the public.
He suggested funding would come from the industry to "attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing."
AI chatbot falsely accuses journalist of crimes
The proposal comes amid growing concerns about AI safety, which have escalated in recent weeks amid warnings from two former workers at major AI developers.
Researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic last week, sounding the alarm that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."
On Monday, former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."
Even top names within the industry have raised similar concerns.
On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the industry's development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Hassabis all supporting the sentiment.
How has the US government under Trump reacted to the calls?
Trump has dismissed the calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy," while a divided Congress, narrowly controlled by Trump's Republicans, has failed to act.
The looming midterm elections make it unlikely any action will come soon despite AI and the power-hungry data centers needed to run it being a concern for many voters.

Trump's dismissal has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.
The dire prediction that AI could destroy humanity "is not grounded on science," Huang said.
Leading Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have, however, expressed caution.
Amid Washington's persistent apathy toward regulation, smaller AI companies have warned any self-regulatory measures would come at their expense.
Canadian AI company Cohere's chief, Aidan Gomez, has accused the dominant American AI labs of forming a "cartel" under the guise of safety.

"AI needs guardrails. That is not the dispute and never has been. The dispute is over who writes them, who gets to participate and whose interests the rules are protecting," Gomez wrote in a blog post on Sunday.
What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy?

articles.title: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat
articles.summary:
Election officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against president

After the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it…

blocks.text: After the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it significantly harder to vote by mail in the midterms, US election officials are redoubling their efforts to convince Americans it is safe to cast their ballots by mail.

The supreme court’s Monday ruling, which sent Trump into an angry froth on Truth Social, averted what election officials of both parties said would be an administrative disaster for this year’s elections. Trump’s order would have required states to comply with cumbersome new rules, including redesigning mail-in envelopes and uploading lists of voters to the USPS, that were not feasible to implement before ballots started going out. The effort was seen as a push by the government to change voting policy as well as one to weaken confidence in voting by mail.

“That is the whole intent of the president. He wanted to build doubt,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat who serves as the top election official in Nevada, where mail-in voting is widely used. “He wanted to create chaos.”

Twenty-nine percent of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election and roughly one third cast a mail-in ballot in the 2022 midterms, according to researchers at the MIT election lab. Democrats were more likely than Republicans to cast a mail-in ballot.

“There’s just concern: ‘Can we trust the mail?’ And I say yes, because it’s not the leadership or the management of the postal service that’s actually going to have their hands on the ballots, it’s the postal workers who are on our side,” Aguilar said. Nevada officials also plan to run a series of public service announcements to educate voters on the election process.

In Wisconsin, election officials have faced questions about voters concerned their ballots won’t be delivered in time. Wisconsin law requires mail-in ballots to be delivered by the close of polls on election day in order to count and in the state’s April election there was an increase in late-arriving ballots. There have been higher rates of late-arriving ballots tossed this year, according to an analysis by the New York Times.

Wisconsin election officials have encouraged people through county websites, social media, and notes attached to their ballots, among other things, to mail their ballots back sooner, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

“We’re really trying to encourage people to act sooner. So hopefully they take that to heart,” said Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin elections commission, which oversees voting in that state. “It’s hard to tell people, ‘No, really, you should trust the post office’ when they came up with this absolutely cockamamie rule that was going to eliminate absentee voting.”

In a video released on Tuesday, Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin elections commission, said: “If you’re going to be returning your ballot by mail, please do so at least two weeks before the election. And you also may want to contact your municipal clerk to find out if there are other opportunities for you to return your ballot in your community. You may have drop-boxes or you may be able to return your ballot in person to your clerk.”
In Washington state, where everyone received a mail-in ballot, more than 20,000 votes were rejected in the August primary because they arrived late at an election office.
“There is a sense of distrust,” said Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state. “Even though there is a victory in the courts, we still are urging our voters to put their ballot in a drop-box.”

As lawsuits challenging the rule wound their way through federal courts this year, Adrian Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, publicly emphasized that the rule had not gone into effect yet and so that nothing around voting by mail had changed. Since the supreme court’s ruling preserved that status quo, he said, officials haven’t had to shift their messaging.

While voters have raised questions about the proposed changes “we continue to tell them until there’s a change, there is no change,” said Fontes, a Democrat “We are still where we were. We never jumped on the paranoia bandwagon.”

“It’s intentionally damaging to the entire elections administration process in this country,” said Fontes, a Democrat and the top election official in a state where voting by mail is widely used. “The administration, by their actions, have proven that they are hell-bent on driving American voters away from their own elections. And we’ve been working very hard to counter that.”

articles.title: House committee recommends Leon Black be held in contempt of Congress over Epstein inquiry subpoenas
articles.summary:
Financier refused to comply with subpoenas seeking his testimony for the investigation into the late sex offender

The House oversight committee voted unanimously Tuesday to recommend that…

blocks.text: The House oversight committee voted unanimously Tuesday to recommend that the House of Representatives hold Leon Black, the billionaire financier, in contempt of Congress, after he refused to comply with subpoenas seeking his testimony and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) sought by the panel as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. Black contends the subpoenas are “invalid” and he is suing to block them.

“Subpoenas are not suggestions; they carry the force of law and require full compliance” the representative James Comer, who chairs the committee, said in the chamber on Tuesday afternoon before the voting began. “Mr Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation because he maintained a close personal relationship with Epstein for years during the time when Epstein was engaged in sex trafficking.
“We made it clear to Mr Black and his attorneys that if he did not comply, then the committee would initiate contempt proceedings” Comer added.
The bipartisan committee passed the resolution 41-0. Comer said that the committee now “moves the report to the full House”.
The office of the House speaker, Mike Johnson, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday about whether the lower chamber would consider the contempt measure.

The markup is the latest escalation in the dispute between the committee and Black, whose name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017.
Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and has said that he had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes.

Comerannounced last week that that the committee would consider the resolution to hold Black in contempt. It came after Black did not appear for his deposition scheduled for 3 September and did not produce all of the nondisclosure agreements sought by the committee.

Instead, Black sued to block the subpoenas, arguing that they were “invalid to the extent they exceed” the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose.

Black’s lawsuit also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee”.

The committee issued the subpoenas in June, after Black appeared voluntarily before the panel for a transcribed interview. The interview ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. Comer then issued the two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party”, and another requiring him to appear before the committee again. In August, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he did not fully cooperate with the committee’s subpoenas.
On Tuesday, during his remarks in the chamber before the vote, Comer said that Black “only produced one NDA to the committee” and noted that Black did not appear for his 3 September deposition.
Attorneys representing Black had asked for a postponement of the committee’s markup earlier on Tuesday, and described it as a “complete abomination”.
after newsletter promotion

The attorneys said they sent two letters to Comer and Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the committee, saying that they would submit a complaint to the office of congressional conduct requesting “an investigation into conduct by Chairman Comer” alleging that ahead of Black’s scheduled deposition, Comer “engaged in what should be viewed as a violation of the Rules of the House of Representatives relating to the deposition”.

“The Committee under the leadership of Chairman James Comer and Ranking Member Robert Garcia has lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power,” Black’s attorney said in a statement on Tuesday.
The lawyers described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens”.

“Mr Black has repeatedly said that he feels terrible for Epstein’s victims and that he regrets ever doing business with Epstein,” the statement added. “He never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein. Mr Black had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct.”

Before Black’s scheduled deposition earlier this month, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse urged him to comply with congressional subpoenas. They argued that his use “of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit”.

Earlier this year, the committee also moved to hold former president Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton in contempt for initially refusing to testify about Epstein. The Clintons ultimately testified before the House.

articles.title: Iran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report finds
articles.summary:
Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild

The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of…
articles.byline: Joseph Gedeon and Andrew Roth in Washington

blocks.text: The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found, in a damaging report less than two months before midterm elections where the war and the cost of living crisis will likely hurt Republicans at the polls.

The economic report comes one day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”.

The Pentagon’s report did not address an internal Pentagon investigation into the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people, including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying the results of the investigation that would show negligence by the Pentagon in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes.

The new $38bn estimate in the CBO report, which is some of the first public accounting of the cost of the war in Iran, was requested by the Democratic congressman Brendan Boyle, ranking member of the House budget committee. It also found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. And it estimated that the cost would grow $3bn for every additional month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation.

Much of that cost has come from missile defenses. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and Navy interceptors that CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”.

In a White House statement responding to reports of the shortage, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, separately dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true” in August.

According to the CBO report, the shortage would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains such an arsenal and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has.

Munitions have been the single largest driver of the Pentagon’s costs overall, CBO found: $21.7bn to replace weapons expended so far, of which $13.1bn went toward missile defense interceptors alone. The office also put a price on damage to American aircraft and equipment, including a destroyed Thaad radar system, and said it was forced to build its estimates largely from public reporting because the Pentagon did not respond to its requests for information.

The report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been.
It also said that the war had led to the “large expenditure of missile defense interceptors, which will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years”.

In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out (including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs), $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs CBO could not examine – a far larger share of secret funding than in past war supplementals.
CBO further added that it still cannot estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

articles.title: All supporting acts withdraw from Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore
articles.summary:
Three openers and live band for Sheeran’s tour depart after removal of Macklemore over ‘free Palestine’ comments

All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of

blocks.text: All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opening act Macklemore, as backlash grows to his removal from the tour over onstage comments in support of Palestine.

Finneas, the singer who was scheduled to open for Sheeran on six South American dates in November, withdrew from the tour on Tuesday afternoon, hours after Sheeran posted his own lengthy statement to Instagram explaining pressure from venue owners to remove Macklemore for pro-Palestine comments made during two shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.

In a two-minute speech on 4 September, the Grammy-winning artist told the audience he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, along with the words “free Palestine”. The remark prompted a petition calling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour from the Israeli American Council and the opposition of some venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and a prominent donor to Israel.

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote on social media. “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”

The decision came shortly after Aaron Rowe, an Irish singer who opened for Sheeran in Australia earlier this year and was scheduled for the 10 remaining dates in North America, announced his own withdrawal from the tour. “I don’t take the decision lightly,” he wrote on Instagram. “Ed has been a friends to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this.

“But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.”
The Irish band Beoga shortly after joined Rowe in departing the US tour to protest the “silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”.

“We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us,” they wrote on social media. “We have been friends with Ed for over 10 years now and will continue to be. We believe in dialogue as a means of progressing the plight of the Palestinian people.”

The Danish pop band Lukas Graham also dropped out of the tour on Tuesday afternoon. “We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them,” wrote lead singer Lukas Forchhammer on the band’s social media. “Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge.”

The abrupt withdrawals of the Sheeran’s opening acts came hours after the English singer confirmed that Kraft, along with several other stadium owners, refused to allow the tour to play at their venues if Macklemore continued to open for him. Though Sheeran wrote that the was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and “the suffering and pain caused on both sides,” he said that attempts to broker conversations between parties was unsuccessful, and the “venue’s and the promoter’s decision was final”.

“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” he wrote in a multi-page post on Instagram. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”

“I have spent this week trying to build bridges, to find a solution and unfortunately, was unable to do so,” he concluded. “I know who I am, both as a person and as an artist, and those who know my heart know my values too.”

The tour withdrawals join a growing chorus of backlash to Macklemore’s removal, including numerous politicians and Ms Rachel, the children’s educator and Youtube star, who wrote on Instagram: “Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won’t be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine. Instead he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak on it.”

Kehlani, the singer whose pro-Palestine activism led to the cancellation of a concert at Cornell University last year, commented on social media in support of Macklemore: “A LOT of the venues / owners are rallied together this way. honored to know you brother.”

In his own statement on Monday, Kraft did not deny refusing to allow Macklemore on stage at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston, and said the decision was based on both Macklemore’s “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.

“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” he said.

articles.title: Search under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playground
articles.summary:
More than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss

Police are urging people to check their gardens and sheds for a…

blocks.text: Police are urging people to check their gardens and sheds for a three-year-old boy who went missing on Tuesday during a visit to a playground near the Suffolk-Essex border.

The boy, named Noah, was last seen at 3pm in Merriam Close in Brantham, near Manningtree, before being separated from a relative. Officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah was reported to have run down an alleyway near the playground towards a housing estate.

He is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey. Police also confirmed that Noah is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss.

The BBC reported that more than 100 people had joined in the search efforts by Tuesday evening and that train services between Manningtree and Ipswich were running at reduced speed while searches continued.
Police have cordoned off the alleyway and there were reports of door-to-door inquiries in the area.

A spokesperson for Suffolk constabulary said late on Tuesday: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches. Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.”

articles.title: Air pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggests
articles.summary:
Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide

Air pollution is associated with an
articles.byline: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent

blocks.text: Air pollution is associated with an increased risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, according to research.

Environmental pollution is known to be associated with poorer mental health but its role in suicide risk is less well understood. Scientists at Queen’s University Belfast examined whether air, noise, light, and water pollution could influence the risk of death by suicide and suicidal behaviours.

Their meta analysis of 29 studies found that exposure to airborne small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide were linked to a heightened risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.

Narrative analysis of a further 16 studies suggested that some other air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and ozone, as well as noise pollution, were also associated with a higher suicide risk. However, evidence for light and water pollution was inconclusive.

The authors said the findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, suggested that environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies and that suicide prevention should also be viewed as a public health issue.
“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they said.

“Integrating environmental health into mental health policy, through cross-sectoral collaboration, pollution reduction strategies, and targeted public health interventions, could play a vital role in reducing suicide risk and improving overall population mental wellbeing.”

But other experts expressed caution about the findings. Dr Jess Moody, the senior research and evidence manager at Samaritans, said: “While the reasons for suicide are complex, evidence shows that a variety of factors can impact suicide risk and we must not ignore the environments we live in, particularly inequalities around living conditions. Samaritans welcomes research that helps awareness of how suicide links to wider public health concerns.”

Dr Jon Van Niekerk, the chair of the general adult faculty at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said the research suggested some forms of air pollution may be associated with a small increase in suicidal behaviour but it did not establish that air pollution itself caused suicidal thoughts or attempts.
He added: “Air pollution is closely associated with other factors which we know can influence mental health, including socioeconomic deprivation, urban living, physical health and housing.

“The study provides further population-level support for reducing harmful air pollution, though the findings should not be seen as supporting individual suicide risk prediction or suggesting that pollution reduction alone could be a suicide prevention measure.”

Dr Rosie Cornish, a senior research fellow in epidemiology and health data science at the University of Bristol, said there were many factors associated with higher levels of air pollution as well as increased risk of suicide.
“If air pollution is not actually a cause of increased risk of suicide then reducing pollution will not help to prevent suicide. The authors do not acknowledge this when drawing their conclusions.”
Dr Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge, said: “This study confuses two fundamentally different concepts: causation and association.
“There are many other factors that could potentially explain the associations observed. For example, areas with higher levels of pollution may differ in other ways that affect suicide risk.
“This research finds factors that are associated with increased suicide risk, but further research is needed to claim that the factors identified are causes of increased risk.”
More than 720,000 people globally die by suicide each year. It is the third leading cause of death among 15– to 29-year-olds, according to the World Health Organization.
