articles.title: Pocock says Labor easing copyright protections for AI datacentre investment would throw creatives ‘under the bus’
articles.summary:
Proposals revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met with Albanese ministers

The Albanese government is considering giving AI companies access to Australian…

blocks.text: The Albanese government is considering giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default as its pursues a compromise with American tech giants.

The proposals were revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met with Labor ministers and warned Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company training models locally.
The independent senator David Pocock said the compromise would throw protections for creatives and copyright holders “under the bus” in pursuit of datacentre funding.
“It would mean putting AI companies’ interests over everyday Australians, giving AI companies access to all Australians’ content, unless they opt out,” Pocock said on Tuesday.
“The burden should not fall on Australians to defend the rights they already hold over content they create and own and invest in.”
The proposals were contained in a document Pocock described as screenshots of government’s consultation proposals, tabled in the Senate on Tuesday and titled “AI on Australian Terms”.
AI companies have sought to train their models on content and data online but cannot do so with Australian content due to local copyright rules.
The document raises as a key issue the vast number of small individual creators of online content, for which voluntary deals with AI companies “is not realistic/possible”.
It suggests requiring rights holders “digitally protect” their material if they do not want AI models trained on it – a proposal rightsholders say is not feasible.
Under one option it proposes, AI companies would gain the right to access and train models on any unprotected online material as long as they made deals with enough businesses.

Under another, AI companies would do deals with creatives’ rightsholder organisations that give the access rights even if the content was made by someone who was not a member of the organisation that won the deal. A licence to access one category of material, such as music or text, would be extended to cover the many different small creators within that industry.
Labor’s industry minister, Tim Ayres, had on Monday said the government’s forthcoming AI rules would “in no way” involve a reduction in copyright protection.

The deputy prime minister Richard Marles, said the federal government was “working at a pace” to respond to the issue of copyright, and maintained the opportunity to work with American tech giants was a “significant moment for the country”.
“The opportunity for Australia economically is enormous in collaborating with frontier companies … and having frontier training occur in Australia,” he told the ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening.
“We want to see this opportunity come to the country [but] it needs to come on terms which are in our national interests.”
Marles confirmed the federal government had spoken with tech companies in San Francisco in the past fortnight on the issue, adding “I think this can be done”.
The Greens senator Sarah Hanson Young said the suggestions of a copyright compromise were “abhorrent” prior to the revelations on Tuesday afternoon.
“Every Australian deserves to get paid for the work that they make and the work that they do,” Hanson-Young said.
“A weakening of the copyright laws letting big tech take the work of Australians for free, not have to pay for it, for their own profit.”
Musicians, writers and artists lobbied against weaker copyright laws earlier this year after reports AI companies were offering $50bn datacentre investments in exchange.
The attorney-general, Michelle Rowland, is running the government’s ongoing consultation with affected organisations.
A spokesperson for Rowland on Tuesday said the government would ensure any future copyright changes deliver “meaningful control and fair compensation”.
OpenAI’s vice president for global policy, Ann O’Leary, met ministers and officials this week, as the company considers investing in Australia.

In an interview with The Australian newspaper about the prospect of training models here, O’Leary said: “Our company isn’t ready to have that conversation if we can’t get through the gating problem of the copyright barriers.”

The newspaper reported the comments as an “ultimatum” that sought to “strong-arm” the government. Marles said the newspaper was “overstating” the comments. OpenAI has asked the paper to correct its headline and article.
Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, told News24 on Tuesday he hadn’t seen any ultimatum and he would reject one if it were issued.
“We want to support Australian artists,” Charlton said. “We want to give them control over their work. We want to make sure they’re compensated, if they choose to have it used.
“We’re not compromising them or trading them off. So if we lose some datacentres over this, so be it.”

articles.title: Alberta NDP flies the anti-separatist flag to steal a UCP riding in Calgary
articles.summary: It's hard to find meaning in one byelection for a general election 12 months away. But the big referendum is only five weeks from now.

image.caption: Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi talks about his candidate's byelection victory on Tuesday, as MLA-elect Kyle Campbell looks on. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis
It's hard to find meaning in one byelection for a general election 12 months away. But the big referendum is only five weeks from now.
A surprise upset 5 weeks before referendum, and a whole year before next election
In among all the splashes of Alberta NDP orange and UCP blue, there was plenty of red adorning the front yards of many homes ahead of this week’s Calgary-Shaw byelection.
No, sorry, I’m not talking about Alberta Liberal Leader John Roggeveen and the 3.8 per cent vote share he snagged.
The red refers to the many Canadian flags homeowners have newly erected, and the pro-unity, anti-separatist lawn signs that have sprung up throughout Alberta.
The campaigning New Democrats sensed the kind of reception they’d get at those doors for their candidate Kyle Campbell, now the MLA-elect.

“If you were flying a Canadian flag or you had a forever Canadian sign … Yeah, we pretty much could mark you down as a supporter,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters on Tuesday, the day after his party’s victory in what was previously a UCP riding in Calgary’s deep suburbs.
It’s often too easy and too foolish to treat the results of a single byelection as a predictor of a general election a year away, although darned if the partisans like Nenshi won’t try.
We’re likely on firmer ground trying to discern what a byelection says about the mood heading into the referendum about Alberta separation that’s set for five weeks from now.
Polls have consistently indicated that Albertans, especially in big cities, resoundingly support the “stay” option and oppose holding a future referendum for independence.

Now, another indication, in the form of voting results. At least in Calgary-Shaw, the public mood has turned against Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservatives, who thrust the province deeper into the unity debate by crafting and scheduling the Oct. 19 vote.

Shaw residents converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. Of the 12 Calgary ridings that Smith’s party took in 2023, Shaw had the third-widest victory margin, a fact that might bring worry to UCP cabinet ministers and backbenchers in the city.

The win in Shaw was somewhat of a surprise to the NDP, judging by, among more publicly available factors, the fact Nenshi said his party’s relatively modest win margin “exceeded my wildest expectations.”

After all, the Opposition party had long been trailing the UCP in public opinion, and Nenshi lagged behind Smith, including in the city he formerly served as mayor. Most voters may have been squarely against separation or even the debate itself, but that dissatisfaction hadn’t been washing up on United Conservative shores. Not yet at least.

Smith and her Shaw candidate Mike Derry might have said repeatedly that they endorse staying in Canada, but Campbell and Nenshi spent much of the campaign trying to remind voters how responsible the UCP government is for the referendum — and that senior organizers in the party favour separation.

How thoroughly did the New Democrats wrap their campaign identity around federalism? After Campbell’s victory speech at a southwest Calgary bar, supporters spontaneously broke into a rendition of O Canada.
After the verdict that got his backers singing, a jubilant Nenshi called the byelection an “earthquake.”
“This means that 35 days from today, we send Danielle Smith and her separatist pals packing, and within a year from now, we give Albertans the NDP government they deserve,” he said.
Sure, Alberta would have a Premier Naheed Nenshi if Shaw’s 18-point swing from UCP to NDP gets translated to the rest of the province in the fall 2027 election.
In the same way that a stunner of a federal Conservative victory in a 2024 byelection in the Toronto riding of St. Paul’s led to Prime Minister Pierre Poilievre in 2025. Or didn’t.

In mid-2024, the Pierre Poilievre Conservatives stole a federal byelection in downtown Toronto, flipping a seat that had been Liberal for three decades. One year and one prime ministerial resignation later, the Liberals took the riding by 28 percentage points, and Mark Carney secured a fourth straight Liberal government term.
Ample time to interpret message

That Toronto byelection sent a political message of sorts that ultimately led to Justin Trudeau’s resignation. There’s ample time and opportunity for Alberta’s premier to interpret the message that voters sent her in the sort of suburban seat her party can’t afford to lose in a general election.

Barring another political “earthquake” on Oct. 19, independence referendums will be a distant memory come next fall. Alberta politics could change a lot before then; heavens knows they’re prone to turbulence.

Smith could pivot her agenda farther away from the independence question. She could give her Opposition less room to cast her as an agent of disunity, and themselves as the exclusive guardians of Alberta’s place within Canada.

It’s also possible United Conservative members give their federalist leader new marching orders on that same matter, and urge her at a November convention to get in line with many party activists and take a more pro-separatist stance.

The future could also be determined by what Calgary-Shaw and other ridings look like in the next election. Alberta’s electoral boundaries are getting revised by an unorthodox UCP-led advisory panel, with the prospect that the cities’ suburban ridings are spliced with more UCP-friendly rural areas.

The October referendum seems to have left its striking imprint in one riding. The boundary revisions will be but one of many factors that will colour in the map when all Albertans get to vote next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

blocks.text: Lambie pleads with voters to reject 'dangerous' and 'delusional' Hanson

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales
Jacqui Lambie has warned Australians not to support a “dangerous” and “delusional” Pauline Hanson, drawing comparisons between the One Nation leader and controversial international leaders.

In a speech during adjournment last night in the Senate, the Tasmanian senator said she had received a stream of abuse after her impassioned defence of Andrew Hastie after he was repeatedly labelled a “traitor” in One Nation’s cartoon series.
Lambie said:

double quotation markOne Nation whips up the anger and they tell people who to blame. That’s the populist trick ... It’s a trick Australia, and we’ve got to wake up to it. Because every time a populist leader, like Trump or Farage, get any power, the lives of working people don’t get better. They get worse.
The outspoken senator criticised Donald Trump’s potential forever war with Iran while singling out Hanson’s support of his actions.
double quotation markYou’d put [Australian soldiers] back in another American forever war? [Hanson] is not only dangerous, she’s delusional!
Lambie said figures such as Trump and Nigel Farage were great at telling people they would fight for them while doing the opposite.

double quotation markSenator Hanson will be fine in her retirement, as will Nigel and Donald in theirs, because once again they are feathering their own nests ... Australia can choose not to follow the ugly politics of populism, we can do better because we bloody are better. And it’s not about right or left, it’s about respect and finding solutions, and not operating from a place of fear – whatever side you’re on.

blocks.text: Gambling company fined $1m for sending 800 messages to 165 people on Betstop

blocks.caption: Henry Belot

blocks.text: Henry Belot

Betting company Dabble has been fined more than $1m for continuing to send more than 800 messages to 165 gamblers who had joined the federal government’s self-exclusion register and asked to be left alone.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority also found the gambling company failed to close the betting accounts of 157 people who registered with Betstop, which helps people break their gambling addictions.
In a statement, ACMA said Dabble sent more than 2000 push notifications to 45 customers without including any information about the Betstop service, which is a legal requirement.
The watchdog has fined the company $1,069,200. According to Acma, Dabble has also given a court-enforceable undertaking to guarantee future compliance with the rules.
Acma member, Carolyn Lidgerwood, said the breachers were serious and undermined the federal government’s harm minimisation strategy.

double quotation markPeople who register with BetStop have made a clear decision to exclude themselves from online wagering. Providers must respect that decision by closing their accounts promptly and ensuring they are not targeted with gambling promotions. BetStop is an important consumer protection measure, but it only works if wagering companies follow the rules. The Acma will take action where wagering providers fail to meet their obligations.
Renters in NSW will be able to transfer their bond from one property to the next from today, meaning they won’t need to come up with thousands of dollars upfront every time they move.
It’s expected Smart Rental Bonds will save more than two million renters across the state up to $4,000 each time they move home – though the online scheme costs $25 to use.
The NSW government will pay the landlord the bond upon the end of the lease, while the renter will repay the government.
Renters will need to pay the difference if the second bond is higher – equally they will be refunded the difference if it is cheaper, provided there is no agreed claim on the bond.
The NSW government scheme has already seen $1m in bond transfers in Penrith, Parramatta and the Central Coast, where it was rolled out early.

It follows similar moves to make renting fairer in NSW, including a ban on no grounds evictions, a limit of one rent increase a year, enforcing fee-free ways to pay rent and making it easier for people to have pets.
NSW One Nation leader fronts rally opposing 'abortion to birth'

blocks.caption: Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy

The head of One Nation in New South Wales has fronted a rally opposing “abortion up to birth” ahead of an expected vote in the upper house on Libertarian member John Ruddick’s bill to ban “sex-selective abortions” during private member’s business today.

Mike Newman appeared alongside members of fringe parties outside the state’s parliament house on Tuesday evening, where he claimed One Nation wanted to “stop” abortion rights. Stumbling upon his words, he told the crowd:

double quotation markWe want to stop it. We want to make sure that same-sex-, sorry, abortion is stopped. We want to make sure that people have the right to life, and we will vote for you in favour of that.

Debate on Ruddick’s bill was adjourned in the June sitting week, and is expected to be decided via a conscience vote. Labor and opposition sources said the vote was expected to be close, or for support for Ruddick’s bill to fall slightly short.
The event follows another anti-abortion rally in June, attended by One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, where he piled pressure on Nationals MPs to vote on favour of the bill.

Some members were expected to be absent for today’s vote, including Shooters, Farmers and Fishers MLC Robert Borsak, who spoke in favour of the bill in June. A senior Liberal source said that without members including Borsak, there did not appear to be “any room or margin” which could deliver Ruddick’s bill.

Richard Marles was also asked about Aukus, and whether he was concerned about reports from the UK which indicated the Labour government was delaying its decision about begginning building the boats by two years to 2028.
He said there was “no change” on Australia’s end in terms of the UK’s position and rejected that they were “red flags”.

double quotation markThe ultimate number of submarines is not the key issue here, the key issue is the development of the design, the pace of that which is happening. The UK is on track to cut steel in respect of its first SSN Aukus submarine next year. It’s on track to have that submarine come off the production line in the UK in the late 2030s. That’s perfect timing in respect of what we’re doing … We are really comfortable with what is happening there.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, says he is “comforted” by a recent essay from the boss of artificial intelligence company Anthropic which warned his industry must slow the pace in developing AI systems.
Appearing on ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening, Marles was asked about Dario Amodei’s comments urging governments to press pause on the AI revolution.
He replied:

double quotation markI actually take comfort in Dario Amodei’s essay and the call he’s made … It’s firstly not about … stopping this all together but rather making sure that the development of the safeguards that are in place in respect of this technology is in front of the technological capability itself … The technology is being developed very quickly, and … from an Australian point of view, our focus is making sure that in seeing this as a revolutionary technology which can be doing so much good in Australia that, we do have in place … AI safeguards in Australia which make sure that this is a technology which is benefit Australians and not the other way around.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.
Jacqui Lambie has launched a fiery attack on Pauline Hanson, urging Australians not to support the “dangerous” and “delusional” One Nation leader. More coming up.

articles.title: Hyrox athlete competed while having diarrhea. Was she right to push through?
articles.summary: The graphic images of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors…

image.caption: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia takes part in Hyrox Beijing 2026 at National Speed Skating Oval on Saturday in Beijing. Hyrox has been criticized online for not stopping Wietrzyk from competing despite having diarrhea. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The graphic images of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.
Hyrox apologized after Australian Joanna Wietrzyk won Saturday's competition in Beijing
Popular indoor fitness competition Hyrox has said it has changed its protocols after allowing an Australian athlete to keep competing — and win — despite suffering from what appeared to be diarrhea.
"It's a biohazard, how they let the competition go on is beyond me," an observer wrote on Reddit.
"Think about how disgusting it is, especially when we use the exact same track," a race participant told the South China Morning Post.

Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23.
"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.

As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.

"Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not," co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement Monday.
"As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again," he added.

The Hyrox official rulebook already had some penalties in place for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited, but until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.
As some people have pointed out in the comments on Hyrox's Instagram apology, perhaps it's "unbelievable that this even needs a rule."
"That’s not a rule. That’s basic human decency," someone commented.
So, what happened?
Hyrox, a structured indoor activity divided into eight segments, each involving a one-kilometre run followed by a fitness exercise, attracts tens of thousands of participants to its biggest events.

The event was developed in 2017 by German entrepreneur Christian Toetzke and Moritz Fürste, who won field hockey gold medals for Germany in the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics. It's since become a global phenomenon, was accepted as a format in World Triathlon this year (under the name Hyathlon) and has its sights set on the Olympics.

items: 'Extreme' workouts drive spike in 'rhabdo' cases among young N.L. women, says doctor
Botched Edmonton Marathon costs 13 runners chance at Boston Marathon

blocks.text: And Wietrzyk is the women's pro world record holder after her performance at the Warsaw Major in April. While she hasn't made an official statement about what happening in Beijing, several reports claim Wietrzyk was suffering from food poisoning.
A spectator at the event told the South China Morning Post that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.

Hyrox China, in a statement posted social media platform Weibo, said a competitor experienced a "sudden medical issue." The statement explained that organizers later disinfected contaminated areas, removed any contaminated equipment and replaced the carpet in the venue.
60-year-old teacher places 2nd at Hyrox world championship

As the TaiPei Times reports, Hyrox China did not apologize, but "admitted in an earlier statement to 'shortcomings' in the regulations which had prevented judges from intervening immediately during the competition."
Wietrzyk's coach, Chris Bayens, defended her in a statement posted to Instagram Sunday, urging people not to judge her "intent, clarity, or morality."
"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," Bayens wrote.
"What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time."
CBC News has reached out to Hyrox, Wietrzyk and her coach for comment, but not yet heard back.
Poop incidents are common

As many high-intensity athletes likely know, shit happens. Sometimes literally. There's even a term for it: runner's diarrhea, which Healthline describes as an inflammation of the colon caused by the intensity of workouts that can lead to frequent bowel movements.

According to a 2014 study, anywhere from 30 to 50 per cent of athletes report gastrointestinal problems. More recently, a 2025 literature review published in the World Journal of Gastroenterology concluded that high-intensity or prolonged exercise may contribute to symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

items: Olympic-bound sprinter trapped in toilet before race unlocks new bathroom fear in fellow runners
Canadian athletes fighting stomach illness at Paris Olympics

blocks.text: There are many well-documented and highly public cases where athletes have soiled themselves mid-competition. Just this past June, for instance, South African runner George Kusche won the Comrades Marathon with feces dripping down his legs.
Meanwhile, U.S. athlete Taylor Knibb won the 2024 T100 World Championship in Dubai, but made headlines for telling a cameraman, "I just shit myself. So can you not get my ass?"
Hyrox is coming to Ottawa and athletes are training at this 24/7 pop-up gym

In 2021, another U.S. athlete, Addi Zerrenner, went viral after soiling herself three times while running the California International Marathon, and told Business Insider, "I'm finally having the true marathon experience."
And U.K. runner Paula Radcliffe famously won the 2005 London Marathon after having to stop at 22-mile mark to defecate on the sidelines, calling it "an embarrassing necessity."
But, as many observers have noted, these incidents have all occurred outdoors.

Meanwhile, another Hyrox competitor, Malaysia's Zarif Zakaria, posted on Threads that he was recently disqualified from the Aug. 13 competition in Bangkok for using the bathroom — before the race. He claimed it's because it meant he had a late start.
"How come people can race while having diarrhea and not get DQ’d?" he posted Monday.
"Maybe it's time for me to retire from HYROX."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Family of missing B.C. mountaineer believes she fell while descending the Alps
articles.summary: The family of famed Canadian skyrunner and mountaineer Kalie McCrystal, who went missing on the Matterhorn in the Alps more than two weeks ago, say she "remains among the mountains where she felt…

image.caption: Athletics Canada National Team trail runner, Kalie McCrystal, is shown in this undated photo posted by Athletics Canada on their X page. (AthleticsCanada/X)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The family of famed Canadian skyrunner and mountaineer Kalie McCrystal, who went missing on the Matterhorn in the Alps more than two weeks ago, say she "remains among the mountains where she felt most at home."
Kalie McCrystal went missing on Matterhorn more than 2 weeks ago
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 4:20 PM EDT | Last Updated: 8 minutes ago
Her mother and sister say in a statement that everything they know after an extensive search suggests she fell while descending the mountain.

The statement that was shared by British Columbia provincial legislator Amelia Boultbee, a friend of McCrystal, praises search and rescue crews for their efforts and says the family is confident everything possible has been done to find her.
McCrystal was last seen Sept. 1 while attempting to break a mountain-running record in the Alps along the Switzerland-Italy border, climbing the 4,481-metre-tall Matterhorn.

items: Helicopter search suspended for Squamish, B.C., mountain runner missing on Matterhorn
B.C. athlete missing in Italian Alps

blocks.text: The family statement says friends and loved ones from around the world mobilized and went to remarkable lengths to help find McCrystal and bring her home.
They say not finding her was not the outcome they were hoping for and is difficult to accept.

The statement describes McCrystal as a special person who moved through life with equal parts determination and fun and says her absence will leave a hole in communities in skyrunning, Squamish and beyond.

"While we desperately wish we could have found her, we find peace in knowing that she was doing what made her feel most alive until her very last moments, and that she remains among the mountains where she felt most at home," the statement says.

articles.title: NBA says it looked at precedent before doling out Clippers' penalties for cap circumvention
articles.summary: NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said the league looked at precedent before taking away five first-round draft picks from the Los Angeles Clippers for circumventing salary cap rules, though he noted that…

image.caption: NBA commissioner Adam Silver, seen during a press conference in February, spoke for the first time about the league's probe into alleged salary cap circumvention from the Los Angeles Clippers on Tuesday at the NBA board of governors meeting in New York. (Ryan Sirius Sun/Getty Images)

blocks.text: NBA·New

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said the league looked at precedent before taking away five first-round draft picks from the Los Angeles Clippers for circumventing salary cap rules, though he noted that the decision was difficult because of the impact it could have on the team's fans.
Commissioner says penalty decision was difficult, in part, due to impact on team's fans
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 4:14 PM EDT | Last Updated: 11 minutes ago

Silver, speaking Tuesday at the end of a two-day Board of Governors meeting, pointed to how the Minnesota Timberwolves were once docked five picks for cap circumvention as the precedent used in this case. And while noting that he doesn't believe the loss of picks will lead to what he called "permanent damage" to the Clippers, it is still a major setback.

"I think that's, in some ways, the most difficult part of adjudicating these disputes," Silver said. "While there have to be competitive consequences, in our view, if these rules are violated, we still want to be a 30-team league and we recognize that in some ways we're unfortunately punishing the fans of that team as well."

Those were Silver's first public comments after the Clippers were found to have circumvented salary cap rules on Kawhi Leonard's behalf — something the team vehemently denied during a yearlong investigation. The NBA hit the Clippers earlier this month with massive penalties as a result of that probe, suspending owner Steve Ballmer for one year, fining the team $30 million US and forcing it to forfeit five first-round draft picks, among other sanctions.

items: Raptors confirm Kawhi Leonard is heading back to Toronto after completing trade deal
Leonard focused on Raptors return with 'clean slate' after avoiding suspension in NBA cap probe

blocks.text: The trade sending Leonard back to Toronto was finally completed Monday after the Raptors and Clippers got the customary league approval required for such deals. And Ballmer, earlier this week, said he would accept the penalties and that the fine has already been paid.
The Clippers were not represented at the board meeting, Silver said, since the team remains in the process of finding an interim governor.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran addresses backlash over Macklemore being dropped from tour
articles.summary: After facing a slew of criticism following Macklemore’s ejection from his tour as an opening act for his pro-Palestine comments during sets, singer Ed Sheeran has issued a statement on the situation,…

image.caption: Ed Sheeran and Macklemore perform during the 2014 iHeartRadio Music Festival in Las Vegas. Sheeran is addressing Macklemore's removal from his tour as opening act over 'Free Palestine' comments, saying it wasn't his call. (Steve Marcus/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

After facing a slew of criticism following Macklemore’s ejection from his tour as an opening act for his pro-Palestine comments during sets, singer Ed Sheeran has issued a statement on the situation, claiming it wasn’t his call and defending his choice to not take political stances.
The rapper was dropped as an opening act after venues boycotted his presence over 'Free Palestine' comments

After facing a slew of criticism following Macklemore's ejection from his tour as an opening act for his pro-Palestine comments during sets, singer Ed Sheeran has issued a statement claiming it wasn't his call and defending his choice to not take political stances.
Sheeran said he is "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," calling the suffering on "both sides" a "human tragedy."

Sheeran said upcoming venues contacted him after his shows at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium earlier this month, saying they would pull his performances if Macklemore, 43, was not removed as his opening act, because of "how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance," the singer said.

Videos from the performances, which have drawn criticism from pro-Israel groups, show the rapper repeating "Free Palestine" to a cheering crowd and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank. In his speech at the second show on Sept. 5, he addressed Jewish audience members, saying, "criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way is a criticism of you.
"My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality."

items: Macklemore cut from Ed Sheeran U.S. tour after onstage 'Free Palestine' remarks

blocks.text: In his statement, Sheeran said, "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
He added that while he tried to "build a bridge," the venues would not change their minds.
Macklemore said in a statement Monday that although Sheeran is "a friend" it doesn't "change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened."

"He told me that the words 'Free Palestine' and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with. I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn't get past his public facing, 'I don't take sides.'"

During his set, Macklemore also displayed images of the devastation in Gaza while performing his song, Hind's Hall, about pro-Palestinian student protests, which references Hind Rajab, a child killed by Israeli forces in Gaza.
Amnesty International and a United Nations commission have said Israel's actions in Gaza constitute a genocide. Israel has denied these allegations.
'I have my personal views'
Billionaire Robert Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, was one of the people behind the call for Macklemore's removal, Sheeran confirmed.

Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel, said in a statement shared with CBC News Monday that his stadium would "not provide a platform for hate speech," stating Macklemore spread divisiveness through "selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas."
Backlash against Sheeran was swift online following Macklemore's exit, with critics slamming Sheeran's apolitical stance.

"I am not complicit," Sheeran said in his statement. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."
Sheeran said he refrains from weighing in on global events because his audience "includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."
But children's content creator Ms. Rachel, pointed out Tuesday the hypocrisy behind Sheeran participating in charity efforts for Ukraine while considering "Palestine too dangerous and political."

"Imagine being a Palestinian kid and seeing he did a concert for Ukraine but when over 20,000 Palestinian children are killed he's silent," she wrote in an Instagram post. Sheeran was one of the artists who performed at the "Concert for Ukraine" benefit concert in Birmingham, England, in 2022.

items: UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
Gaza doc NAZA earns 24.5-minute standing ovation at Venice premiere
In search for senior Hamas operative, Israeli raid on Gaza City camp kills 3 children

blocks.text: The situation has put a renewed spotlight on how artists who speak up about Gaza often face increased scrutiny. Actors have been dropped from projects or agencies for taking public pro-Palestinian stances.

Sheeran's tour will continue for its remaining eight dates without Macklemore. It ends its run at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Fla., a venue which hosted two Kanye West shows earlier this summer despite calls for cancellation over West's well-documented history of virulent antisemitic statements.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Cree chief says Canada blocking community efforts to take back control of child welfare
articles.summary: A Cree chief in Ontario is accusing the Carney government of blocking his community's effort to take back jurisdiction over child welfare by imposing financial terms on any handover of jurisdiction —…

image.caption: Taykwa Tagamou Chief Bruce Archibald says he started noticing 'barriers being put in place' as his community negotiated with Canada to implement its child well-being law. (Taykwa Tagamou Nation)

blocks.text: Indigenous·New

A Cree chief in Ontario is accusing the Carney government of blocking his community's effort to take back jurisdiction over child welfare by imposing financial terms on any handover of jurisdiction — a move that he fears could have an impact on other First Nations.
Taykwa Tagamou Nation leader concerned about Ottawa imposing funding reforms
A Cree chief in Ontario is accusing the Carney government of blocking his community's effort to reclaim jurisdiction over child welfare by imposing financial terms on any handover of authority.
Warning of potential serious consequences for other communities, Taykwa Tagamou Nation Chief Bruce Archibald told CBC Indigenous the situation has him feeling concerned, ignored and disheartened.
"They're not giving us self-determination," said Archibald, whose community is in northern Ontario, about 270 kilometres north of Sudbury.
"They're basically forcing the colonial way of how things were done in the past, which didn't work for our people."

Archibald's concerns arise from an Aug. 6 letter he got from Indigenous Services Canada, which informed him about "updates to Canada’s funding approach" for First Nations negotiating self-government over child and family services under federal law C-92.

The Trudeau-era legislation empowers First Nations to assert jurisdiction over child welfare by passing laws that supersede both federal and provincial authorities. The caveat is that First Nations must negotiate a "co-ordination agreement" to get any money to implement their laws.

In a ruling two years ago, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld and praised C-92 as "legislative reconciliation by means of an innovative statute." Sixteen co-ordination agreements have been signed since the law was passed in 2019, according to ISC.

items: Ottawa to begin $8.5B rollout for Ontario First Nations to reclaim child welfare
How one First Nation aims to break the cycle of trauma with new child 'well-being' law

blocks.text: After two years of talks, ISC's latest letter told Archibald that funding for on-reserve services "will align" with Canada's broader child welfare program reforms — which Archibald's community has not endorsed — and that "this funding approach will guide fiscal discussions" during negotiations for a co-ordination agreement.

The chief responded with a list of 10 detailed questions outlined in a six-page open letter to Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, arguing Canada's new approach raises issues that may impact every Indigenous government that has or intends to invoke C-92.
"The consequences are immediate and serious both for our children and our rights," Archibald wrote on Aug. 21.

Funding for First Nations laws must be sustainable and connected to each community's service model and children's needs, not subject to Canada's predetermined program constraints, the letter continued.
"Recognition of jurisdiction without the means to implement it is not reconciliation."
Negotiation as a 'Trojan horse'
Another chief in Alberta is echoing the concerns.
"Canada's actions and Canada's words are reminiscent of Trump's signature in pencil," wrote Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko in his own open letter to the minister.

"Statements that could be intercepted by the general public, and our membership, say one thing while your actions in court, in front of the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal, and in the details of the terms and conditions of your programs say another."
Jacko told CBC Indigenous he's worried Canada wants to tell First Nations that Ottawa knows best when it comes to the design of their laws.
"And that is not reconciliation, it might not even be legal," Jacko said via text message.

The chiefs are right to speak out, according to children's rights advocate Cindy Blackstock, who said Canada is at serious risk of undermining this once-touted promise of jurisdiction by offloading responsibility while retaining control of all the money.

"What it's saying is, 'We're going to make all the major decisions here, and there's very little room for you to actually be able to negotiate what's needed to give your law effect and protect your kids.' So it's negotiation almost as a Trojan horse," Blackstock said.

As executive director of the First Nations Child and Family Caring Society, Blackstock and the Assembly of First Nations have been successfully fighting at the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal since 2007 to end racial discrimination in funding the on-reserve child welfare system.

The complaint revealed how chronic underfunding fuelled the mass removal of First Nations kids from their families, with more youth being taken into government custody than at the height of the residential school system.

items: Canada's call to rejig tribunal panel on child welfare reform a delay 'tactic', says chief
Tribunal chair dismisses Canada's request to rejig panel on First Nations child welfare reform

blocks.text: Their work culminated in a $23.4-billion class-action settlement and a proposed $47.8-billion reform deal, though chiefs voted down the latter in 2024. Since then Ottawa began trying to sign regional agreements, concluding an $8.5 billion deal with First Nations in Ontario.
The future of the program's reform outside Ontario is unclear, however, as litigation continues.
Blackstock said the record shows "when Canada makes decisions without qualification and without oversight about funding, kids get hurt and taxpayers end up paying more money."

A spokesperson for Gull-Masty did not provide comment by publishing time. Her department's letter to Archibald concluded by saying ISC's funding approach remains guided by the principle that Indigenous peoples are best placed to make decisions about their children's well-being.
Archibald is unconvinced, however, since Taykwa Tagamou Nation did not support the reforms in Ontario that his agreement may now have to align with, he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.

articles.title: Criticism of LGBTQ+ raids in Turkey is growing
articles.summary: Several raids and arrests of LGBTQ+ persons in Turkey have triggered sharp criticism from numerous Turkish organizations — and also from Brussels.

image.caption: Police raids in Turkey targeted the LGBTQ+ community (file photo from Istanbul's Pride march in June 2022)Image: Kemal Aslan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Raids targeting LGBTQ+ activists and organizations took place in Turkey over the weekend. Several people were arrested by the Turkish authorities and many social media accounts were blocked. The Turkish government's actions have drawn sharp criticism from across the country and also from Brussels.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had announced the operation as part of the "Decade of Family and Population” scheme, a national strategy proclaimed in May 2025 that was to counter the drastic decline in the country's birthrate and strengthen the traditional, conservative family view in Turkey.
On Tuesday, Istanbul saw demonstrations again. Turkish LGBTQ+ associations emphasized in a joint declaration that it wasn't a crime to set up an association and advocate for rights.
"Freedom of assembly, freedom of opinion, protection of privacy and presumption of innocence apply to LGBTQ+ people as well," the declaration stated.
The LGBTQ+ community also received support from the women's movement. 120 women's rights organizations signed a joint declaration in which they criticized authoritarianism in Turkey.

"As women, we stand against the operations carried out in the name of 'keeping the family safe.' We know that the repression of our bodies, our lives, our identities, and our right to organize is part of the same authoritarian politics. Being [LGBTQ+] is not a crime! Organizing as [LGBTQ+] people is not a crime!", the organizations stated.
'The aim is criminalization'

The government is trying to criminalize the LGBTQ+ community, says Yildiz Taghizade of Women for Women's Human Rights (WWHR), an organization that co-signed the declaration. This criminalization did not just start with the operations of the past few days, but had already been going on for a few years, according to Taghizade.

"The aim is not only to target LGBTQ+ people, but to practically ban the LGBTQ+ community from engaging in politics, getting organized, claiming rights and showing presence in the public sphere," Taghizade said.
It was no coincidence that the operation came with the slogan "My family is safe."

"The government is trying to justify its actions by invoking the protection of families and children, but this narrative doesn't work. Because when we look at Turkey today and what is actually a factor of uncertainty for families, we come across very concrete issues such as poverty, the housing crisis, unemployment, care work [caring for and tending to relatives, the ed.] passed on to women, and male violence against women," Taghizade said.
Criticism from medical community, trade associations, politicians

Other organizations also criticized the government's actions. The Turkish Medical Association (TTB) described them as a violation of human rights, demanding an end to the politics of discrimination. It was unacceptable, it said, to treat gender identity and sexual orientation as a crime, take people out of their homes at night and block digital channels — all in the name of family protection and security.
The chairman of the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP), Erkan Bas, called for the immediate release of those arrested, arguing that the mere existence of LGBTQ+ persons was no crime.

But all those who did not share the government's views were "'called to order' by judiciary, truncheon and censorship. If they had their way, they'd love nothing more than to enshrine the criminal offense of 'being an opponent of the government' by law and sit back," Bas said.

blocks.caption: According to human rights activists, the criminalization of the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is nothing newImage: Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the name of 'national security'

The raids took place on Sunday in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir. Over the weekend, numerous websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, various organizations and activists were blocked. On the day of the raids, another 32 accounts were suspended. On the following day, the number of blocked accounts reached a total of more than 100.

Among those affected were Amnesty International Turkey, the left-leaning Evrensel newspaper, the Academics for Peace initiative, the Lawyers for Justice association, the women's rights organization Mor Dayanisma, the LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA).

The legal basis was a ruling by an Istanbul court announced on September 13. The Public Prosecutor's Office in Bakirkoy justified the suspensions by citing investigations into accounts that had spread "obscene content and LGBTQ+ propaganda."
According to several media outlets, the accounts were also blocked on grounds of "national security."
Critics called the move digital censorship.
Homosexuality not a criminal offense
Homosexual relationships are not a criminal offense in Turkey. However, the Turkish government had repeatedly referred to the LGBTQ+ community as a movement of "perverts."

Justice Minister Akin Gurlek had previously accused LGBTQ+ organizations of "promoting immorality." He declared in a social media post that "no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated."
EU: stigmatization incompatible with our values
The EU expressed concern as well.

Commission Spokesperson Christian Wigand pointed out that Turkey, as an EU accession candidate, "should promote and ensure respect for the human rights and dignity of all individuals, irrespective of their gender identity or sexual orientation." He added that "stigmatization and discrimination are contrary to the values of the union."
Emma Sinclair-Webb, Turkey director at Human Rights Watch, interpreted the arrests as proof of the government's intention to criminalize LGBTQ+ persons without enacting new laws.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election
articles.summary:
Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates

Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.

The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.

During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”
“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.
Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.

“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”

The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pits Moraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.

Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.

Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.

With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.

The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.

Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.

Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.

Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealed an explosive police dossier relating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. In one text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”

Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.

The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.

The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.

“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.
Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.

Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.
In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.

“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.
“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.

articles.title: Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat
articles.summary:
Prime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment Summit

Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic…
articles.byline: Leyland Cecco in Toronto and Jennifer Rankin in Strasbourg

blocks.text: Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”.

Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States.
Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation.

“The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies.

“Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”

While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country.

That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks.

Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels.

European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy.

Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence.

“Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.”

The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe.

But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force.

French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.”

Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain.
EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 when Ceta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn.

Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner.

“We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”
In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US.

Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.”

Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted.

Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed.
But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some.

Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for the Many vs the Money counter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects.

“Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.”
Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s office announced nearly C$500bn in new domestic investment.

“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”

articles.title: People from ethnic groups feel racial equality is worsening, UK study shows
articles.summary:
Nearly half of ethnic minority respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past year

Many Britons feel inequality is worsening and that discrimination has become more…

blocks.text: Many Britons feel inequality is worsening and that discrimination has become more common, according to a thinktank study.
The report by British Future has found that people across ethnic groups believe racial equality is worsening in Britain. One in six people are from ethnic minority backgrounds.
“Most ethnic minorities in Britain feel there was a positive change against racism in our lifetimes yet now fear that progress being reversed,” said the thinktank’s director, Sunder Katwala.

The research found nearly half of ethnic minority respondents had faced racial or nationality prejudice over the past year, with the problem notably higher among those aged 18 to 24. Prejudice was most often reported in public spaces, followed by on social media and in the workplace.

The research found that 62% of ethnic minority Britons saw racial inequality as a serious problem, a view supported by 57% of the white population. White respondents were less likely to see structural barriers in education, work and public services and more likely to believe minority communities received equal or preferential treatment.

The report, part of a three-year study funded by the Nuffield Foundation, found a growing polarisation over perceptions that minorities received preferential treatment. Among white respondents, 37% felt ethnic minorities were treated better than white British people, while 33% disagreed. Among ethnic minorities, 23% agreed and 48% disagreed.

The report found divisions by age and politics were deeper than those relating to ethnicity. “In both the white and ethnic minority surveys, gaps between rich and poor are seen as the most important divide impacting the UK,” the report said.
The research was driven by two online surveys of 2,009 white adults and 3,014 ethnic minority adults between 30 March and 29 April. It was supplemented by information from 12 focus groups.

The study noted a difference within ethnic minority attitudes, finding Black respondents were frequently more positive about the UK making progress on racial equality. By contrast, Bangladeshi and Pakistani heritage respondents were found to be more pessimistic, with heightened anxiety seemingly linked to the 2024 riots.
“Women, particularly ethnic minority women, are also more pessimistic than men throughout,” the report said.

The study found that ethnic minority Britons would like to see more effort to promote equal pay and tackle disparities in essential services and unequal treatment in media reporting. This was brought into “sharp focus”, the report said, by the intense media scrutiny on Jason Arday, a Cambridge University professor who died at his London home after allegations of plagiarism.
after newsletter promotion

The report, which criticised successive governments for having “rarely held” a sustained focus on race, laid out 10 recommendations for the government, including challenging zero-sum thinking, supporting grassroots activities and pushing the watchdog Ofcom on compliance against online racism.

Overall, it found low trust among political parties. While the Green party and Labour led narrowly in terms of treating people of different backgrounds fairly (+15 and +13 in net trust scores respectively), Reform UK had a net score of -31 (16% trust/47% distrust).
Katwala said leaders should “counter the sense of a zero-sum contest over race equality: that fairness for ethnic minorities comes at the expense of the white majority, or vice versa”.
He added: “The antidote to that is to pursue a broad and proactive fairness agenda – with the confidence and tools to tackle racism and discrimination where it is most needed.”

articles.title: Nigeria arrests alleged Mexican drug kingpin at international airport
articles.summary: Arturo Carrera Loaiza denies allegations he was involved in meth production, the Nigerian authorities say.

blocks.text: Image source, NDLEA
Arturo Carrera Loaiza has denied allegations that he was involved in methamphetamine production, Nigeria's drugs control authority says
BySimi Jolaoso
Africa correspondentReporting fromLagos
An alleged Mexican drug kingpin was arrested in Nigeria last month as he tried to leave the country, the drug enforcement authority has just revealed.
That arrest resulted in the discovery of a suspected industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory - the third such find allegedly linked to Mexicans in four months.

When Arturo Carrera Loaiza, 40, was detained at Lagos international airport, officials allegedly found digital images of him wearing what they believed to be a laboratory coat alongside equipment consistent with meth production.
The pictures' location data led officers to a property in Ebonyi state, where they said chemicals and drug-making equipment were found.

Loaiza has denied involvement in methamphetamine production and said he had been invited to Nigeria by a local contact for a restaurant business venture, according to a statement from the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA).

The agency's investigators found a CCTV memory card at the suspected laboratory in Ebonyi with footage from the property showing someone who looked like Loaiza wearing a blue laboratory coat. A Nigerian man was also identified directing people as they removed chemicals and equipment from the site.

NDLEA chairman Gen Mohamed Buba Marwa said further intelligence led officers to an isolated house in a neighbouring community, where they recovered chemicals, dehydrators, condensers, a reaction pot, weighing scales, mixers, drums, gas burners and a sieve containing traces of methamphetamine.
No estimate has yet been given for how much methamphetamine the alleged laboratory was capable of producing.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The NDLEA released pictures of some of the things investigators found after raiding a suspected laboratory

blocks.text: The NDLEA released pictures of some of the things investigators found after raiding a suspected laboratory

Investigators have alleged that Loaiza had recruited and brought a fellow Mexican to work at another suspected methamphetamine laboratory hidden in a forest in Oyo state, which was raided in June. Four Nigerians were also arrested after the raid.

A month earlier, NDLEA officers arrested three Mexican nationals and seven Nigerians at what the agency described as an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory hidden in a forest in another part of the country.
Marwa said the operations showed international criminal groups were attempting to establish drug-production facilities in Nigeria's forests and rural communities.
"Nigeria will not be allowed to become a haven for transnational drug cartels seeking to relocate their laboratories from other jurisdictions into our forests and rural communities", he said.
The NDLEA said its investigation into the network is ongoing, including into those it believes financed or helped facilitate the operations in Nigeria.

Unlike plant-based drugs, such as cocaine or heroin, which can only be grown and processed in certain places, a synthetic drug like meth can be produced anywhere with the right chemicals and expertise, making it easier for organised crime groups to quickly scale up production.
West Africa poses numerous attractive benefits to Mexican syndicates, starting with swathes of forested land which serves well for secluded production sites.

articles.title: Judge blocks Kennedy Center board from putting Trump's name on building, grounds in any way
articles.summary: A U.S. federal judge blocked the Kennedy Center on Tuesday from returning President Donald Trump's name to the performing arts venue, saying it would violate an earlier ruling that his name was…

image.caption: Visitors walk at The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts last Sunday. A judge ruled today that Donald Trump's name may not be added to the building or grounds in any way without the approval of Congress. (Jose Luis Magana/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A U.S. federal judge blocked the Kennedy Center on Tuesday from returning President Donald Trump's name to the performing arts venue, saying it would violate an earlier ruling that his name was illegally added to the building when an inscription on the facade was approved that acknowledged his role in renovating and restoring the building.
Judge rules no one can add memorials for Trump or anyone else without Congressional approval

A federal judge blocked the Kennedy Center on Tuesday from returning President Donald Trump's name to the performing arts venue, saying it would violate an earlier ruling that his name was illegally added to the building when an inscription on the facade was approved that acknowledged his role in renovating and restoring the building.
Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that, "Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."

The Trump-aligned board at the Kennedy Center voted in August to inscribe the president's name on the venue's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts restored and renovated by President Donald J. Trump."
And if the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, it had voted for another inscription to be added reading: "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would have also been renamed in Trump's honour, as part of the board's vote.
Months-long saga

Cooper ruled in May that only Congress can approve changes to the Kennedy Center's name. In an emergency hearing on the matter in August, the administration argued it was no longer attempting to rename the building and that the vote was simply a recognition of Trump's effort to secure money for much-needed renovations.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose wife sits on the Kennedy Center board, compared the move to the way hospitals and colleges recognize high-dollar donors.
But a lawyer for U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, argued the changes amounted to "déja vu" and violated Cooper's earlier ruling.
"The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else," Beatty said in a statement Tuesday.

"But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial. The court just rejected this proposal for the second time. This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop."

Tuesday's ruling is the latest twist in a months-old naming saga that first saw the board installing Trump's name above Kennedy's. After Cooper shot down that move, an elevated tarp was erected, which obscures Trump's name and most of Kennedy's.
Workers remove Trump's name from Kennedy Center

A more recent board proposal floated multiple options for getting Trump's name on the grounds, including inscriptions such as, "Renovation and endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund." Another option: "With gratitude for support from President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
'Turn down the temperature,' judge asks

The proposed board resolution was submitted to the court by Beatty as part of her effort to prevent the board from proceeding with the planned closure. It flatly states that "without such appropriate recognition," it's unlikely that Trump will financially support what the board says are desperately needed renovations.
Cooper, in his Tuesday ruling, tartly notes "the government plays word games."

In a scheduling hearing Tuesday morning, prior to the release of his ruling, Cooper appealed to lawyers for both sides to find a mediated solution to the fate of the performing arts centre. The centre's board has claimed the building is in desperate physical shape and the institution is desperately close to insolvency.
"Is it possible to turn down the temperature a little bit?" Cooper asked. "I'm not ordering you to do it, but there is a larger public interest here."
