articles.title: Historic mandate: Unionized health-care workers in Sask.'s biggest local vote 99% for strike
articles.summary: Unionized health-care workers with CUPE 5430, by far the biggest local in Saskatchewan, have voted 99 per cent in favour of job action in the province's largest strike vote. The workers have been…

image.caption: CUPE 5430 workers from from Prince Albert, Saskatoon, North Battleford, Yorkton, Estevan, Moosomin, and many rural communities gathered in North Battleford to demand fair wages and respect for frontline workers. (Jeremy Warren/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·Updated

Unionized health-care workers with CUPE 5430, by far the biggest local in Saskatchewan, have voted 99 per cent in favour of job action in the province's largest strike vote. The workers have been without a contract since March 2023, and have gone more than 4½ years without a pay raise. They're asking for higher wages and safer staffing.
More than 13,000 members of CUPE 5430 secure province's largest strike vote
Health-care workers represented by CUPE 5430 have voted 99 per cent in favour of job action in the largest strike vote in Saskatchewan's history

Between Sept. 8/14, 13,358 members of the Canadian Union of Public Employees local, which represents nearly half of all unionized health-care employees in support, long-term care, and administrative roles in the province, cast ballots, securing a decisive strike mandate.

“This vote is about respect, fair wages, and safe staffing. It is about having a health-care system where people can build a career, support a family, and actually stay in their community,” CUPE national president Mark Hancock said in a statement.

The results were announced Tuesday morning in North Battleford, where streets were flooded with pink banners and calls to action. The rally was held outside of Minister of Health Jeremy Cockrill's constituency office.
The union represents 14,000 health-care workers who say they've been without a contract since March 31, 2023 and have gone more than 4½ years without a wage increase.
“It’s shameful how long the minister of health has allowed our members to go without a wage increase or the respect they deserve,” Bashir Jalloh, president of CUPE 5430, said in a statement.

CUPE says the latest employer offer from the Saskatchewan Association of Health Organizations would move health-care workers farther from their homes, leave its members earning less than with the same role in Western Canada, and would not reflect the rise in the cost of living.
Opposition NDP Leader Carla Beck expressed her support for the workers in a statement on Tuesday.
"The very people on the front lines who have kept our health-care system running against all odds haven’t had a contract in four years," Beck said .
"We will continue to fight for fair contracts, competitive wages and a serious plan to recruit and retain the people our health-care system depends on."
CBC News has reached out to the provincial government and is awaiting a response.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Halyna Mihalik is a journalist and weather specialist for CBC Saskatchewan. She holds a degree in journalism from the University of Regina. Halyna enjoys stories about advocacy, local politics and rural communities. Send Halyna news tips at halyna.mihalik@cbc.ca

articles.title: South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg
articles.summary: Police have not linked the deaths to a serial killer but are investigating this possibility.

blocks.text: South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings of several women in and around the town of Kempton Park, north-east of Johannesburg, over the last two months.
Another body was discovered on Tuesday morning and police say their investigation now includes the deaths of seven women most of whom have been found either partially or fully naked.
"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," the president said.
Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.
"[It] could be that it's a copycat crime that is happening right here but so far, no linkages as yet," police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said.
One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody.
So far only two of the seven women have been identified.
On Monday, police said that one of them was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a runner whose disappearance last week sparked a frantic and public search for her.

President Ramaphosa said he had directed that the cases be prioritised: "Our law enforcement agencies are working urgently to establish the facts, keep communities safe and bring the perpetrator or perpetrators to justice."
South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.
The discoveries of the bodies have sparked outrage and fear across the country, with many criticising the authorities for failing to adequately protect women.

Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after her body was discovered on Saturday. It was the 38-year-old's young daughter who raised the alarm about her disappearance after she failed to return from her daily run last Wednesday.
The body of the first woman was found in mid-July, the second in late August - the others were discovered this month, two in the last two days.
On Tuesday, police said that the body of woman found on 7 September in a town nearby Kempton Park was also being included - bringing the total number of bodies being investigated to seven.

"After noticing that there are bodies being picked up, we went back to our police stations… and unfortunately it came to light that a body of a female in her late 20s was observed in a river next to a mall," Maj-Gen Fred Kekana, acting police chief for Gauteng province, said at a briefing.
Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area - which is by South Africa's main international airport - to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".
South Africa's Commission for Gender Equality urged residents of Kempton Park to work with the police to find the perpetrators.
"These deaths are indicative that women in South Africa continue to face environments in which their ordinary freedom of movement can become a matter of life and death," it said.

"Women should be able to run, walk to work, use public transport, return home, visit friends and participate in community life without having to calculate whether an ordinary activity could place their lives at risk."

articles.title: Houthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in Yemen
articles.summary:
Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait

Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across…

blocks.text: Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across Yemen led the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced.

As oil prices remained well over $100 (£74) a barrel, Qatar warned of a catastrophe if the Iran-backed Houthi militants won full control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea dominating the key naval route to Asia. The strait has become vital to Saudi crude oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

An emergency meeting of the UN security council in New York heard repeated calls for Houthi forces to show restraint. In a sign that Iran is still seeking a broader solution, its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, travelled to Beijing to discuss China’s possible role in solving the related strait of Hormuz dispute.

The future of the strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime and which the US and Iran are now mounting blockades of – is the diplomatic key to unlocking the conflict between the US and Iran, and to a lesser extent the related conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Oil prices rose sharply after Reuters reported that ⁠loadings at Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Red ⁠Sea port ​of Yanbu had ⁠been suspended, citing shipping industry sources. The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose nearly 3% to $108 a barrell.

Prices have risen this week after the ⁠world’s biggest ​crude ‌oil exporter, Saudi Aramco, ‌closed its East-West ‌pipeline due to an attack by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Aramco had increased ⁠use of the ​Yanbu terminal since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.

blocks.caption: A screen grab from a Houthi video released earlier this week purporting to show militants on an armoured personnel carrier during an offensive near Yemen’s Red Sea city of Mocha. Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPA

blocks.text: Qatar, acting as a mediator in the Iran war, is still trying to revive a postponed meeting planned for Monday between Iran and most Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The planned talks in Oman were delayed at the insistence of Saudi Arabia in protest at what it regarded as Iranian-inspired Houthis attacks on Saudi cities.

The Houthis had claimed responsibility for a new “large-scale” attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” against King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, southern Saudi Arabia, on Monday. Air raid sirens were activated in six governorates including Jeddah on Tuesday. The warnings were lifted relatively quickly, but reflect an unprecedented new state of insecurity across Saudi Arabia.

The Oman meeting had been organised with the intention of reaching a regional agreement on an authorised route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, spoke with Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday amid US concern that Oman will cede excessive control of the waterway to Iran.

blocks.caption: A shipping vessel anchored off Yemen's coast in the Bab al-Mandab strait, pictured earlier this week. Qatar has warned a blockade of the waterway could have a significant impact on world trade. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The prospect of the strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab strait both being under the long-term control of anti-western forces would be a significant strategic reversal for the US and Europe.

Qatar foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi told reporters: “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandab into that equation.” He added that the closure of the southern entrance to the Red Sea would be “catastrophic for the entire world … and we are already seeing the consequences”.

The strait of Hormuz remained largely closed for commercial traffic on Monday and Tuesday, with a Qatar ship disabled by Iran and only four ships recorded as crossing the strait on Monday compared with a prewar average of about 130 ships.

So far Donald Trump has rejected Saudi pleas to join the fight to drive the Houthis back north up the coast of the Red Sea. Houthi leaders have also spoken to the US vice-president, JD Vance, reassuring the White House that their forces are seeking only to hinder Saudi-owned shipping, and that their overall goal is to end what they regard as a Saudi blockade of Houthi-controlled areas. The Houthis have signed a ceasefire agreement with the US, but are still subject to US sanctions.

The UK is unlikely to offer direct military, as opposed to political, support to Saudi Arabia unless there is a clear instruction from Washington to do so. Inside Yemen the next military engagement is likely to focus on the city of Marib where Saudi air raids have been trying to weaken Houthi formations.
Yemen’s ministry of foreign affairs and expatriates said: “If the world wants stability and calm in the region, it must tell the Saudis: enough interference in the Yemeni affair.”

Rather than giving direct military help, western governments are providing intelligence, including targeting advice as well as strategic help in the task of trying to integrate the disparate anti-Houthi forces in Yemen.

But Maysaa Shuja al-Deen from the Sana’a Centre said: “Any renewed military campaign must be accompanied by a serious reassessment of past mistakes, meaningful reform of the Yemeni government, stronger coordination among anti-Houthi forces, and a more balanced relationship between Yemeni actors and their regional partners.”

She added: “In many cases, the Saudis choose Yemeni figures who are weak, easily manipulated, and willing to follow their orders. If they instead chose competent, strong actors who could implement a shared agenda, they would also gain the respect of other competent Yemeni figures.

“This approach contrasts with the Iranian and Emirati models, which have generally given their local allies more room to manoeuvre while building relationships around specific objectives and clearer mandates.”

Due to the weakness of the UN-recognised government in Yemen, various militias with different ideological or regional loyalties operate alongside the official national army. Together on paper, the number of anti-Houthi forces could reach as many as 500,000 troops but in practice not all these forces cooperate or are willing to fight outside their area.

Saudi Arabia gives support to Yemen’s Homeland Shield Forces while the United Arab Emirates had backed both the 80,000-strong Southern Transitional Council’s Giants Brigade and a 20,000-strong force led by Tareq Saleh. But the UAE, after backing separatist forces in the south, has now pulled out of Yemen.

articles.title: ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors
articles.summary:
Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason

Film industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed…
articles.byline: Catherine Shoard in London and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Film industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”.

NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.
The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025.

The 80-minute documentary won the special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.

blocks.caption: Jonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and James Wilson in Venice.  Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.

Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage.

“Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.”

Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.”
They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”.

NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at the Bologna film festival tonight, before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month.

Tricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”

Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”

Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position came under threat after several prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stage at the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including from Israel, rallied around Tuttle.

blocks.caption: Laura Poitras in Venice last week.  Photograph: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers have signed a petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally.
Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz.
The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor.

“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.
So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so.
Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials.

“The facts about the mass killing of civilians in NAZA have been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA.

blocks.caption: No Other Land co-director Hamdan Ballal with his Oscar in March 2025, shortly after he had been attacked by Israeli settlers at his home, in his village of Susya in the occupied West Bank.  Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: She called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government.
“Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists in Gaza and has normalised the murder of journalists.”

Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.”

British film industry veterans offering their support include director Richard Eyre, who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”.

Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.
Additional reporting by Andrew Pulver and Philip Oltermann

articles.title: High fuel prices challenge the German government
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to provide relief to motorists. But exactly how this is to happen remains unclear.

image.caption: In Germany, a liter of fuel now costs about three euros — that is over €11 for a gallonImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter.

Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage. On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office.

Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany.
German government expresses 'great and growing' concern

But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz(CDU) has promised. "Many people who need their cars every day, have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action." However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined. "We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," he assured.

But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, Deputy Government Spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices. "So, it's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer explained.

The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before. "From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman.
Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices
Price gouging at the pumps

Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly. "They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper. He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it.

However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt. "Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer.
A new fuel rebate or tax relief?

Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter.

"We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network. But she says that won't be possible again. "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment." As an alternative, the Conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments.

But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crisis situations. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump.
Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices
AfD standing to profit from bickering

But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%.

The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%.

"There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin. She criticized the federal government's inaction. "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration."
A solution from the EU?

According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday.

Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level. "Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the finance ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin.

"Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Knobloch: 'It is a very dangerous situation at the moment'
articles.summary: Charlotte Knobloch survived the Holocaust by passing as the daughter of non-Jewish farmers. She recently spoke with DW to express her shock following the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.

image.caption: Charlotte Knobloch is appalled by the AfD's election victory in Saxony-AnhaltImage: DW

blocks.text: Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria, is dismayed by the electoral victory of the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Knobloch told DW that there were now once again a number of Jewish people who, in the wake of such events, were considering leaving Germany.
It took decades, Knobloch said, for Jews in Germany to regain trust in the country after the Holocaust. That had ultimately been achieved.

But now, there were great fears again: "That is, in sum, the biggest problem for me, because we successfully tried to rebuild the Jewish communities after 1945, to give the Jewish people a home again, which they hadn't had for a long time..."

blocks.caption: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund's (center) party received nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Standing up against the far-right 'requires some courage'

In Saxony-Anhalt's September 6 state election, the AfD, classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, had received almost 44% of the vote. Although AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority, he still has a good chance of becoming the next premier in the state parliament, meaning he'd become the first head of a state government from a right-wing extremist party after World War II.

Charlotte Knobloch issues a stark warning: "We can't allow any of those people to become state premier. It is a very dangerous situation at the moment, in my view. I hope the other parties realize that and stand up against it. They can do it. It requires some courage of course."

blocks.caption: The nonagenarian, seen here with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is still present in Germany's public lifeImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Charlotte Knobloch, who is almost 94 years old, is one of the most prominent and well-known representatives of Jewish life in Germany and one of the last surviving witnesses of Nazi dictatorship between 1933 and 1945. Born in 1932, she was initially raised by her grandmother, who was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942 and died there. A family acquaintance saved the girl by accommodating her on her farm in Middle Franconia and passing her off as her own child.
Knobloch: 'danger looming' today did not exist like this 10 years ago

Asked by DW when and how she still thinks about that horrible era, she said: "There were times when this happened only rarely. When it was mentioned by the media from time to time, but not permanently. These days, I wake up thinking about it, and I also go to bed thinking about it."

blocks.caption: Knobloch spoke to DW correspondent Tina Gerhäusser in MunichImage: DW

blocks.text: Knobloch served as vice president of the World Jewish Congress between 2005 and 2013, and as president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany from 2006 to 2010. For a long time, she has been warning against growing antisemitism in Germany. However, she herself did not foresee the rise of far-right extremist parties like the AfD.
"There's a danger looming that did not exist in this form ten years ago," Knobloch said. "There have always been Nazis, there have always been Jew haters, but not in the way as it's the case today."

In Knobloch's view, the established parties have up to now failed to speak out decisively against the AfD: "Today's political parties must jointly, not alone, address the issue. I still see a chance here, that people will at least be willing to listen and discuss it. And that's very, very important."
Young people need to be included in the conversation
Politicians have to speak to young people in particular more intensively and address their fears, which isn't happening enough, Knobloch says.

"There's talk about it, but there is no real discussion, because young people are naturally afraid that what they say will become public. What I want to say is, we'll have to find ways to bring young people back into the fold."

Last week, Knobloch received death threats. On Thursday, a witness discovered the scrawled threats on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the English Garden in Munich and informed the police, according to a police headquarters statement. Knobloch subsequently canceled her attendance at an event. The threats were directly linked to the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a spokeswoman said in response to a query from the dpa news agency.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: South Africa now probing deaths of 8 women near Johannesburg
articles.summary: Police have warned women to take extra care in parts of Johannesburg as similarities between at least eight deaths fuel fears that the cases could be connected.

image.caption: South African police have warned women to exercise caution amid fears the cases could be connectedImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South African police are now investigating the deaths of eight women found east of Johannesburg over the past two months, after another body was discovered on Tuesday and an earlier case was added to the widening investigation.

The deaths have raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers could be operating in the area. Several of the victims were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of sexual violence.
"The challenge is ahead of us and the deaths of these young women must not be in vain," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia told reporters following a meeting to discuss the killings.
What have South African police said?
The South African Police Service (SAPS) has issued a public warning urging women to exercise caution when jogging or carrying out similar activities in the area.

"While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.
President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday ordered police to prioritize the investigations, saying the deaths were causing "fear and uncertainty" and promising that "no stone will be left unturned."
What do we know about the victims?
The bodies have been discovered at several locations across the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.
Police said the first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.
A 32-year-old woman was found partially clothed on August 24. Another woman's body, found in a river near the Tembisa township on September 7, has now been included in the wider investigation.
One of the victims, aged 38, disappeared after leaving her eight-year-old daughter at home to go jogging. Her partially clothed body was found behind a hotel on September 12.
Another woman's body was discovered in the Kwa-Thema township on Tuesday.
Why are women still unsafe in South Africa?
Are South African police investigating a serial killer?
Police have not confirmed that the deaths are the work of a serial killer.
"We are still investigating whether we are dealing with one perpetrator or a group of men that are behind the murders of these women," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.
Police said similarities between the cases were sufficiently concerning to issue a public warning, including advising women to exercise caution while jogging in the area.
How serious is violence against women in South Africa?
Violence against women is a longstanding problem in South Africa. UN Women says the country has some of the world's highest rates of violence against women and children.
Around one in three South African women experience physical or sexual violence during their lifetime, according to the United Nations.
The killings come as violent crime remains a major source of public concern ahead of municipal elections in November.

articles.title: Why do authoritarian regimes target the LGBTQ+ community?
articles.summary: A recent crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is symptomatic of a wider rights regression, according to experts. It's worse under authoritarian regimes, but why is it such a popular policy for…

image.caption: Members of the Turkish LGBTQ+ community were targeted by authorities, and they are not alone (file photo from June 27, 2026)Image: Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Raids on gay bars and homes, hundreds of arrests and rhetoric about state responsibility to "protect families and children." Turkey's latest crackdown on LGBTQ+ communities is not such an outlier.
"It's not uncommon, we've seen it before," Dr Koen Slootmaeckers, from the international politics department at City St George's, University of London, told DW.

"Turkey's been doing this for a while, but it seems like a much higher intensity," Slootmaeckers said. "We've seen it in different places too. I think what we are seeing with the rise of the far right is a crackdown on anything that looks different. It's really about an us versus them narrative and a reinforcing of 'traditional family values.'"

Those values were cited by Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek after the weekend's crackdown: "As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!"
Attack on LGBTQ+ rights accelerating

The reference to protecting children from harm is also typical of authoritarian government actions against LGBTQ+ communities on a wider scale, added Slootmaeckers, whose work often focuses on gender and sexuality policy.
Slovakia debates marriage equality
"They're trying to bring back discourses around paedophilia and homosexuality being intertwined. It's not always direct but there is a definite tendency."
Sentiments such as those expressed by Gurlek have become increasingly normalized of late, according to a 2026 report from South Africa-based civil rights nonprofit, Civicus.
"Women's and LGBTQI+ people's rights are under the most coordinated and wide-ranging attack in decades," the report reads.

It adds that "The USA has set the global narrative" under President Donald Trump and points to the recent criminalizing of same sex relationships in Burkina Faso and Trinidad and Tobago among its evidence of rights regressions.
While the methods of oppression vary, Slootmaeckers said the underlying reasons are often, at least partly, opportunistic rather than ideological.
Scapegoating a common strategy

"In authoritarian regimes, as we've seen in Hungary and Poland in the past, there is often a tendency when political power becomes threatened to use these issues as an easy way to scapegoat and distract — by claiming that LGBT people are a threat to the social fabric because they challenge family and the future of the nation, so to speak. It's an easy way of creating a scapegoat and often distracting from other crises," he said.

Turkey was ranked 47 of 49 countries in the annual Rainbow Map compiled by the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association. Countries ranking lower means laws and polcies there aren't LGBTQ+ friendly.
But, for many observers it is countries that are dropping in such rankings that are troubling. One of those is Serbia. It has gradually slipped to 29th spot, below the European average.

Groups associated with President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, have been linked to a wave of violence against an LGBTQ+ community which feels increasingly marginalized. A recent survey from the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights found that 80% of respondents said they avoided holding the hand of their partner in public, for example.
EU hopes put up 'guardrails' amid violence in Serbia
While Serbia is not one of the 64 countries around the world which have laws that criminalize homosexuality, some of which carry the death penalty, there is a definite sense of unease.

"In the Balkans, most countries still want to join the EU, so there ar some kind of guardrails on how far they can go. But we see things like [Vucic] trying to cancel [pan-European LGBTQ+ event] EuroPride in 2022 in Belgrade when he felt threatened surrounding Kosovo," said Slootmaeckers, who wrote a book called "Coming in: Sexual politics and EU accession in Serbia" in 2025.
Will Hungary's new govt. bring real change on LGBTQ+ rights?

"We can see this tactic of pandering to family values and then positioning LGBT rights as an expensive frivolity, as a means of redirecting the attention of people from the actual political problem," Slootmaeckers said.

"I think across Europe, not just in the Balkans or Eastern Europe, we see the return of homophobia and transphobia. We see a culture where anything considered 'out there' is threatened and it becomes normalized that we can exclude people again."

Exclusion appears to be the word for many in the Turkish LGBTQ+ community, with rights group Kaos GL, whose offices were raided, calling the latest crackdown "state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society."
For those living under authoritarian regimes elsewhere, the threat of similar scenes continues to loom.

articles.summary: U.S. prosecutors said Tuesday that they won't pursue the death penalty for Nick Reiner in the killings of his parents, actor-director Rob Reiner and his wife Michele Singer Reiner, who were stabbed…

image.caption: Nick Reiner, charged with two counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, is seen here during his arraignment on murder charges in Los Angeles in February. (Chris Torres/Pool for Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

U.S. prosecutors said Tuesday that they won't pursue the death penalty for Nick Reiner in the killings of his parents, actor-director Rob Reiner and his wife Michele Singer Reiner, who were stabbed at their Los Angeles home late last year.
Trial unlikely before 2027, says Los Angeles County district attorney
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 12:03 PM EDT | Last Updated: 9 minutes ago

Nick Reiner, 32, was charged with first-degree murder on Dec. 16, two days after the stunning killings of the couple. A grand jury allegation from this summer said he was lying in wait before killing them.

Special circumstances in the allegations against Nick Reiner made him eligible for the death penalty, but Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said the issue would be deferred while his office decided whether to pursue it. Those circumstances include multiple killings and the use of a dangerous weapon, a knife.
Hochman said his office did a thorough review, including speaking Rob and Michele Reiner's families and evaluating mitigating factors in Nick Reiner's favour, before reaching its decision.
Hochman said the maximum sentence Reiner will be eligible to receive if convicted will be life without the possibility of parole.

Nick Reiner has not entered a plea after two court hearings, but his former defence attorney Alan Jackson said adamantly, shortly after resigning from the case, that "pursuant to the laws of California, Nick Reiner is not guilty of murder."
Jackson had to withdraw for undisclosed reasons that he said were beyond his and the client's control, and a public defender took over for him.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
articles.summary: The star says tour promoters took the decision, after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian statements on stage.

blocks.text: Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.
The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.
His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.

In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.
"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."
The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.
"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."
He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.
"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.

"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."
The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.
Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.

The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.
The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.
Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.
In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts.

Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".

"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.
However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.

Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."
In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.

"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.

He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

“My job there is to convince our counterparts that after stealing $1 billion from a very poor country like the Philippines, he does not deserve asylum and he needs to be brought back to the Philippines,” Remulla said yesterday.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla will block former lawmaker Zaldy Co’s asylum bid in his upcoming visit to France.
Remulla will meet with the International Criminal Police Organization in Lyon to follow through on the government’s request for an Interpol red notice alert.
He is expected to fly to France in the next 10 days.
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla will also go to France, but the interior chief said they have different missions.
Co and former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s co-accused in a P7.4-billion plunder case, Joselyn Sereno and Felicito Guevarra, are still in the Philippines and remain at large, Remulla said.
Roque on asylum denial: Fake news
Former presidential spokesman Harry Roque denied yesterday that his application for asylum in Europe had been denied, as announced by Remulla.
“It is absolutely fake news. Asylum procedures worldwide are considered strictly confidential,” Roque told “Storycon” on One News.
Malacañang maintains that Roque’s request for asylum has no basis.

“This is not political persecution. Records, evidence speak for themselves,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said, citing human trafficking, land grabbing and tax evasion cases filed against Roque.
Remulla said the government needs to secure an Interpol red notice to arrest Roque.
Speaking from Vienna, Roque said his asylum application had been submitted for resolution and he has yet to receive a decision from Austrian authorities. — Helen Flores, Mark Ernest Villeza

articles.title: Ferry June Aster captain surfaces, faces PCG
articles.summary: Five days after a fire struck the passenger and cargo ship MV June Aster, its captain, Roel Sarmiento, showed up at the Philippine Coast Guard’s Palawan field office yesterday to shed light on…

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 12:00am

In a statement, PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said Sarmiento voluntarily appeared and was accompanied by Dindo Macalinao, human resources generalist of Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., which owns the June Aster.
PCG photo

MANILA, Philippines — Five days after a fire struck the passenger and cargo ship MV June Aster, its captain, Roel Sarmiento, showed up at the Philippine Coast Guard’s Palawan field office yesterday to shed light on the incident that claimed 76 lives.

Cayabyab said investigators are scheduled to interview the ship captain regarding the circumstances surrounding the incident, including his whereabouts following the fire and what transpired before his appearance on Sept. 14.
Based on the latest figures, joint authorities have accounted for 44 survivors, including Sarmiento, with 76 bodies recovered and 12 persons still remain missing.
The ticket manifest listed 134 passengers, including two who later reported that they did not board the vessel, bringing the total number of passengers to 132.
On Sept. 9, the June Aster was sailing to Coron from the Port of Manila when, at 6:45 p.m., an explosion was heard in the cargo hold, followed by thick smoke and fire.
The vessel remains grounded at 7.6 nautical miles northeast of Barangay Turda, Coron, Palawan.
Many of the 76 fatalities were found in the accommodation and cabin areas of the 53-meter-long steel-hulled ship.

Authorities in Coron have temporarily buried 41 unidentified bodies out of the 76 fatalities while waiting for results of DNA testing being done by the Philippine National Police (PNP), an ABS-CBN report said.
The mass grave would be at the San Nicolas Public Cemetery.

Police Lt. Col. Richard Allan Mangalip, commander of the Disaster Victim Identification Unit of the MIMAROPA Regional Forensic Unit, on Sunday said it might take them weeks or even months to complete the identification of the bodies.
The PNP has sent additional forensic experts to Palawan to assist in the identification of the bodies.

articles.title: Congress urged: Permanently remove system loss charge
articles.summary: It’s now the turn of Congress – the Senate and the House of Representatives – to do its part in giving relief to consumers burdened by high electricity bills, by passing a law that…

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 12:00am

“The Bureau of Internal Revenue did its part. Congress must now do ours,” Yap said, referring to Revenue Memorandum Circular 97-2026 removing the 12 percent value-added tax on allowable system loss charge.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — It’s now the turn of Congress – the Senate and the House of Representatives – to do its part in giving relief to consumers burdened by high electricity bills, by passing a law that would permanently remove the system loss charges, Rep. Arthur Yap of Murang Kuryente party-list said yesterday.

“Look at what this took. No new agency. No new appropriation. A few weeks from the President’s instruction to a signed circular. Commissioner Charlito Martin Mendoza found the legal basis and used it. That is the benchmark, and Congress will be measured against it,” Yap, vice chairman of the House committee on energy, noted.

In a statement, Yap expressed full belief that the House leadership under Speaker Faustino Dy III and House energy committee chairman Rep. Jose Alvarez (Palawan) is “ready to match the executive and pass the law.”

“Remove the system loss charge from consumer bills entirely – technical and non-technical losses, not just the tax on top. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin has confirmed that is what the President asked for,” Yap pointed out.
The administration lawmaker said the Department of Energy has already sent lawmakers “draft measures to repeal Section 43(F) and bills to the same end are pending in the House.”

In a statement, Dy praised the BIR for removing the VAT on system loss charge. “Every peso we can remove from the electricity bill matters, especially to families already stretching their budgets for food, education, transportation and other basic needs,” the congressman from the sixth district of Isabela province said.

Opposition Rep. Leila de Lima also commended the BIR and called for colleagues’ support for House Bill 10677, which prohibits distribution utilities from imposing any cost caused by non-technical loss, whether through system loss or any other charge or fee.

“We welcome the BIR’s removal of VAT on the allowable system loss charge in electricity bills. Filipinos deserve more. We should not be content on the small reduction of costly power bills. They should stop collecting fees for services that have not been felt by consumers,” she said.
Meanwhile, Malacañang said the government will rely on efficient tax administration and existing tax measures to offset the revenue losses arising from the removal of the VAT on system loss charge.
“There are no discussions on the imposition of new taxes, because it’s not the concern of the government,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing.

“There are many ways the BIR and the DOF can raise funds to cover the P10-billion revenue loss: efficient tax administration, proper tax collection and reforms on VAT on digital service,” Castro said.
She also cited the CREATE More Act, which aims to attract more investments, as another measure to increase the government’s tax revenues. — Helen Flores

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has urged the judges handling the crimes against humanity case against former president Rodrigo Duterte to declare him fit to stand trial.

In a seven-page request made public on Monday night, ICC acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang argued that Duterte should be declared fit for trial based on the reports submitted by the panel of medical experts tapped to examine the former president.

articles.title: P16.03 billion for ARAL sought to sustain PISA gains
articles.summary: Education Secretary Sonny Angara on Tuesday urged Congress to approve a P16.03-billion supplemental budget for 2027 to sustain the gains made by Filipino students in the 2025 Program for…

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 12:00am
Students attend their classes after their holiday break at Araullo High School in Manila on Jan. 4, 2024.
The STAR / Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — Education Secretary Sonny Angara on Tuesday urged Congress to approve a P16.03-billion supplemental budget for 2027 to sustain the gains made by Filipino students in the 2025 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) through the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program.
Angara said Filipino students’ scores in reading, mathematics and science improved significantly in PISA 2025 amid the implementation of ARAL.

“These latest PISA gains are an encouraging checkpoint, not the finish line. They prove that system-wide progress is possible, but they also highlight why sustained funding and structured interventions like ARAL remain non-negotiable,” Angara said.

The proposed additional P16.03 billion for next year would cover remediation consultations, learning resources, training of DepEd tutors, the ARAL Summer Program, compensation for external tutors and teaching overload honoraria.

“To sustain this momentum, the Department of Education (DepEd) is appealing to lawmakers to restore funding for the ARAL Program under its Fiscal Year 2027 budget after the initiative received zero allocation in the National Expenditure Program,” DepEd said.
During school year 2025-2026, ARAL formed part of DepEd’s intensified learning recovery efforts by providing targeted support to struggling learners.
The program helped reduce the number of struggling readers nationwide from 6.7 million to 2.2 million while increasing grade-level reading readiness from 3.3 million to 5.8 million learners.
The Philippines recorded a mean score of 373 in science, 371 in mathematics and 367 in reading in PISA 2025, up by 17, 16 and 20 points, respectively, from the country’s 2022 results.

articles.title: Marcos to ASEAN: Strengthen cooperation on disasters

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos has called on members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to strengthen cooperation on disaster resilience as risks confronting the region are “changing faster than ever.”

At yesterday’s ASEAN ministerial conference on disaster resilience at the Conrad Hotel in Pasay, Marcos highlighted initiatives to strengthen disaster preparedness, early warning systems and anticipatory action while improving coordination and mutual assistance among member-states.

Initiatives include the proposed Manila-ASEAN Strategic Protocol for Emergency and Comprehensive Transformation,- or Manila-Aspect Framework, which seeks to boost disaster response and improve coordination in ASEAN.
Marcos cited the government’s enactment of the Declaration of State of Imminent Disaster Act, which allows the state to mobilize resources in anticipation of highly probable and imminent disasters.

Gaps among ASEAN members include differences in knowledge, communication, hazard detection and monitoring capabilities, Marcos said, citing the 2024 report “Strengthening ASEAN Multi-Hazard End-to-End Early Warning System for Natural Disasters.”
The Sept. 15 to 16 conference will conclude with the Manila Declaration on Advancing ASEAN’s Disaster Resilience Agenda Towards 2030 and Beyond. — Pia Lee-Brago

articles.title: ‘Blanket class suspensions deepen literacy challenges’
articles.summary: Blanket class suspensions could deepen literacy challenges as schools continue to lose significant teaching days to weather-related hazards, a new study released by the Second Congressional…

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Blanket class suspensions could deepen literacy challenges as schools continue to lose significant teaching days to weather-related hazards, a new study released by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2) warned.

The study – “The Hidden Cost of Class Suspensions: How Blanket Orders Could Deepen the Learning Crisis” – found that blanket class suspension orders may be imposing a learning cost even on schools that are not directly exposed to unsafe conditions.
The report noted that the increasing number of class suspensions has become a routine feature of the school calendar.
In school year 2025-2026, a typical public elementary school forfeited about 20 teaching days to hazard-related suspensions.
“That is roughly one in every 10 days in the official school calendar,” the report said.
More recently, from Aug. 1 to Sept. 15, 12 out of 28 class days were canceled in the National Capital Region and several provinces.
“This is already 43 percent of total class days in that period and has significantly affected the delivery of learning for Term 1,” the report said.
According to the study, class cancellations in the past four school years have compounded learning loss from two years of school closures during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“Unless we all take this issue very seriously, efforts of DepEd to improve learning outcomes would not progress simply because children are not in school when they should be,” the study said.
Weather-driven hazards, including typhoons, monsoon rains and shearlines, coupled with excessive risk aversion, account for the bulk of school day suspensions.

Previous EDCOM2 findings highlighted the wide range of disruptions across the country, with regions such as the Negros Island Region, Region 1 and Region 5 experiencing much higher numbers of class suspensions than some areas in Mindanao.

Lanao del Sur, Davao del Norte and Tagum City each recorded only one class suspension, while seven school division offices in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao had no recorded suspensions.
The report said more granular decisions could make class suspensions more effective.

“Each and every class cancellation should be accounted for, and the cost and benefit of such decisions should be considered. Given the volatility of weather, the government needs to also assess accuracy of forecasts against actual weather to further improve forecasting technique,” the report said.

It noted that national and local governments should recognize that school heads have better information about conditions in their respective areas and can make more balanced decisions on whether to suspend or resume classes.

“Surrendering close to a month each year to hazards, even when warranted by circumstances, is already a large setback for a system still working hard to ensure that every learner can read by Grade 3. Against this backdrop, sparing the rest of our schools from suspensions when unnecessary should not be a choice, but an imperative,” it added.

The study was authored by University of Auckland PhD Economics candidate Tristan Piosang, EDCOM2 executive director Karol Mark Yee and former National Economic and Development Authority secretary Karl Kendrick Chua.
Damage
Aside from further worsening the country’s learning crisis, the continuing weather disturbances have also caused extensive damage to school facilities.

The DepEd estimated that P8.267 billion will be needed for response and recovery following the impact of the southwest monsoon and Tropical Cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Obet and Pilandok since Aug. 3.
In its final report, the DepEd Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Service said 2,537 schools reported damage involving 11,995 classrooms.
Of these, 2,362 classrooms were destroyed, 2,550 sustained major damage and 7,083 had minor damage.

“Correspondingly, the estimated response and recovery requirements have reached approximately P8.267 billion, comprising P74.908 million for clean-up and clearing operations, P347.067 million for minor repairs, P1.275 billion for major repairs and P4.905 billion for reconstruction. These figures reflect the continuing receipt, validation and consolidation of school-level reports,” DepEd said.
Based on the Incident Management Reporting System, 509 schools across seven regions were being used as evacuation centers, with 2,185 classrooms accommodating 19,242 families.
DepEd also reported that at least 37,376 learning materials, 965 information technology equipment and 28,975 chairs were damaged.

“Downloading of clean-up and clearing operations and minor repair fund has now been initiated. DepEd ensures the immediate restoration of damaged facilities to ensure continuity of learning,” the department said.
Light rains

The weather situation remains a factor in potential disruptions as the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) returns and brings cloudy skies, scattered rains and thunderstorms to parts of the Visayas and Mindanao, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration said yesterday.
The ITCZ is the line where winds from the northern and southern hemispheres meet, resulting in cloudy skies and light rains.

Cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the ITCZ are expected in the Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Masbate, Lanao del Sur and Davao Oriental.
The rest of the Visayas and Mindanao will experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms due to the ITCZ.
Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon will also experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.
Meanwhile, a tropical depression formed outside the Philippine area of responsibility and was last located 2,785 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon.
It was packing winds of 55 km per hour and gusts of up to 70 kph while moving northward at 20 kph.
Despite its low chances of entering the Philippine area of responsibility, state meteorologists are not ruling out the possibility.
Should it enter, it will be given the local name Queenie, which would be the first tropical cyclone to enter the Philippine area of responsibility this month. — Josiah Antonio

articles.title: VP Sara ready to replace Marcos, says spokesperson
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is ready to replace President Marcos in case the latter resigns, according to her spokesman.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte is ready to replace President Marcos in case the latter resigns, according to her spokesman.
Lawyer Paolo Panelo, the spokesman, defended the Vice President amid criticisms that her call for Marcos to resign was self-serving as she would benefit from it.

“She was elected as the Vice President so she was actually the one the people voted for to replace the President if he would resign, so I don’t think this is self-serving or, as some might say, a conflict of interest because for her and for many Filipinos, it’s not really good for the country for the President to remain in office,” Panelo said.

During an interview in Quezon City, Duterte branded Marcos as the “problem of the nation,” accusing his administration of corruption, abuse and political harassment amid the cases filed against her and members of her family.
Duterte counsel Michael Poa said Duterte in effect has declared her candidacy for the 2028 presidential elections.

“It means, she believed in her ability to change the system or the government’s practices. Because we saw here under President Marcos’ leadership massive corruption, including the flood control scam, violations of the law that almost every month we have a new creative way to interpret the law that we didn’t study in law school,” Panelo added.
Poa noted that as early as 2023, Duterte has issued statements against former House speaker Martin Romualdez and former representative Zaldy Co.

“It all started, if you remember, Vice President Sara was the first to call out Martin Romualdez and Zaldy Co for controlling the budget. President Marcos ignored her then but you see now they are the ones being flagged as big fish that the government is pursuing for corruption,” Panelo added.
According to Panelo, Duterte resigned as secretary of the Department of Education (DepEd) in 2024 “because she didn’t want to be part of that scheme.”
Inhibition motion rejected
Duterte’s camp has confirmed that Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 denied the motion it filed seeking the inhibition of the presiding judge.
Paul Lawrence Lim said QC RTC Branch 98 Judge Maria Angelica de Ramos junked the motion for inhibition filed by Duterte.
De Ramos is handling the grave threats case filed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) against the Vice President and issued a warrant of arrest against her.

“The Vice President will exercise all available remedies. We also received the court’s order requiring both parties to strictly comply with the sub judice rule and to refrain from publicly discussing the merits of the case,” Lim added.
Former Commission on Elections commissioner Rowena Guanzon said it was Marcos who appointed De Ramos to her post in March 2025.
Duterte’s arraignment on Friday was deferred after her lawyers filed a motion challenging the proceedings.
The defense also filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition with a temporary restraining order before the Supreme Court questioning a DOJ resolution, alongside its filing before the trial court.
Defense explains decision

The defense team defended its decision not to file a motion to quash to block the testimony of retired Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang after the impeachment court spokesman said it failed to avail of such remedy.

Poa said the Duterte camp agreed with impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol that a motion to quash could have been a remedy, but maintained that it did not avail of such as it would have been premature, considering that the legal team has yet to hear the offer of testimony.
“While the purpose was indicated in the subpoena, the extent of her testimony, including whether the witness will testify on factual matters, was unknown to the defense,” Poa said.
The prosecution presented Cabotaje-Tang as witness on Monday as it began tackling the article on the alleged unexplained wealth of the Vice President.
Meanwhile, despite raising doubts on her security detail, the Armed Forces of the Philippines assured the Vice President of continued protection. — Michael Punongbayan, Josiah Antonio, Alexis Romero

articles.title: BARMM polls: Federalist party gets big bloc slot
articles.summary: The Bangsamoro Federalist Party ranked first in the Sept. 14 elections for bloc nominations to the 80-seat parliament of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, based on initial tallies…

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) ranked first in the Sept. 14 elections for bloc nominations to the 80-seat parliament of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), based on initial tallies released by the Commission on Elections yesterday.

Comelec officials said the BFP led the regional parliamentary political party vote with 181,246 votes, followed by the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front with 135,932 and the BARMM Government Coalition (BGC) with 102,891.

BFP is headed by BARMM Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua, who was also elected as representative of a district covering parts of Cotabato City and several barangays in nearby towns in Maguindanao del Norte province.
Up to 14 BFP candidates for parliamentary seats in the 32 districts defeated rivals from other parties during Monday’s first Bangsamoro parliamentary electoral exercise.
The Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) received the first electronic transmission of votes from BARMM at 7:08 p.m. Monday.
Its analytics showed that Tawi-Tawi, which had a smaller number of voters, posted the highest vote completion rate at 41 percent as of 7:20 p.m.

It was followed by Maguindanao del Sur with 30.51 percent, Maguindanao del Norte with 26.67 percent, Basilan with 24.53 percent, the Special Geographic Area with 19.85 percent and Lanao del Sur with 14.97 percent.

Meanwhile, PPCRV data showed Marjanie Macasalong leading the parliamentary sectoral representative race for traditional leaders with 335,443 votes, followed by Sultan Pax Mangundadatu with 240,452 and Panga Ibay with 129,745.
For the Ulama sector, Muhammad Nadzir Ebil led with 330,011 votes, followed by Alibasher Abdullatif with 283,382 and Marhan Borhan with 216,200.
As of yesterday morning, Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said 1,168 of the 1,186 polling centers, or 98.48 percent, had completed voting.

“We are keeping our personnel engaged and our lines of coordination open until the remaining election activities are completed,” he said. “The voting may be winding down, but our responsibility does not end there.”
More than 10,439 police personnel were deployed in BARMM, including 5,045 who secured voting centers across the region.
‘Very successful’

Despite cases of violence during the election, Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity Secretary Mel Senen Sarmiento described the first parliamentary elections in the BARMM as “very successful.”
“It was relatively very successful,” Sarmiento told The STAR in a phone interview Monday.
Sarmiento said the Sept. 14 elections compared favorably with previous elections held in areas that formerly comprised the ARMM, noting that the death toll was definitely lower.
He also stressed that voting was orderly in most areas of BARMM.
“Last night, when the results were out, we learned that calm and silence descended all over the region,” Sarmiento said. “That means the electorate accepted the results.”
He said BARMM old-timers told him there would have been trouble, if not violence, if voters were dissatisfied with or rejected the election results.
Sarmiento also congratulated the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and the PNP for their crisis management and quick response to isolated cases of violence.
“I salute them for a job well done,” Sarmiento said.
At least three people were killed and 20 others, including three police officers, were wounded in shootings and other forms of violence in the region during the elections.
Four people were reported killed and 19 others injured in election-related incidents in Cotabato City, although police described the incidents as isolated.

There were 14 incidents recorded on election day, including two shootings, an explosion, commotions, firefights and a strafing incident. — Evelyn Macairan, Rainier Allan Ronda, Emmanuel Tupas, Alexis Romero, Roel Pareno, Christine Boton
