articles.title: LGUs to seek P58.53-B local funding via online portal -- DBM
articles.summary: Local government units (LGUs) must directly apply for government funding through a digital platform, bypassing political intermediaries and ensuring greater transparency in the allocation of public…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 7:24pm

Local government units (LGUs) must directly apply for government funding through a digital platform, bypassing political intermediaries and ensuring greater transparency in the allocation of public funds, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said on Tuesday.

During the Development Budget Coordination Committee briefing at the House of Representatives, DBM Secretary Kim Robert De Leon, through House Appropriations Committee Chair Mikaela Angela Suansing, said the government has proposed P58.53 billion for the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
"We are proposing Php 58.53 billion for the (LGSF), covering financial assistance to LGUs, the Growth Equity Fund, and the Barangay Development Program," she said.
"By strengthening local fiscal capacity, we bring resources and decision-making closer to communities and give every region a stronger voice in the nation's development," the DBM added.
Under DBM Local Budget Circular No. 169, local chief executives must apply directly through the digital Ugnayang Bayan Portal.

Suansing, who was defending the committee report on the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, said LGUs must submit their funding requests directly to the DBM through the portal, ensuring that allocations are based on local priorities rather than requests coursed through third parties.
The circular eliminates intermediaries, while submission of an application does not guarantee that an LGU will receive funding, she said.

The proposed P58.53-billion allocation for 2027 is reportedly 1.14% higher than the 2026 budget. The DBM said the proposal incorporated inputs from groups such as the Union of Local Authorities of the Philippines (ULAP) and various LGU leagues to better address local infrastructure and social development priorities.

In a separate statement, the DBM said funding requests are evaluated based on several criteria, including governance standards, fiscal management, transparency, absorptive capacity, service delivery, economic development, environmental management, public safety and citizen engagement.

"The evaluation considers governance standards; financial management, fiscal transparency, and absorptive capacity; service delivery; economic development; environmental management; public safety; and citizen engagement," it said.
"DBM also considers the necessity of the proposed assistance, just and equitable distribution of funds among LGUs, and availability of funds," the DBM added.

During the House hearing, Suansing also noted that the Supreme Court had previously affirmed the constitutionality of the LGSF, saying it serves a clear policy purpose and is governed by sufficient legal standards.

"The ruling reinforces that LGSF releases operate within defined purposes, eligibility requirements, evaluation criteria, and accountability mechanisms. LGUs themselves identify and request assistance based on local needs, while approved funds remain subject to transparency, monitoring, audit, and applicable government rules," she said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
articles.summary:
Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir

The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad

blocks.text: The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions.

Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges.
They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to lobby for his release.

On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft.

blocks.caption: Imran Khan outside court in Lahore after a hearing in February 2023. Photograph: Mohsin Raza/Reuters

blocks.text: Later this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release.

Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”.

“The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.”

blocks.caption: Left to right: Sulaiman Khan, Jemima Khan, Imran Khan’s daughter Tyrian White and Kasim Khan at a film premiere in London in February 2023. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

blocks.text: Late last month, Sky Sports aired an interview with Khasim and Sulaiman during its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister, made a formal complaint to Sky Sports after the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break.

“It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.”

The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.
Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said.
Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief.

blocks.caption: Asim Munir praying after laying a wreath on the martyrs’ monument during a ceremony in Rawalpindi last year. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: When Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and the bad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2023, the persecution of Khan increased notably.

“It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman. Munir’s powers expanded over the past year as he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”.

Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention.
Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party.

“There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off.
“The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.”

In a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.
“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said.

It was widely acknowledged that Khan came to power in 2018 with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption, press censorship and persecution of his opponents.
He was toppled in 2022 after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government.

By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor to the persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power.
Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf display a poster of Imran Khan at a rally in February on the second anniversary of the 2024 general elections, which the party alleges were rigged. Photograph: Bilawal Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Sulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case.
Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying.
They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence.

“We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.”

Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.”

Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”

articles.title: No sign of drilling from Chinese ship lurking in Bajo de Masinloc - AFP
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said the Chinese vessel that was spotted in Bajo de Masinloc for 28 days was conducting research and surveillance, but did not conduct any…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 7:17pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said the Chinese vessel that was spotted in Bajo de Masinloc for 28 days was conducting research and surveillance, but did not conduct any drilling.

AFP Special Spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad reiterated the country’s claim over the disputed waters, particularly Bajo de Masinloc, also known as the Panatag Shoal.

“On the Chinese research vessel that was spotted for 25 days...28 days in Bajo de Masinloc, the presence and the track would indicate that they were conducting surveillance or research activities,” Trinidad told reporters.
“As to any report of drilling activities, there was none that was confirmed, nor were there any reports given by our monitoring capabilities,” he added.
Trinidad explained that for the vessel to be able to drill, it needed to remain stationary. He said the AFP also has other sensors to determine such activities.
“The tracks indicated not a continuous pattern. It was not only transiting. But to be able to conduct drilling activities, it should be stationary,” the Navy officer added.
The presence of the Chinese vessel was initially called out by Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela.

China has continuously laid its claim to Philippine waters despite the 2016 ruling of the Permanent Court of Arbitration, with numerous maritime encounters between Filipino and Chinese personnel. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: SPD governor campaigns as one-woman bulwark against AfD
articles.summary: Manuela Schwesig, of the center-left SPD, has governed the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic Sea coast, since 2017. Ahead of this weekend's election, she is campaigning against…

image.caption: Manuela Schwesig has made a point of meeting as many voters personally as she canImage: Philip Dulian/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The late-summer warmth is lingering in the countryside of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Lavender-infused cocktails and savory onion cakes are being served on the spacious terrace of Hasenwinkel Castle, an old country house turned conference hotel not far from the Baltic coast. The largest business association in this northeastern German state has invited members and guests from the political world to a convivial gathering. State Premier Manuela Schwesig, of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), is also in attendance.

It could be a relaxed evening, were it not for the upcoming state election on September 20. "We live in politically turbulent times," says association president Lars Schwarz in his welcoming remarks. But the evening is also meant to serve as an opportunity to "recharge," he says. Days before the election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading in the polls with around 37%. But the SPD is not far behind, with 33%, and has narrowed the gap in recent weeks. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which leads the federal government with the SPD under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is far behind and hoping to remain above the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
The economy needs immigration, the AfD opposes it

The term "remigration" is playing a major role in the AfD's campaign. But as far as the state's business leaders are concerned, sending people of immigrant background out of Germany would be a disaster for the economy.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a significantly older population than most other German states. It's also less densely populated and more severely affected by demographic change. "International skilled workers and laborers have long been an important part of our economic future," said Schwarz. "Openness to the world is not an abstract political formula, but a concrete prerequisite for ensuring that businesses in our state can continue to produce, offer services, train employees, and grow."

In a brief speech at the event, Schwesig recounted encounters she had during the election campaign. She speaks of a conversation with a baker who is concerned not only about high energy prices but also about her employees. "She said, 'Ms. Schwesig, I have employees with immigrant backgrounds working here, and I'm very worried that I'll lose them — because I value them, and because I care about them as people.'"

The head of a planning firm approached the state premier and explained that his Moroccan employee wanted to leave the country. "Because when he goes to the café at the market in Stralsund and waits for his German friends, the people sitting near him either make snide remarks or move to another table." Who, Schwesig asks, would want to live in such a climate?
Fear of social division

Preventing the AfD's victory — that is what the 52-year-old Schwesig has made her stated goal. In the final stretch of the campaign, her posters feature just her face on a red background — no name — above the slogan "The Woman Against Blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."
Anyone who doesn't want those things must support her, she says. "To do that, you have to go to the polls and vote for the SPD — and that's why I'm the woman against blue."

Perhaps tellingly, the SPD isn't mentioned on most of her campaign posters, however. Only Schwesig herself is visible, dressed in red. The SPD's party color must suffice as a reference. Schwesig is the driving force: She represents the political comeback of the past twelve months. In September 2025, the SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was languishing at just 19% in opinion polls, while the AfD stood at 38%.
Recipe for success: Close to the people and distance from Berlin

Manuela Schwesig managed to close the gap, in part, by trying to stay closely connected to the people of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, seeking direct dialogue with voters as often as possible. She is friendly and approachable, yet also firm. Schwesig listens, answers questions with confidence, marshals the facts, and engages in discussions where she attempts to demonstrate that she is well-informed about everything happening in the state.

Above all, however, she scored points by maintaining maximum distance from the federal government — and thus from her own party too. In Berlin, the SPD governs as the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) parties, and the government is more unpopular than any before it. As Schwesig has gained ground, the SPD's support at the federal level has plummeted to 12%.
Imported care giver: Skilled, needed, stalled by bureaucracy
Strong criticism of Friedrich Merz

Schwesig believes much of what is decided in Berlin is wrong — and she says so. "I expect the chancellor and the entire federal government to chart a new political course,” she demanded following the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt in early September.

She has long believed that the reform of the social welfare systems planned by the CDU/CSU and the SPD is heading in the wrong direction. "I expect that the reforms will ensure that those who have worked their entire lives and made contributions are not the ones who bear the heaviest burdens," she says regarding the plans to eliminate the retirement age of 63 for people who have contributed to the pension fund for a particularly long time. "And I'm glad that my criticism is now receiving a lot of support."
Will Manuela Schwesig become SPD leader?

She also receives support from within her own party. Discontent is growing within the federal SPD over the two co-chairs, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas. There is open speculation about whether Manuela Schwesig should replace them at the party's helm. Amid the SPD's crisis, there are strong arguments for making one of the last Social Democrats who is popular with voters the party leader.

A woman who entered politics relatively late in life. Born in Brandenburg, she was already nearly 30 years old when she joined the SPD in 2003. Prior to that, she had studied public finance and worked as a tax official.

blocks.caption: Schwesig served in Merkel's cabinet before returning to Mecklenburg Western-PomeraniaImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Schwesig: Underestimated by opponents?

Her political rise was rapid: Local politics in the state capital of Schwerin, Social Affairs Minister in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and finally, in 2013, Federal Family Affairs Minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. By then, she had become well-known nationwide.

Her opponents often underestimated her, especially men. A CDU politician once derisively called her the "coastal Barbie." "Young, blonde, East German" was the headline when she became a federal minister.
Perhaps this was also because Schwesig never came across as a classic power-seeking politician. Her strengths, say her supporters, lie in her calm perseverance, fighting spirit, and pragmatism.
Nord Stream 2

This tenacity nearly proved to be her undoing in the dispute over the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline. In 2017, Schwesig returned to Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania to succeed State Premier Erwin Sellering, who was seriously ill at the time. Sellering had maintained very good relations with Russia, and Schwesig continued his policies.

This included defending the construction of the Baltic Sea pipeline — which was intended to transport even more Russian gas to Germany — in the face of criticism from Eastern Europe, the US, and some in Germany. When the US threatened sanctions in 2021, Schwesig even attempted to secure the completion of Nord Stream 2 by establishing a "climate foundation" funded by Moscow.

blocks.caption: Schwesig's support for the Nord Stream pipeline became a political liabilityImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: State premier with a 60% approval rating

After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, her stance became a political liability. Schwesig made a political about-face and admitted to mistakes. To this day, however, she defends the logic behind her decisions at the time.
This has not caused her any lasting damage. Currently, in a direct election, 60% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania would vote for Schwesig as head of government.
The current state government, made up of the SPD and the socialist Left Party, is also performing well in polls. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to secure another term.
This article was translated from German.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines– The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte questioned on Tuesday, September 15, the competence of an official of the Office of the Ombudsman to testify on alleged irregularities in the Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) of the country’s second-highest official.

On Day 25 of the impeachment trial, defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular underscored that Ombudsman records division officer-in-charge (OIC) Karen Batu has no personal knowledge of the contents of Duterte’s SALNs including her personal properties, liabilities, net worths, and disclosures of business interests and financial connections.
Batu also has no personal knowledge whether or not there were irregularities, unusual entries, or errors in Duterte’s records, he added.
“In testifying in today’s trial, you cannot conclude whether the Vice President has or does not have ill-gotten wealth,” said Gular.
The prosecution swiftly objected, saying “it was clear from the very start that the witness was only testifying based on the [Ombudsman’s] records.”
“We’ve been fair with the witness in our direct [examination] only asking her to that,” private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said.

Duterte’s financial records were scrutinized during the trial, with prosecutors presenting her SALNs from 2007 to 2025. The defense initially objected to the presentation, explaining that she was not an impeachable officer prior to 2022. Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, however, allowed the presentation, citing the need to establish a baseline.

“The Chair would like to remind counsel for the respondent of the ruling of the Chair with respect to the issuance of the subpoenas covering the period 2007 up to 2025, that pursuant to OMB, Office of the Ombudsman vs. Bernardo GR No. 181598 dated March 2013, there is a necessity to establish the baseline, not for the prosecution but equally for the respondent, in order to find out what is the base figure for the computation of the SALN during her term,” Escudero said.

Defense spokesperson Michael Poa, in a press briefing, said Batu was not the proper witness to interpret the SALNs, adding she was called to testify to identify Duterte’s SALNs that were in the custody of the Ombudsman. He also said the defense will present a strategy, during their presentation of evidence, to address questions on the SALNs.

“We have our strategy on that matter, actually. Because obviously, I will not, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny na siyempre, napag-isipan na ng depensa kung paano natin gagawin yan at ipapaliwanag ang mga bagay-bagay,” Poa said.

(We have our strategy on that matter, actually. Because obviously, I will not, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny that we have already formulated ways on how we will explain the SALNs.)

“Meron naman kaming mga naisip na paraan at estratehiya… Asahan niyo na lang po at abangan niyo na lang po ‘pag kami naman ang nag-present ng ebidensya kung sakaling may mga kailangan ipaliwanag doon sa mga nakalagay,” he added.
(We thought of ways and strategies. We will show that to the public during our turn to present evidence.)
In a related development, the Senate impeachment court is now preparing for the presentation of the amici curiae, or “friends of the court” on Wednesday, September 16.

The impeachment court has tapped four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices to provide guidance on the resolution of the voting threshold for Duterte’s trial. They are: retired Chief Justices Artemio V. Panganiban, Reynato S. Puno, Hilario G. Davide Jr., and retired Associate Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna.
Panganiban, Puno, and Azcuna will physically attend the presentation while Davide will submit an advisory to be read before the court.
RELATED STORY: ‘Amici curiae’: Where do invited ex-justices stand on conviction threshold debate?

Each senator-judges will be provided five minutes to pose a question to the retired SC justices. Following their presentation, an oral argument between the defense and prosecution panels on the matter will be held on September 23, with each side given 15 minutes to present its position.
Senator-judges are expected to cast their votes on the voting threshold issue on the same day. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Communauto says it was hit by data breach initiated by its own employee
articles.summary: The Montreal car-sharing company said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.

image.caption: The Montreal car-sharing company Communauto says it has about 50,000 customers in Quebec alone. (Olivia Laperrière-Roy/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal
The Montreal car-sharing company said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.
Breach affected 'some thousand members' across the country, says company
The Montreal car-sharing company Communauto said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.
In an email sent to affected customers on Monday evening, Communauto said the incident happened during the night of Sept. 3 to 4.
"Our investigation determined that an automated script had been deployed without authorization by an employee in an attempt to access and download customer records," the email reads.
The company says police executed a search warrant the next day at the residence of the employee suspected of carrying out the breach to seize their computer equipment.

Communauto says account passwords and payment information were not affected by the breach, but that personal information, including people's names, addresses and driver's licence numbers, was. If the customer had a photograph of themselves or of their licence attached to their file, then those were downloaded as well.
In a statement to CBC, Communauto's vice-president of strategic development, Marco Viviani, said the breach affected about two per cent of its users, representing "some thousand members" Canada-wide.
"At this stage, we hope that no data was disclosed externally," he said.

"Based on the information available to us, we did not believe it was necessary for anyone to be taken into custody, but we have not received any additional details since law enforcement became involved."
Viviani says the company hired a specialized consulting firm to monitor the web and dark web for any signs of data exposure.

Communauto says those affected by the breach should "remain vigilant regarding unsolicited emails, phone calls, and text messages, particularly those requesting personal information, payment, urgent action, or encouraging you to click on a link or open an attachment."
It says customers should set up multi-factor authentication and make sure their account password is strong and unique.

articles.title: Venice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victory
articles.summary:
Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive

The winner of this year’s best actress prize at…

blocks.text: The winner of this year’s best actress prize at the Venice film festival has revealed that she is on unemployment benefits and had to fly to back to Copenhagen to report to the job centre before receiving her award.

On Saturday night, Danish actor Mathilde Arcel won the prestigious Volpi Cup for her first leading role in a feature film, May el-Toukhy’s post-second world war drama Woman Unknown, which also won the Golden Lion award for best film.
Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal said the judges had been able to relax Venice rules around not awarding more than one prize per film because the vote for Arcel had been unanimous.

After her triumph, the 30-year-old actor revealed in interviews with Danish media that she had returned to Denmark after her film’s premiere to sign on at the job centre, as she is on unemployment benefits when not working on films. She then returned to the Lido after being told it would be wise to be present at the awards gala.
In the UK, actors’ trade union Equity said in a 2023 report that 63% of its members have been in receipt of social security at some point in their life.
Set in the direct aftermath of the Nazi occupation of Denmark, Woman Unknown tells the story of Marie, a young housemaid and nanny who is about to marry her widowed industrialist employer.

But a chance encounter with an old schoolfriend threatens to reveal a shameful secret, exposing Marie to the retributive hounding of female “horizontal collaborators” who had intimate relations with German soldiers.

At Venice, Arcel drew wide critical praise for the contained inner anguish she brings to the role of Marie. “Mathilde is going to blow our socks off,” Gyllenhaal said in a press conference after the awards ceremony.

The actor said her agent had received several calls with new job offers since she scooped the Volpi Cup, the male version of which went to Hollywood veteran John Malkovich. “There are a lot of calls and a lot of interest from abroad and things like that, and we need to talk about what’s going to happen,” she told Danish broadcaster DR.

Speaking in Venice on Saturday night, Arcel joked that her ultimate dream would be to play a part in one long-running British TV detective drama she was particularly fond of. “I really want to keep on working and meet some new artists”, she said. “I’m looking so much forward to what the future will bring, perhaps even a role in Midsomer Murders”.

articles.title: Poland seeks new defense deals with Philippines
articles.summary: Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewsk says Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines

blocks.text: POLAND FLAG. The flag of Poland.
Darwinek, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewsk says Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines – Poland is seeking new defense partnerships with the Philippines, a senior foreign ministry official said on Tuesday, September 15, after completing the delivery of Black Hawk helicopters to Manila last month.

Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, who was in Manila for annual political consultations with the Philippines, said Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines.

items: Bartoszewski said Poland could sell both reconnaissance and fighting drones, radar equipment, anti-aircraft missiles and armored personnel carriers. A Philippine military delegation recently visited Poland to look into equipment that Manila can buy, he said.

The Philippines acquired 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from Polish Sikorsky subsidiary PZL Mielec in a deal worth P32 billion ($509.60 million) in 2022. The delivery of the last seven helicopters was completed last month, the Philippine military said.
Bartoszewski said separately talks were ongoing between Ukraine and Poland for the transfer of Warsaw’s MiG-29 fighter jets in exchange for drone technology from Kyiv.
Bartoszewski said the two sides are discussing whether to refurbish the jets before transferring them to Ukraine as well as the kind of technology Warsaw gets in return.
Poland has been one of Ukraine’s strongest backers since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022, providing military aid and serving as a ​key logistics hub for Western assistance.

blocks.text: (Reporting by Mikhail Flores; Editing by Martin Petty)

articles.title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
articles.summary: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.

blocks.text: Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.
The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".
Moscow has not commented on the incident.

It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."
Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.
The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.

President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".
Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone over Lithuania
articles.summary: An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania ‌shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.

image.caption: Debris of what the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre says is a drone shot down by a NATO fighter jet lies on the ground near Pratkunai, Lithuania, on Tuesday in this screengrab from a handout video. (Lithuanian Army/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania ‌shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.
It was not immediately clear if the drone was fired by Russian or Ukrainian forces

The drone, which was likely to have entered from Belarus, was shot ​down near Pratkunai village in southern ​Lithuania, near Kaunas, the second-largest city, the centre's spokesperson said. Its origin had yet to be ​determined, he said.
Military drones ​straying into the ⁠airspace of Russia's neighbours have stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that strikes close to the alliance's territory would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Kyiv. Rutte also pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defences along its long eastern border with Russia.
Concerns grow over Russia’s incursions into NATO nations

Officials did not say whether ⁠the drone was ⁠believed to be Ukrainian ‌or Russian. In recent months, Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace in the Baltic region. Kyiv says they were steered off course by ⁠Russian signal jamming.
A drone alert was issued earlier in the capital Vilnius and surrounding region.
The Lithuanian army shared video ‌from the site of the crash, showing debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood and some appeared charred.

Fighters ​with the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission have patrolled the skies of ⁠Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined ⁠the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray ⁠Ukrainian ⁠drones over Estonia ​in May, and over Latvia in June and August.
Denmark reports encounter with Russian ship

Separately, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter on Monday. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called the incident "unacceptable" and said it could have endangered human lives.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident was serious but not surprising, calling it part of a ⁠pattern in which an increasingly aggressive Russia has intensified its hybrid warfare against Europe and is testing NATO.
How NATO is tracking airspace threats over eastern Europe
The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Baltic Sea region is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline ​outages, airspace violations and drone sightings.
Russia has dismissed accusations over such incidents and repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe.

In fighting on Tuesday, a Russian drone attack ‌killed one person ​and knocked out ​power in parts ​of the ⁠city ⁠of Zaporizhzhia ‌in southeast Ukraine, the ⁠acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

As well, the regional governor of Odesa, Oleh Kiper, said that Russia hit port ‌infrastructure in ​Ukraine's southern ​Black Sea region overnight, ‌with residential buildings, ‌logistics facilities and transport infrastructure ​coming under attack.
‌Russian ​forces hit ​a cargo ship ​and ⁠a ⁠ferry ‌carrying ⁠military supplies ‌in ​Ukraine's ⁠port ⁠of Chornomorsk, ⁠the ⁠Russian Defence ​Ministry ⁠said on ⁠Tuesday.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday posted on social media that Russia and Ukraine had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure. He had earlier called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying ​the attacks were causing a shortage of the fuel that is "hurting ​the world."
Trump didn't offer further details on the purported agreement.
Zelenskyy said late Monday that Kyiv was "ready to support de-escalation," but expressed doubts Russia would adhere to such a demand.
With files from the Associated Press

articles.title: Democrats say supreme court rejection of Trump mail ballot restrictions will ensure ‘safe, secure and accurate elections’ – US politics live
articles.summary: Comments come after court on Monday rejected the president’s mail ballot restrictions ahead of the November midterm elections

blocks.text: Key events

items: 10m agoTrump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies
28m agoSupreme court rejection of Trump mail ballot restrictions will ensure 'safe, secure and accurate elections'

blocks.text: Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies

blocks.caption: David Smith

blocks.text: David Smith
Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies.
Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity.

Trump dismissed the anxieties on Monday, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy” and insisting on social media: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

But the 80-year-old president, who has sidelined Congress on numerous issues during his second term, looks increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late.

Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia, said: “History will look very poorly on that tweet. He’s not paying attention – or he’s paying attention to the wrong people. He’s being really foolish: not the first time he’s been really foolish but perhaps catastrophically foolish in this case.”

Recent surveys by the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation found 85% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want a new federal agency to monitor and regulate AI; and 82% of Democrats and 78% of Republicans favour government safety tests for AI making critical decisions.
Supreme court rejection of Trump mail ballot restrictions will ensure 'safe, secure and accurate elections'
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Lawmakers have given their support to the supreme court’s rejection of Donald Trump’s bid to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections.
The decision capped a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already underway, with states allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes used for years.

Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active.

Washington’s secretary of state Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said the decision means work “to carry out a safe, secure, and accurate election” can continue ‘without having to upend our election processes to meet unrealistic ballot mail requirements.”

In Arizona, another largely vote-by-mail state, Democratic secretary of state Adrian Fontes said “it is crucial for us to continue rejecting the notion that access and security are mutually exclusive when it comes to running strong elections.”

Utah Lt Gov Deidre Henderson, a Republican serving as the state’s chief election officer, said on social media that the supreme court’s decision means “Utahns can have confidence that the 2026 election will proceed as normal.”
In other developments:

items: Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old former Senate majority leader from Kentucky, was seen in Washington for the first time in months on Monday, minutes before his office released a statement saying that he was back at work.

With a slip of the tongue reminiscent of Joe Biden, Gavin Newsom, California’s Democratic governor, told CNN that he would not run for president in 2028 if his fellow Californian, former vice-president Kamala Harris, decides to run again, since “I know what that means: I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the zen diagram on that is just pure crossover.”
Donald Trump claimed there is a “SICK conspiracy” against artificial intelligence and data centers in response to the growing calls for greater checks on AI development.

In a statement posted on social media, Barack Obama, the former US president, called for the pace of AI development to be slowed to allow time for the federal government to develop regulations to address “serious safety concerns”.

articles.title: Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter
articles.summary: Denmark has summoned Russia's ambassador over a Baltic Sea encounter that Copenhagen says is part of an increasingly aggressive pattern of Russian behavior.

image.caption: Denmark's military uses the related Fennec helicopter for tasks including surveillance and reconnaissanceImage: gemeinfrei

blocks.text: A Russian warship fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea, with one passing close to the aircraft, Denmark's armed forces said on Tuesday.
The confrontation comes amid heightened security concerns on NATO's eastern flank during Russia's war in Ukraine.
How has Denmark responded?
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident fitted a broader pattern of increasingly aggressive Russian behavior in Europe.
She accused Moscow of intensifying its "hybrid war against Europe" and testing and challenging NATO, and called on European countries to strengthen their defenses.

"Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver," Frederiksen said in a statement on X.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen condemned the incident as "completely unacceptable" and summoned Russia's ambassador, saying the action could have put lives at risk.
The foreign minister accused Moscow of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour," adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
What happened in the Baltic Sea?
Denmark's armed forces said one of its Fennec helicopters was carrying out a routine photographic reconnaissance mission when the incident occurred.
The helicopter was observing a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser, a Danish port on the Baltic Sea.
The Russian vessel fired two flares towards the helicopter, according to the Danish military.
"One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter," it said. No one on board was injured.

The incident came against a backdrop of growing tensions along NATO's eastern flank. Poland has repeatedly scrambled fighter jets during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine and reported incursions by Russian drones into its airspace.

NATO members in the region have stepped up air patrols and other defenses as Moscow's war in Ukraine has increasingly raised fears of spillover and direct confrontations between Russian and alliance forces.

articles.title: Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
articles.summary: Trains were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday after objects were found on tracks at multiple locations.

blocks.text: Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway operator has said.
ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while several level crossings were also malfunctioning.
Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action".
It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating. The BBC has contacted police for comment.
The network's website showed that 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected.
ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved".

Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands.

articles.title: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating
articles.summary: Nova Scotia officials are investigating after the new owners of a funeral home in the Annapolis Valley discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has…

image.caption: Kristina Sweeney says she was shocked to learn an urn was discovered with what's believed to be her mother's cremated remains. Sweeney's mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 and a funeral was held at that time. (David Laughlin/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·Exclusive

Nova Scotia officials are investigating after the new owners of a funeral home in the Annapolis Valley discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned. Several families were recently told ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.
New funeral home owner discovers ‘significant number’ of human ashes in storage
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating after the new owners of an Annapolis Valley funeral home discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned.

It comes as several Nova Scotia families who used the services of Serenity Funeral Home say they were shocked and horrified to receive calls letting them know that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.
“I kind of started internally freaking out because I buried my mom in 2024,” said Kristina Sweeney.
“I don't even think the shock has worn off yet … I thought I buried my mom, all of her. I put her in the ground by myself.”

Sweeney wasn't the only one contacted by East Coast Memorial, which recently purchased the buildings from Serenity Funeral Home. Serenity’s head office and crematorium was located in the small community of Coldbrook. The company also had other locations in the Annapolis Valley.

Michelle Carey and her sister Amanda Sabean used Serenity when they buried what they believed were the cremated remains of their father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, in the spring of 2018. On Sept. 8, Carey was informed by East Coast Memorial that her father’s full remains were found in storage.
“Having to, you know, bury him and to do this all over again. It's really hard,” said Carey.
The sisters are also left wondering whose remains they buried.
“There’s a family out there that's missing remains of their family member,” said Sabean.

In an email, Andrew George, the owner of the new business East Coast Memorial, explained that his company discovered “a significant number of cremated remains that had been left in storage, some for many, many years.”

George said he and his staff are carefully reviewing the home’s information to “make every reasonable effort to locate and contact families so that these loved ones could be returned to their families or otherwise laid to rest appropriately.”
‘Dozens’ of other urns found, daughter told
Sweeney said when her mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 at the age of 60, her body was cremated. Sweeney chose a green urn, which she received and buried.

This month, the employee of East Coast Memorial who returned what’s believed to be the rest of her mother’s ashes gave her a green urn with a different pattern. It had been identified with a sticky note label as her mother’s. Sweeney said the employee told her that there were “dozens” of other urns found.
Another family told CBC their loved one’s remains were delivered to them in a cardboard box.

Sweeney wrote a post on Facebook about her experience and started receiving responses from other families. They recounted similar experiences, believing that they had received and buried their loved ones. Then they were contacted by East Coast Memorial years later suggesting otherwise.
“Every single person I've spoken to was under the impression that they had taken care of all the remains,” Sweeney said. “They were either buried or they took the urn home.”

George said his company is still assessing all the cases and doing its due diligence “as thoroughly as possible for each family,” and so he isn’t able to say exactly how many persons’ remains were found.
Former owner responds

When CBC reached Tony Facey, a former owner of Serenity Funeral Home for 12 years until December 2025, he confirmed there was a “whole stack” of cremated remains dating back as far as 25 years that had never been claimed by families. He said unclaimed remains is a wider issue all funeral homes are dealing with, and this has been an ongoing discussion at the regulatory board. Facey declined an interview.
The president of the Funeral Service Association of Nova Scotia, Kollin Weatherbee, said he’s never heard of a funeral home keeping decades of unclaimed remains.
“It is unusual that a funeral home would hold a portion of someone's ashes without the family knowing,” he said.
Weatherbee added that if a funeral home held ashes for a family, it would only be for a matter of weeks.
And in situations where a next of kin can’t be identified or reached, he said the public trustee usually gets involved within the first 12 days of a death.
Provincial inspectors visit
The province licenses and regulates funeral homes through Service Nova Scotia, while an arm’s-length board licenses and regulates funeral home directors.

The province learned of the stored ashes on Sept. 9 when it was contacted by that board and George, the owner of East Coast Memorial. It assigned two provincial inspectors to visit the crematorium the next day to learn more.

Adam Tipert, the chair of the Nova Scotia Board of Registration of Embalmers and Funeral Directors, told CBC in an email the board is taking the concerns “very seriously” and will collaborate with Service Nova Scotia in its investigation as more information emerges.
The province and the board also conducted an investigation at Serenity Funeral Home in 2018, when the location in Berwick mixed up the bodies of two women. A funeral director had his licence revoked.
That case eventually led to a change in the legislation surrounding funeral homes in 2025.

items: Family horrified after funeral home mixes up bodies, cremates wrong one
New law coming aimed at preventing body mix-ups at funeral homes

blocks.text: A provincial spokesperson said Serenity was routinely inspected in 2022, and some non-compliant administrative matters were resolved.
Following the sale to East Coast Memorial, Serenity is no longer licensed to operate funeral homes in Nova Scotia.
George said right now he is keeping focused on doing what is right for the families.

“We do not want to speculate about decisions or practices that occurred before our involvement,” he said, adding that his company will treat the remains with respect and dignity, as they were “received into our care when we acquired Serenity.”
George said his company is making plans for a community burial ceremony for any remains that can’t be reunited with a family, or if the families direct his company to do so.
Hank Sabean’s daughters still have many unanswered questions, especially since their father had been so clear about his own funeral arrangements and being laid to rest with his family.
“He had strong morals and values, and I know that he would think that this is so wrong that this could happen,” said Carey.
Kristina Sweeney said her mother would also be “really, really disgusted.”
“I felt like my mom and I had been violated,” she said. “I expect when someone passes away that, and I'm sure most people do, they're treated with dignity and respect.”

Angela MacIvor is a reporter with the CBC Atlantic investigative unit. She has been with CBC since 2006 as a reporter and producer in all three Maritime provinces. articles.title: Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services
articles.summary: A major outage has hit parts of the Dutch railway system after objects were found placed across lines, authorities say. The company responsible for rail infrastructure says it suspects deliberate…

image.caption: The disruption began during Tuesday's morning rush hourImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Train services in various parts of the Netherlands have been severely disrupted, with ProRail, the company that maintains the nation's rail infrastructure, saying that sabotage was possibly at play.
National railway company NS said that train services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort have been affected since the morning rush hour.

blocks.caption: The national railway company said it is not clear when services can resumeImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: What do we know about the causes of the disruption?

In a statement, rail authority ProRail said that "[m]aterials deliberately placed on the tracks have been found at several locations. This is causing track-circuit failures. It appears to be a case of sabotage."
The ‌objects caused failures ‌across ​the network, affecting several level crossings, which disrupted ​road traffic, Pro Rail said.
ProRail ​workers ​were clearing the ​objects and ‌working to restore safe conditions, it ​added.
Though the company itself did not say what the "materials" were, a ProRail spokesperson told the daily de Volkskrant that "pipes had been found attached to the line" in several places.
This caused the disruptions, as the railway security systems can register a train's presence on a line because of an object placed on it and thus block access for other trains.
The spokesperson told the paper that one train had even collided with one of the pipes laid on the tracks, but that no accident or injuries had occurred.

blocks.caption: The disruption originated at 13 locations on tracks in the central NetherlandsImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Important event in The Hague
It remains unknown whether the incident has to do with so-called Prinsjesdag, the day the Dutch government presents its annual budget to parliament, where the reigning monarch gives a speech.
On the day, thousands of people go to The Hague to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages.

articles.title: Why AI researchers warn humanity could face extinction
articles.summary: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.

image.caption: Some researchers argue that artificial general intelligence could pose unforeseeable risksImage: Marc Asensio/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Dramatic warnings about the existential risks posed by artificial intelligence to humanity are nothing new.
As early as the 1940s, the renowned scientist and science fiction author Isaac Asimov explored potential risks and unintended consequences of intelligent machines.
In 1991, Hollywood blockbuster "Terminator 2" imagined a dystopian 2029 in which an out-of-control military AI called Skynet directs killer robots in a war against humanity.
If the warnings of several of the biggest names in AI are to be believed, a similar scenario could become a reality — even before 2029.

blocks.caption: The opening sequence of 'Terminator 2' depicts a dystopian future where AI has spiraled out of control and turned against humanityImage: Columbia/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Growing calls for strict regulation
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," AI researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X last week, without exactly explaining how it might happen.
"No other human activity poses this level of danger," he added.

Coxon also revealed that he had quit his job at Anthropic, a US-based AI company, in protest against what he saw as an irresponsible race among AI companies to develop an ever better, self-improving superintelligence.

He warned that algorithms could begin to analyze and improve their own source code independently, which could shrink development cycles from several months to just a few minutes and thus make them uncontrollable.

Coxon is not an isolated voice. Nobel Prize-winning physicist Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has been warning for years about the serious consequences of artificial superintelligence.

In 2023, he left his job at Google to publicly warn of the dangers of AI technologies he helped pioneer. Yoshua Bengio, a pioneer of artificial neural networks and deep learning, has also expressed concern about current developments and called for government regulation.

As recently as July 2026, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI companies warned in an open letter of an imminent loss of control if the race for "superintelligence" were not subject to significantly stricter regulations.
Caught in an unregulated race?
Despite the growing warnings, US President Donald Trump's administration has clearly shifted its AI policy toward minimizing regulatory hurdles and accelerating AI development.

In his X post, Jacob Coxon indirectly criticized the consequences of this policy: "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."
Coxon, who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic in early 2026, is familiar with both corporate cultures.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he said that under the "most aggressive scenarios," things could spiral out of control as early as the end of 2027.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for his part, is currently calling for a coordinated, industry-wide slowdown in development to buy time to address the risks and prevent any misuse of AI.

In a lengthy essay shared on X over the weekend, he wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable ​of taking over the entire internet" and potentially cause "hundreds of billions of dollars in damage" without proper guardrails.
Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei.
The alignment problem

In recent years, numerous experts have voiced concern about the rapid AI advances, particularly the development of artificial general intelligence, which refers to systems that not only solve individual tasks but also match or exceed human intellectual capabilities in nearly all areas.
Sophisticated AI models, for instance, may pursue goals in ways that diverge from human intentions, something AI security researchers refer to as the "alignment problem."
On top of that, even developers can't always fully understand how AI makes certain decisions.
And so, it's no surprise that Coxon's former colleague Evan Hubinger came to his defense.

"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger, who himself is the team lead for alignment stress tests at Anthropic, wrote on X.

In his post, Hubinger made clear that Anthropic hasn't yet found a solution to the alignment problem and warned that an AI model might begin to resist being shut down, because that would limit its ability to achieve its programmed goal.
Exaggerated hysteria?
Other AI experts, however, consider such doomsday scenarios to be extremely unlikely.
Among the most prominent critics of the so-called AI doomers is Meta's chief scientist, Yann LeCun. In October 2024, he dismissed such concerns as "complete nonsense."
Still, other experts note that developing AI systems requires enormous amounts of computing power, energy, data and infrastructure.
They argue that an AI model cannot simply take over the world because it would need to rely on servers, power grids, communication systems and physical resources that are controlled by humans.
China's humanoid robots put to the test
Does the real danger lie elsewhere?
In fact, many experts see the short-term risks not so much in the extinction of humanity as in the numerous indirect consequences of AI systems that already exist even without superintelligence.
These include disinformation campaigns on an unprecedented scale and the related manipulation of democratic processes, an expansion of mass surveillance, and job losses across numerous industries.

Just last week, Anthropic revealed that there had been several attempts by users to misuse its Claude AI models for research that could support biological weapons development. The company said it had banned the accounts involved.
In August, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI caused a stir when they announced that their AI systems had unintentionally carried out autonomous hacking activities.
Following reports of further AI hacking attacks during testing, even top US AI frontier labs are now expressing a willingness to slow down the development of the technology.
This piece was originally published in German.

articles.title: Denmark summons Russia’s ambassador after warship fires flares at Danish army helicopter – Europe live
articles.summary:
Danish PM says action was ‘reckless’ as Moscow-attributed security incidents continue to intensify across Europe

Separately, Dutch authorities are investigating a major outage that…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Russia-attributed security incidents intensify across Europe

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Denmark has summoned Russia’s ambassador after a Russian warship fired two emergency flares at a Danish army’s helicopter in the Baltic Sea in the latest of incidents attributed to Moscow.
The incident took place during what Denmark said was “a routine” monitoring of the frigate.

“Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver,” prime minister Mette Frederiksen said.

blocks.caption: Denmark's prime minister Mette Frederiksen, leader of Denmark's Social Democrats. Photograph: Henning Bagger/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Denmark’s foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the frigate’s behaviour was “completely unacceptable.”
The incident took place amid worsening security situation in Europe.
Separately, Nato fighter jets stationed on the alliance’s eastern flank shot down a drone – believed to be flying from Belarus – over Lithuania last night.
“With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region,” Lithuania’s president Gitanas Nausėda said.
Meanwhile, Poland discovered remains of a suspected Russian drone near its Baltic Sea coast, just a day after a Russian drone hit a train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday.
It’s Tuesday, 15 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

blocks.text: Lithuania briefs EU, Nato allies about drone incident, minister says

Separately, Dutch authorities are investigating a major outage that affected parts of the country’s railway system, suspecting a possible sabotage after objects were placed on tracks.

“Because safety always comes first, signals automatically turn red. As a result, trains must stop or slow down. Level crossings can also malfunction,” it said.
It did not comment on who could be behind the incident.

Former Danish defence minister Troels Lund Poulsen warned that the frigate incident was a further proof of Russia’s “extremely aggressive” behaviour seeking to “provoke potential conflicts.”
“We should be very aware of that,” he said in comments reported by Danish broadcaster DR.
Defence minister Jeppe Bruus called an all-party meeting on the incident this morning to give political leaders a more detailed read on what happened, DR said.

articles.title: Iran and US: Two countries and the pistachio between them
articles.summary: The pistachios sold across the United States have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now, both regions face the same threat — their farmland is sinking as groundwater…

image.caption: Pistachios like these sold across the US trace their roots back to IranImage: Svetlanasf/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hand-width cracks crisscross Armin's pistachio orchard in southeastern Iran, damaging irrigation pipes and swallowing precious water as the ground beneath him sinks.

"You look, and the earth has opened its mouth, and the water just pours in," Armin says. He has seen the cracks spread rapidly over the past five years, and worries that his children may not be able to work the land as his father and grandfather did before him.

Armin, whose real name DW has chosen not to reveal for security reasons, lives in the arid region of Rafsanjan. For generations, farmers there have cultivated the pistachio tree for its small green edible seed used in everything from ice cream to the viral Dubai chocolate.

The region has long covered much of the world's demand for pistachios, but a combination of drought and groundwater extraction for irrigation has made Rafsanjan one of the fastest-sinking areas in Iran. One study found parts of the ground are dropping by up to 37 centimeters (14 inches) annually. And that is impacting production.

It's a similar picture in California, where some pistachio farmers are also seeing their ground sink. Joe Coelho's family has cultivated the crop since 2000, and he says while his farm in Fresno is not directly affected, "growers are very aware of the risk."

Some areas nearby are facing serious water problems, says Coelho, who is the director of sustainability at American Pistachio Growers. "Subsidence is absolutely a serious issue in parts of the San Joaquin Valley."

blocks.caption: A pistachio orchard in California's Central Valley, now the world's largest producing regionImage: Photosoundsplanet/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The same pistachio and the same problems

The link between growers in the two countries goes back to the 1960s when US famers started building a pistachio industry. They did it using an Iranian variety — the pistachio that now dominates most Californian orchards is called Kerman, named after a city near Armin's farm.

California has recently overtaken Iran as the world's largest pistachio producer, with most of the crop grown in the Central Valley, where Coelho has his orchard. And though it is one of the world's most productive farming regions, there are places where the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a year.
Like in Iran, the problem is that more water is being pumped from underground aquifers for crop irrigation than is flowing back in.

"As surface water reliability has declined, growers have relied more heavily on groundwater," Coelho told DW, adding that he has witnessed the land change. "In certain areas, the soil does not have the same structure or water movement it once had."
Pistachio orchards in the Central Valley use around 4% of the valley's crop water. In Rafsanjan, more than nine in 10 liters of groundwater go to pistachio orchards.
As groundwater levels drop from overpumping, spaces within the aquifer collapse, and the earth above begins to sink in a process called land subsidence.

"Land subsidence in Iran is a man-made hazard, not a natural one like an earthquake," says Ali Beitollahi, who leads subsidence research at Iran's Road, Housing and Urban Development Research Center. "Much of the damage cannot be undone. When an aquifer collapses, it can never hold as much water again as before."

Older farmers in Rafsanjan remember reaching water at depths of just 20 meters (66 feet), says Armin. Today, many have to drill down to 300 meters. Some farmlands near Armin's are dead or dying, he says, while other orchards have been abandoned as wells dried up.

It's another blow to the struggling farmers, who says the boom driven by food trends like Dubai chocolate never reaches them because international sanctions and global competition have stripped Iran of the markets it once held as the world's biggest pistachio producer.
"We used to be known for quality," he says. "Now we are known for the low price."

blocks.caption: Ripening pistachios in Wasco, California, where growers, like farmers in Rafsanjan, are pumping more groundwater than flows back in and watching their land sinkImage: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Two pistachio regions, two different responses
The biggest difference between the two regions is how they are responding to the crisis.
In California, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), passed in 2014, requires water agencies to balance pumping and recharge in groundwater basins by 2040.

Managed aquifer recharge is one method the state is using to do so. It entails allowing water to recharge aquifers in rainy years, by flooding farmlands for instance, as a store for drought. Coelho is taking part in a pilot project that does just that.

SGMA has seen some progress. According to California's Department of Water Resources, groundwater levels have risen in four out of 10 monitored wells. But large parts of the Central Valley are still sinking.
Helen Dahlke, professor of integrated hydrologic sciences at the University of California, Davis, says recharge alone is not likely to offset decades of overexploitation of groundwater.

"Agriculture is by far the largest consumptive use of water in the Central Valley, so bringing groundwater basins into balance will likely require aligning crop water demand with the long-term water available under a warmer and more variable climate."

In Iran, awareness of groundwater management and subsidence has grown over the past decade among scientists but remains limited, says Ali Beitollahi. He worked on draft subsidence regulations that are currently awaiting government approval.

Pointing to the example of Japan's capital Tokyo where subsidence rates fell dramatically after authorities restricted groundwater pumping, he believes the problem could be managed if the state were to act quickly. Though given the current political situation in Iran, swift action is unlikely.
Another urgent step, he says, "is changing how farmers water their fields immediately, and teaching them why it matters."
Most of Rafsanjan's orchards are still flood-irrigated, meaning large amounts of water are lost to evaporation before it reaches plant roots.
Armin says he is trying to learn from US growers, but that many older farmers are set in their ways.

blocks.caption: Rows of pistachio trees in California's Central Valley, where in some areas the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a yearImage: Photosoundsplanet/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The meaning of a pistachio
Across California's Central Valley, the pressures of a warming climate, drought and diminishing groundwater are hard to ignore.
"We live with it every day," Coelho says, adding that California's pistachio farmers also need better water policy as well as better infrastructure and protection of water rights.
"Financial sustainability, water sustainability and environmental sustainability are connected," he told DW.

Armin doesn't see a future in pistachio farming. But when he looks at a single pistachio, he sees more than a crop competing for water or a snack on a shelf half a world away. He sees the history and the present of his family and his region.
"This pistachio sometimes comes from a tree 100 years old," he says. "It has paid for a wedding, for a child's education, for someone's happiness. Its money comes, and it creates a life."
How a Swiss farmer reshapes his fields to fight drought
