articles.title: EU seeks Arctic strategy amid growing power rivalry
articles.summary: Russia's aggression, Trump's threats against Greenland and the race for critical raw materials are pushing the Arctic to the top of Europe's agenda.

image.caption: Looking ahead: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders gathered in Finland to discuss the future of the ArcticImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia's war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention.
"There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition."
The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest."
A changing security environment in the High North

The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North.
"We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said.

The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and … uses its presence for hybrid activities every day."
Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials.

blocks.caption: European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as wellImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Confrontation replaces cooperation
"From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland.

For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe.

The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies.
Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities.

"But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW.
The United States as an additional stress factor

The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies.

"Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland, these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation."
Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkilä believes the region is increasingly divided.
"In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW.
He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights.
"Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkilä.
Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis
Climate change is transforming the Arctic

At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova.
Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners.

"Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said.

He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change."
Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience'
At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience.
"We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said.

Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown.

articles.title: Bolsonaro 2.0: Brazil braces for the return of the far right
articles.summary:
With Lula mired in scandal, Flávio Bolsonaro is firing up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing

A giant banner of Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Juiz de Fora

blocks.text: A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.

“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.

With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro supporters float a giant balloon depicting the US president, Donald Trump, holding Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”

“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s president Lula at a reelection campaign rally in Curitiba on Saturday. Photograph: Rodolfo Bührer/Reuters

blocks.text: Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.

A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.

Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.

blocks.caption: Davi Frederico at the airport in Juiz de Fora. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.
But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.

blocks.caption: Street hawkers at Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign event pay tribute to the US connection. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.

“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.

blocks.caption: Supporters gather to greet Flávio Bolsonaro at Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.

“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro addresses supporters at the spot where Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in Juiz de Fora during the 2018 presidential campaign. Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.

Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.

Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.

Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.

blocks.caption: Lennon César: ‘Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.’  Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.

“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”
As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.

César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”
A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

blocks.caption: Graffiti on Flávio Bolsonaro’s headquarters in the city of Juiz de Fora. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

articles.title: Wild dogs record 2,500-mile trek across Africa in search of a mate
articles.summary: Scientists say the record-breaking journey by three brothers offers hope wildlife can survive growing pressures.

blocks.text: A pack of African wild dogs has completed a record-breaking 2,485-mile (4000km) journey across the continent.
Scientists say it is the furthest recorded distance for any African land mammal searching for a mate, offering hope that wildlife can travel across vast distances despite growing human pressures.
The three brothers zigzagged across Zambia, navigating a landscape increasingly shaped by people and avoiding obstacles including major cities.
However, other wild dogs tracked with GPS collars in the study died in illegal snares, underlining the dangers they face.
Three sisters almost completed an equally epic journey, but stopped when one became trapped in a snare.
African wild dogs are among Africa's rarest predators, with only about 6,000 remaining in the wild.
They live in highly social packs, hunt together and are known for their vast roaming in search of new territory and breeding opportunities with other packs.
They cannot breed within the pack they are born into, so they either wait and may eventually inherit their pack, or set off at the age of two or three in search of a mate.
The brothers covered about 260 miles in a straight line over the course of eight months, but travelled nearly 10 times that overall while crossing through a broken-up landscape.

These sorts of journeys are known as dispersals - travelling one way in search of a mate, which is a behaviour distinct from migrations, where animals move back and forth with the seasons in search of food or habitat.
The UN Convention on Migratory Species identifies Africa's longest migrations as wildebeest moving seasonally between Tanzania and Kenya in search of grazing and water covering more than 400 miles.
Globally, caribou undertake the longest single land migrations of any animal - travelling 839 miles in a round trip, while grey wolves have been recorded travelling more than 4,350 miles over a year.
Perhaps even more significant than the distance itself was the route the wild dogs took through Zambia.
They moved between wildlife strongholds, skirting areas containing major human obstacles, including the capital, Lusaka, and heavily developed industrial areas.
The findings suggest wild dog populations across eastern and southern Africa may remain more connected than conservationists previously believed.
Professor Scott Creel of Montana State University, the paper's lead author, who has been studying African wild dogs since 1991, said the study provides cautious optimism.
"It's plausible to believe that every major wild dog population in eastern and southern Africa, other than fenced ones, are potentially connected," he said.
But he said, in conservation,"the glass is half empty and the glass is half full", highlighting the threat of poaching snares.
While the three male wild dogs successfully completed their extraordinary journey, two of the three females died.
Researchers identified a pattern in which surviving pack members repeatedly returned to the same location, a behaviour that often signals the death of a companion.

The research, published in the journal, Ecology, external, adds weight to calls to create strips of natural land outside protected areas that connect separate wildlife areas broken apart by roads, towns, or farms.

Bruce Ellender, one of the paper's co-authors and Kafue Conservation director for the environmental charity, The Nature Conservancy, said species that roam over large areas, such as wild dogs and elephants, need connected landscapes if they are to survive into the future.
"We can't see these protected areas as islands and expect them to be functional in the long term, we need to think much broader than that," he said.

articles.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
articles.summary:
St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans

Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately…
articles.byline: Written by Morgan Ofori and David Conn; Animation by Alexander Purcell; Photography by Wayne Crichlow

blocks.text: Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.

The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.

The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.

It reveals how wealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.
The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.

Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.

blocks.caption: The grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

Ornate boards adorn the walls of the Great Hall in St Barts, where governors recorded their philanthropic donations, many while investing in the companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
The church of St Bartholomew the Less, in the grounds of St Barts hospital.  Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
A portrait of King Henry VIII in the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, surrounded by the boards commemorating the hospital’s benefactors. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

blocks.text: Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.

Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.
The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

blocks.caption: A diagram of a ship showing the cramped conditions in which enslaved Africans were trafficked. Composite: Guardian

blocks.text: The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.

Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.

Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.

These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.
His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.
After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.

blocks.caption: Several leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans formalised to become a lucrative source of funds for merchants. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

The Great Hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message. Its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – are tied to themes of healthcare. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
The stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored last year and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

blocks.text: The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.

He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.

Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.

Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.

St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.

A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.

“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”

A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

articles.title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO
articles.summary:
Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two thirds

The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn…
articles.byline: Eromo Egbejule in Abidjan and agencies

blocks.text: The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.
If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.

Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.

The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).
That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.

Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”

Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.

His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.

The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran. The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrel on Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.
after newsletter promotion

Dangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.

“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”
After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.

articles.title: Indonesian police investigate deaths of Australian man and two children in Bali as suspected murder-suicide
articles.summary:
Police in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own life

Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of…

blocks.text: Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life.
The man, 57 and his two children, aged seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning.

According to Denpasar Police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at around 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach.
Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar Police said in its statement.

The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located.
“Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read.
“From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.”
The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Denpasar Central General hospital for further examination and handling.
Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta Police officers were investigating the incident.

“Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said.
Simatupang said Kuta Police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate.
after newsletter promotion
A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians.
“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement.

articles.title: Carney to speak at investment summit as Liberals discuss airport privatization

blocks.text: Carney to speak at Canada Investment Summit
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to speak Tuesday at a Toronto investment summit aimed at pitching Canada to business leaders and money managers from around the world.
The Latest

items: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to deliver remarks and hold a news conference at his government investment summit in Toronto today.
Hundreds of executives and global asset managers are attending the summit, as Carney looks to attract $1 trillion in new investment to Canada over the next five years.
A special Liberal Party caucus meeting was held last night to discuss private investment in major city airports.
Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. have announced a new $50 billion fund for large-scale investments in Canada.
More than 1,000 demonstrators gathered in downtown Toronto yesterday to protest against the summit, arguing Canada's economic future should not be put in the hands of CEOs.

blocks.text: Pinned
167 projects on the table at investment summit
Carney's $1 trillion investment summit draws powerbrokers, protesters

Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted a slew of global investors at the Canadian Investment Summit in Toronto, where he hopes to raise $1 trillion in capital. The event also drew hundreds of protesters concerned about giving CEOs more control over Canadian resources.
Canada's investment summit is entering its second day today. The summit comes as a new suite of 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump kicked in, amid the Canada-U.S. trade war.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is seeking to turn high-level meetings with global investors into major deals that could make Canada less dependent on trade with the U.S.

The government has set a goal of attracting $1 trillion in new investment to Canada. But landing major deals could depend on whether Canada can address some of the concerns that have deterred investors in the past — including lengthy approval processes and uncertainty around getting major projects built.

Some 167 projects, ranging from a proposed pipeline carrying oil from Alberta to B.C.'s coast to developing satellite technology for Earth observation, are among the investment opportunities on the table, according to a 66-page prospectus obtained by CBC News.
Follow along here for the latest announcements and developments.
-With files from Abby Hughes

articles.title: AI-linked stocks fall after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development
articles.summary: Shares in tech firms tumble across Asia with Nasdaq also likely to dip later after Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX leaders back call

blocks.text: AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.

Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer of OpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chip makers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.

In Taipei, shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%. Futures for the Nasdaq pointed to a 1.3% drop in the tech-heavy index when the US stock market opens this afternoon.
The sell-off comes after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”.
He said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.

Amodei’s claims have been disputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.
The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support for Amodei’s essay on slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.
Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.

Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world has laws sufficient to contain them.

However, Donald Trump rejected the calls to pace AI development. The US president told reporters over the weekend: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.

“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.”
after newsletter promotion

“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.

“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”
Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.

The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year.
OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 due to safety concerns with the technology.

articles.title: Questions mount over what an AI 'slowdown' would look like
articles.summary: While pacing AI development might sound like a quick fix, it is far from an easy solution.

blocks.text: There has been no shortage of warnings from AI's top bosses about existential threats over the years.
I attended the world's first AI safety summit in Bletchley Park in November 2023 where the focus was on the most serious threats imaginable, posed by the most powerful AI models.

At the time, many thought this was in the realm of sci-fi and the real threats were comparatively far more mundane: job losses, cheating in exams. Three years later, many of those same voices don't seem to be so sure.

On Saturday head of AI company Anthropic, Dario Amodei, urged the pace of development to be slowed down - the bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk said they agreed with him.
Meanwhile AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic - told the BBC on Sunday staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.
They all add up to a chorus of serious voices urging a slowdown, but although it might sound like a quick fix, it is far from an easy solution.
America is widely understood to be terrified of losing the race to build the most powerful AI to China.
On Sunday President Trump made his own views clear, claiming the US was ahead of China in the AI race and declaring: "Whoever wins AI, wins."

China isn't renowned for wanting to come second. Everyone I speak to says that even if their company pauses, others will not and they will just get left behind. It reminds me of the height of the campaign for nuclear disarmament. The problem then too was that nobody wanted to go first.

There is also the question of how on earth a slowdown would be enforced. Who would police it? Would we be relying on the AI companies to be transparent about what they are doing, and more importantly what they are choosing not to do? That would require an epic level of trust, which arguably the tech sector has never earned.

Although Amodei in his post proposed a three-point plan that included independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation, some observers question how this would work in practice.
"Nobody has given a substantive explanation of what 'slowdown' means," said Ed Zitron, CEO of EZ Primary Research.
"Putting a plant from METR, where one of the guys who quit Anthropic went, in every AI company? Democratic and global 'co-ordination'? Doesn't mean anything to me."
Zitron said stopping training AI models would leave them vulnerable to Chinese rivals.
"Their margins might improve but their products will be captured in amber and distilled by Chinese labs. They may have to change pricing. I truly don't know how it all works.
"This could burst the bubble. But right now we are very thin on what a 'slowdown' means."

In the UK, we have heard about plans to roll out the tech more widely within the NHS to improve patient care, and how AI gave the UK economy a much-needed boost over the summer. We are all being encouraged to use it more and more at work, in education and in our personal lives.
The industry is a key part of the UK's strategy to drive economic growth. "There is no plan B" a former government adviser told me, so could a slowdown wreck future prospects here in Britain?

The AI industry is burning through enormous amounts of money and natural resources and so far, is not creating nearly as much revenue. There are multiple reports suggesting a number of firms adopting the technology are disappointed by it.

Economists widely speculate that even the current giants are not all likely to survive and that some kind of "levelling" is coming – also known as a bursting bubble. But those firms which do make it could end up becoming the most powerful mega-corporations the world has ever seen, and that comes with its own issues.

OpenAI choosing to halt its march to the stock market could be seen as an epiphany-like moment of taking responsibility for public safety – but it could also be the move of a company which has realised it might not get the lucrative payout it needs while its entire product is perceived to be lethal.

"One of the probably the biggest challenges that we have right now is that no one can predict with certainty how this technology is going to evolve," says Alexander Voicu from the UK AI company Synthesia.

"We know that these systems are getting more powerful, but we don't know where and how they're going to be used, and we haven't figured out essentially a way of taking full advantage of their potential. My only concern in rushing to regulate now, where there's still a lot of open questions, is that it could actually backfire."
We also can't deny the fact that underpinning this entire tech revolution is an ocean of investor cash.
"I'm not worried about the existential risks of AI, I'm worried about the corporate greed of the companies that are creating it," says Sasha Luccioni, the founder of Sustainable AI.
Leading computer scientist Professor dame Wendy Hall, who has advised the UN about AI, says the current crisis is all about the companies not behaving responsibly enough.
She likens the current situation to a farmer having a bull in a field which escapes and causes destruction – and the farmer blames the bull.
"Of course it's not the bull's fault – it's the farmer," she says. Clearly, the fences weren't robust enough, and that is exactly what she says we are seeing with AI guardrails right now.
But if those guardrails become too restrictive, could this spell the end of AI?

Some believe there is a more secretive, politically-motivated push for a rules-based clampdown in order to "regulate AI into oblivion" as Parker Thayer, an investigative researcher at the Conservative-leaning Capital Research Centre think-tank, put it on X this week.
His post was viewed nearly eight million times. It is an extreme and unproven view but it shows that not everybody is on board with the idea of regulation saving the day.
Whatever the reality, the storm currently engulfing the AI industry could already have caused reputational damage to the firms currently in pole position forever.
As Professor Hall puts it: "Would you invest in a company that says it's going to bring about human extinction?"

articles.title: Indonesian rescue crews searching for 140 people after ferry hit bad weather
articles.summary:
More than 100 others on board were evacuated from the Virgo ⁠Transport 8 ship, including one who died

Indonesian rescuers were searching on Sunday for 140 people from a ⁠passenger ship that…

blocks.text: Indonesian rescuers were searching on Sunday for 140 people from a ⁠passenger ship that was earlier reported missing in the Java Sea ​after 103 others were evacuated, ‌one of whom ‌died, a search and rescue agency official said.
A passenger ship carrying more than 240 people was reported missing after losing contact during bad weather in the Java Sea early on Sunday, the country’s ⁠search and rescue agency said.
The Virgo ⁠Transport 8 ship set sail ​on Saturday from ‌the East Java ‌city of Surabaya to the South ‌Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin before losing contact.
I Putu Sudayana, the head of the agency’s Banjarmasin office, ​said in a video statement that 103 people had been evacuated using different ships and some of them would be taken to an East Java port.
Rescuers launched a search, deploying a ⁠team, ships and a helicopter toward the passenger vessel’s last ​known position, ​he said, without stating what happened ​to the ship.

The search and rescue office in the city of Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan, which is located on Borneo island, said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 at about 2am on Sunday.

“The ship’s operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather,” Sudayana, who heads the search and rescue office, said in a video briefing.
Indonesia, an archipelago of 17,000 islands, relies ⁠heavily on ferries as a key mode ​of ​transportation, with sea ​routes more affordable and readily ​available than ‌air travel.
However, ​safety ​standards are not always rigorously enforced, resulting in a relatively high accident rate.
This is a developing story

articles.title: One dead and more than 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast in rough seas
articles.summary:
Prime minister’s office tells families of those missing ‘the nation stands with you’ as search and rescue efforts continue

One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank…

blocks.text: One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the country’s government says.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail with more than 40 passengers and crew on Friday from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones,” Vanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office said in a statement on Sunday.
“Search and rescue operations are continuing.”
Fifteen of those onboard have been “accounted for alive” and one body has been recovered, the statement said.
“Over 30 people remain missing at sea,” it said.
“To the survivors, we ⁠pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of ​those ​missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands ​with you ‌in this time ​of ​grief.”
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in New Caledonia said it was assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
Matai Seremaiah, the member of parliament for Luganville who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the south-east coast where currents may have carried survivors.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion
articles.summary: Officials say more than 300 Russians remain missing after the 2024 Kursk offensive, but no-one really knows the true figure.

blocks.text: "The state channels were convincing viewers that 'everything is under control: two or three days, and it'll be just as it was before'," she recalls.

She still fails to understand why Russian authorities could not stop Ukrainian soldiers storming two border checkpoints in August 2024, taking around 40 prisoners and bombing a convoy carrying Russian soldiers.
Within six days they had overrun more than 777 sq km (300 sq miles) of Russian territory, as Ukraine's military sought to divert Russian forces away from their front-line offensive.
For most of the next eight months, mobile and internet links were down.
Russia's foreign ministry repeatedly accused Ukraine of war crimes against civilians: allegations rejected in Kyiv as completely unfounded.

Nearly 200 Russians sent a letter to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the United Nations, asking them to organise a humanitarian corridor to evacuate civilians.
It never happened and, by late autumn, battles raged as Russian forces sought to retake the territory.
Lyubov and others who had lost contact with their loved ones began to form groups.

One resident, whose family friends had also stayed behind, began compiling a list of people she saw on videos published by the Ukrainian military and journalists. Then she began detailing those believed to have died and where they were buried.
"At first, in a panic, you try to do something – anything – to find some sort of information," she said. "Taking action brings a certain sense of relief, and that's how you can cope with the stress."
Soon about 1,000 names were on the list.
Lyubov wrote to the Red Cross and Kursk interior ministry appealing for help, but had no response.

Early in 2025, Russia's human rights commissioner published a list of 517 Kursk residents reported missing. The list mixed up names of the missing with those who were searching for them, and the families said it was like a "slap in the face".
"Publishing something like this is the height of incompetence and a lack of basic respect for people," said one young woman whose parents had gone missing, in a video shared online.
Heavy fighting had been reported in late 2024 in the village of Darino, where Lyubov and mother were from, and authorities said that 90% of it had been destroyed.
The Russian military regained control of the village and then began evacuating those who had survived, and the bodies of those who had not.

One of the evacuees got in touch with Lyubov, telling her she had lived with her mother for the past few weeks. Her mum had passed away, she explained, following a head injury in circumstances that remain unclear.
A few other elderly people had also died, she said, unable to cope with wartime conditions.
Lyubov waited in vain for her mother's body to be brought out, while other families had no idea if their relatives were alive or dead.
People complained no-one was searching for their loved ones and that there was no single list of those missing.
Lyubov heard that the bodies of neighbours who died alongside her mother had been taken away from Darino in April, but her mother's body was still missing.
She tried and failed to get an answer from the authorities: "They wouldn't listen, and everyone just kept saying that it was dangerous there, and no-one was going to deal with it right now."
The head of one local village council, Yuri Tkachev, was among volunteers who went to retrieve the bodies of civilians, from the streets or from nearby fields.
"It's hard for people to know – or rather not to know – what has happened to their loved ones, whether they're being held captive or have died, and where they died," he said.
Body bags and fuel for vans taking part in the evacuations were paid for either by the volunteers themselves or with donations, but not by authorities.
Although regional officials met the group searching for the missing several times in the second half of 2025, relatives complained it made little difference.
Lyubov was still searching for her mother's body, until she visited the mortuary last October during a trip to the regional capital Kursk.
"I just asked: 'A woman born in 1949 from the village of Darino – are there any unidentified bodies?'"
The official turned his laptop screen towards her and immediately she recognised her deceased mother in a photograph from April 2025.
She was lying on her side in the street, her knees bent. Lyubov tried not to look too closely. She recognised her mum's face and an old jumper, which she wore while she worked.
She had provided a DNA sample in January but was told it had been lost, so her mother's body had been in the mortuary unidentified for several months.
She had wanted to bury her mother in their home village, but for now that is impossible, so she has been cremated and her ashes sit in Lyubov's apartment in Belgorod, about 100 miles away.
She is bitter that the government failed to stop the incursion, that it did not evacuate residents when it could, and that it persuaded them the situation was not serious.
Asked by the BBC to comment on this story, there was no response from the Kursk governor, Russia's human rights commissioner or the Russian Red Cross.
The command of Ukraine's Territorial Defence Forces and Ukraine's human rights commissioner of Ukraine said all the civilians they had evacuated from Kursk region had been handed over to Russia.
Lyubov thinks back to when she used to ride her bike across the border into Ukraine to shop for sausages, yarn and ice cream.
"We went to see them, and they came to see us. And now not one of these villages exists any more."

articles.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
articles.summary:
Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma

Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest…

blocks.text: Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.

Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.
Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.

blocks.caption: King Oyo of the Toro kingdom was for a long time the world’s youngest monarch. Photograph: Sipa/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.
Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.
At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.
“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.

Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.
The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.
A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.

But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.

blocks.caption: UBC news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma. Photograph: UBC Uganda

blocks.text: Supporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.

A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.
The archbishop of the ⁠Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.
“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he ​told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy ​of the king we are mourning.“
Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.

In ​addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning ‌against HIV and Aids, ​Oyo cultivated close ties with former ​Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.
The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a lower profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.
Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.
